articles.title: A member of one body

claims.t: I share one mind with all who reason, and with it the reason that commands what to do or leave undone. If law too is common, we are citizens, and the universe is, as it were, a city.
claims.shared: Pilot wording kept. The shared mind has three witnesses. The commanding reason, the conditional step and the city come from 4.4 alone, so the “if” and the “as it were” are retained. The sun image of 12.23 goes to the margin because that passage treats light as truly divided and mind as only seeming so.

support.quote: The relation that the limbs of the body have in things that are united is the relation that rational beings have in things that stand apart
support.follows: Rational beings, who stand apart, have the same relation to one another that the limbs of one body have.
support.note: Rational beings, who stand apart, have the same relation to one another that the limbs of one body have.

support.quote: we are citizens. If that is so, we share in some civic body. If that is so, the universe is, as it were, a city.
support.follows: We are citizens, we share in a civic body, and the universe is like a city.
gives: we are citizens, and the universe is, as it were, a city

support.quote: you yourself help to complete a civic whole
support.follows: I am one of those who make a civic whole complete.
support.note: I am one of those who make a civic whole complete.

support.quote: One light of the sun, even if it is divided by walls, by mountains
support.follows: The light of the sun is one, even where walls and mountains divide it.
support.note: The light of the sun is one, even where walls and mountains divide it.

support.quote: One soul that has mind, even if it seems to be separated.
support.follows: There is one soul that has mind, even though it seems to be separated.

support.follows: The beings that reason share one soul, the soul that has mind.
gives: I share one mind with all who reason

support.quote: If mind is common to us, then reason too, by which we are rational, is common.
support.follows: Marcus begins with shared mind and shared reason.
gives: I share one mind with all who reason

support.quote: If that is so, law too is common.
support.follows: Shared reason directs conduct, and Marcus draws common law from it.

claims.t: We are made for one another and for one common work, and that shared life is our own good.
claims.shared: Pilot wording restored verbatim. “Made for one another” joins 5.15 with the pull of mind towards its kin in 9.7. The common work is from 7.10 alone. 7.10f supports “our own” only by implication, since it describes a person who does not yet do good as doing good to themselves.

support.quote: being built to do a single task together
support.follows: Rational beings are built to do one work together.
gives: one common work

support.quote: everything that shares in a common nature of mind hurries towards its kin in the same way, or even more
support.follows: Whatever shares in the common nature of mind hurries towards its own kin.
gives: We are made for one another

support.quote: therefore the good of a rational animal is community
support.follows: Living with others is what is good for a reasoning being.
gives: that shared life is our own good

support.quote: For it has long since been shown that we were born for community.
support.follows: It has long been shown that we were born for community.
gives: We are made for one another

support.quote: the worse things are for the sake of the better, and the better for the sake of one another? And things with a soul are better than things without one, and rational things better than things with a soul.
support.follows: The better things are for the sake of one another, and rational things rank above everything else that has a soul.

support.quote: doing good does not yet delight you fully; you still do it as no more than the proper thing, not yet as doing good to yourself
support.follows: Doing good is also doing good to myself; while I do it only as the proper thing, I have not yet grasped that.

claims.t: Each thing I do should aim at the common good, directly or at a distance, and holding to that one aim is what makes me one person.
claims.shared: Pilot wording kept without the opening “So”, which has nothing to refer to when the line stands alone. The allowance for a remote aim is from 9.21 only. “Common good” renders the social goal of 9.21 and the social and civic aim of 11.19.

support.quote: so too let every action of yours help to complete a civic life
support.follows: Every action of mine should help to complete a civic life.
gives: Each thing I do should aim at the common good

support.quote: any action of yours that does not look, whether directly or at a distance, to the social goal tears your life apart and does not let it be one
support.follows: An action with no reference to the social goal, not even a distant one, tears my life apart and keeps it from being one.
gives: directly or at a distance
holding to that one aim is what makes me one person

support.quote: so too the aim to be set up must be the social and civic one

support.quote: whoever directs all their private impulses towards this aim will make all their actions alike, and in this way will always be the same

claims.t: When I turn away from a neighbour in hatred, I cut myself off from our community. When I act against others or refuse to accept what has happened, I set myself against the natural order I belong to.
claims.shared: Pilot wording restored verbatim at the owner’s direction. The common act of cutting myself off is anchored in 11.7 and 8.32. Only 8.32 counts unsocial action and not wanting what happens as a break with the union that accords with nature. “Refuse to accept” means not wanting the event, not denying it. The severed hand and the hedge “as far as it is in their power” are kept in the margin.

support.quote: it is the human being who separates themselves from their neighbour, by coming to hate and turning away
support.follows: A person separates themselves from a neighbour by coming to hate and turning away.
gives: When I turn away from a neighbour in hatred

gives: I cut myself off

support.quote: If you have ever seen a hand cut off, or a foot, or a severed head, lying somewhere or other apart from the rest of the body: that is what a person makes of themselves, as far as it is in their power, when they do not want what happens
support.follows: A person who does not want what happens makes of themselves, as far as they can, something like a hand or foot cut off from the body.
gives: refuse to accept what has happened

support.quote: or when they do something unsocial
support.follows: A person who does something unsocial also makes of themselves something like a severed limb.
gives: act against others

support.quote: he put it in the human being’s power not to be broken off from the whole in the first place
support.follows: It is in a person’s own power not to be broken off from the whole.
support.note: It is in a person’s own power not to be broken off from the whole.

support.quote: like the person in a citizen body who, for their own part, stands apart from such harmony
support.follows: An action that does not refer to the social goal is seditious, like a citizen who, for their own part, stands apart from the harmony of the citizen body.
gives: from our community

support.quote: You lie somewhere or other, thrown away from the union that accords with nature; for you were by nature a part, but now you have cut yourself off.
support.follows: One who does not want what happens, or acts unsocially, was by nature a part and has cut themselves off from the union.

claims.t: Even after I have cut myself off, god has granted me the power to grow together again and take up my part in the whole.
claims.shared: Pilot wording restored verbatim. It states a permission, not a duty. 8.32 names god and 11.7 names Zeus. The detail that no other part is granted this return is from 8.32 alone and goes to the margin. The difficulty of repeated return is left to 11.7f.

support.quote: we are allowed to grow together again with the one next to us and again to help to complete the whole
support.follows: We are allowed to grow together again with the person next to us, and again to help make the whole complete.
gives: god has granted me the power to grow together again
take up my part in the whole

support.quote: for one who has been broken off, he made it possible to come back again and grow together and take up again the place of a part
support.follows: A person who has been broken off has been given the power to come back and grow together again.
gives: Even after I have cut myself off
god has granted me the power to grow together again
take up my part in the whole

support.quote: though they run away, they are overtaken and hemmed in all the same; for nature prevails
support.follows: Those who run away are overtaken all the same, because nature prevails.
support.note: Those who run away are overtaken all the same, because nature prevails.

support.quote: when this kind of division happens many times, it makes what withdraws hard to unite and hard to restore
support.follows: Each further separation makes a return harder.
support.note: Each further separation makes a return harder.

support.quote: To no other part has god granted this, to come together again once it has been separated and cut through.
support.follows: God has granted the human part the power to come together again after being cut off.
support.note: God has granted the human part the power to come together again after being cut off.

support.quote: Yet there is this gift from Zeus, who put the community together
support.follows: The permission to grow together again is a gift from Zeus.

single.label: A practice
single.t: I often say to myself: “I am a limb of the whole made up of reasoning beings.”
single.quote: you often say to yourself: “I am a limb [melos] of the whole made up of rational beings.”
single.why: Single source 7.10, resting on its own quote. Narrowed to the saying itself. The contrast with “a part” lies outside the supplied quote and depends on a Greek pun, so it goes to the margin. “I shall” was dropped because the source recommends a habit and does not make a vow.
single.follows: I should often tell myself that I am a limb of the whole that rational beings make up.

single.label: A warning
single.t: If I cut myself off many times, I become hard to unite and hard to restore.
single.quote: when this kind of division happens many times, it makes what withdraws hard to unite and hard to restore
single.why: Single source 11.7, resting on its own quote. This is a warning and is kept as one. The source says “many times” and “hard”, so the sliding scale of “the more often, the harder” was not warranted.
single.follows: When this division happens many times, what withdraws becomes hard to unite and hard to restore.

single.label: The regrafted branch
single.t: A branch that has grown with the tree from the beginning and stayed, sharing one breath, is not like one cut off and grafted in again, whatever the gardeners say.
single.quote: the branch that sprouted together from the beginning and has stayed together, sharing one breath, is not like the one grafted in again after being cut off, whatever it is that the gardeners say
single.follows: The branch that has stayed with the plant from the start is not like the branch grafted back in after being cut off, and Marcus says so against the gardeners.
single.why: Single source 11.7, resting on its own quote. Pilot wording restored verbatim, with the image in the third person as the speaker framed it. It qualifies the unreserved praise of return in 8.32.

single.label: Dyeing the soul
single.t: My soul is dyed by its impressions, so I choose the dye and keep the run of those impressions unbroken.
single.quote: the soul is dyed by its impressions. So dye it with an unbroken run of impressions such as these
single.follows: Repeated impressions colour the soul, so Marcus urges the reader to choose the impressions they repeat.
single.why: Single source 5.15, resting on its own quote. Narrowed because the supplied quote names no example. “Born for community” already stands in c2, and the frequency clause lies outside the quote.

single.label: Flight that fails
single.t: Only beings with mind have now forgotten their hurrying towards one another. Yet though they run away, they are overtaken and hemmed in all the same, for nature prevails.
single.quote: only the beings that have mind have now forgotten their hurrying towards one another and their leaning together, and only here is the flowing together not to be seen. And yet, though they run away, they are overtaken and hemmed in all the same; for nature prevails.
single.follows: Rational beings alone have forgotten their tendency towards one another, yet even in running away they are overtaken and hemmed in, because nature prevails.
single.why: Single source 9.7, resting on its own quote. “Now” is kept because the forgetting describes present behaviour, not nature. The earthy comparison lies outside the supplied quote and goes to the margin.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. In modern editions 9.7 is 9.8 and 9.9, 5.15 is 5.16, 8.32 is 8.34, 7.10 is 7.13, 9.21 is 9.23, 12.23 is 12.30, 11.19 is 11.21, 8.52 is 8.54 and 11.7 is the first part of 11.8; 4.4 is the same.

Pilot wording kept. The limb relation of 7.10 meets the civic body of 4.4 and 9.21, and “made for” joins born for community in 5.15 with built for a single task in 7.10. The contrast of limb with mere part stays with 7.10 alone.
articles.limit: The passages do not name a single whole. 4.4 and 8.32 speak of the universe or the union that accords with nature, 7.10 of rational beings, and 9.21, 11.7 and 11.19 of the civic community. The opening joins them only at the level of belonging. Every step of 4.4 is conditional and its city is a likeness. Only 8.32 treats not wanting what happens as severance, and it hedges with “as far as it is in their power”. In c4, “refuse to accept what has happened” means not wanting the event, not denying that it occurred. 8.32 praises return without reserve and grants it to no other part, while 11.7 warns that repeated division makes it hard and that the graft is not like the branch that stayed. The single-source lines 7.10c, 5.15d and 9.7d are narrowed to their supplied quotes, with the limb and part contrast, the frequency of impressions and the earthy comparison held in the margin. No political programme, loss of individuality or abolition of private impulses is stated or implied.

aside.8.52: A wish to think together with the mind that surrounds all things, as we breathe together with the air around us. Close to claim 1, but a wish and not a statement.

articles.title: The work that belongs to me

claims.t: Being social comes first in my make-up. I hold goodwill towards my own kind and aim only at social acts. I must do good to people and bear with them.
claims.shared: “This comes first” lacked a referent when read alone. The first place is a single-source detail from 7.30. The duty to do good and bear with people is from 5.17 alone and keeps its “must”.

support.quote: So what comes first in the human make-up is being social.

support.quote: what is proper to a human being is goodwill towards their own kind

claims.t: I do not give way to what my body undergoes. My mind is to hold first place and not be overpowered by the senses, because it is by nature fitted to make use of them. The virtue in my make-up that rises up against pleasure is self-control.
claims.shared: Text unchanged. First place and the mind’s use of the senses are from 7.30 alone. Joint support from 7.30 and 8.25 covers only not being overpowered by the senses. Self-control is from 8.37 alone, and its unstated moral about pleasure is not added.

claims.t: I take care not to be hasty and not to be deceived. I assent to nothing false and nothing unclear, and I tell the persuasive impressions apart. What is just will not be kept if I am easily deceived, hasty and changeable.
claims.shared: Text unchanged. Haste and deception are named in both 7.30 and 11.9. Assent is from 8.6 alone and impressions from 8.25 alone. The link to justice is from 11.9 alone and stays a warning, not a vow. The same sentence’s clause about caring for the things in between is omitted.

claims.t: My joy is to do what is proper to a human being, and my nature is content with itself when its road goes well. For a rational animal, the same action is in accordance with nature and with reason. So long as I am doing a human being’s work, pain is not against nature for me as a human being, and so pain is not bad for me.

single.label: Only in one list
single.t: It is proper to me, as a human being, to contemplate the nature of the whole.
single.quote: contemplating the nature of the whole

single.label: A direction
single.t: Let my ruling part hold to being social, to not giving way to the body, and to not being hasty or deceived. Let it carry its straight road through.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. In modern editions 7.30 is 7.55, 8.25 is 8.26 and 8.27, 8.6 is 8.7, 5.17 is 5.20, 8.37 is 8.39, 11.9 is 11.10, 6.31 is 6.33 and 6.34, 7.8 is 7.11, 9.14 is 9.16 and 8.33 is 8.35; 5.14 is 5.14 and 5.15, and 4.1 is the same. Of the passages set aside, 11.18 is 11.20 and 7.42 is 7.72; 9.1 is the same.

First-person opening of 133 characters. “I am social” is replaced by the act the sources name: goodwill towards one’s own kind in 8.25 and impulses directed to social acts in 8.6, which is what 7.30 calls being social. “Common good” is not used because no cited quote says it. The senses clause now names the mind as the thing not to be overpowered, following 7.30 and 8.25. No ranking is asserted, because only 7.30 ranks.
articles.limit: The sources’ lists do not match: 7.30 ranks three works with the social first, while 8.6 and 8.25 each give four unranked. The article therefore fuses only the three shared works and marks the first place as 7.30’s alone. In the opening, “goodwill towards other people” renders the sources’ being social, goodwill towards one’s own kind and impulses directed to social acts. It does not mean enjoying company, and the sources cited for it do not use the phrase “common good”. Contemplation and welcoming what is allotted stay as separate single-source lines, and welcoming is one of four conditions in 8.6, not a sufficient one. The claim about pain holds only for a human being as a human being, and only while that person is doing a human being’s work. It does not say that pain is good or unreal. The opening and c2 name the senses alone, although 7.30 also names impulse, and the mind is to make use of the senses, not suppress them. Turning obstacles into material is a power over impulse and disposition, and the outward activity may still be hindered. People count as indifferent only as obstacles, and the duty to do good to them and bear with them remains. Our first-person wording is editorial interpretation of third-person and second-person texts.

aside.11.18: The elements keep their place; the mind that resents does not. An argument for submission, nearer to Article 3.
aside.9.1: A long passage that calls injustice, lying and pleasure-seeking impious. It argues for the same three works from piety, a ground the article does not use.
aside.7.42: What the rational and civic power finds to be neither of mind nor social, it judges inferior to itself. A test for objects, not a description of the work.

statement.t: I do a human being’s work when I act with goodwill towards other people, do not let my senses overpower my mind, and judge with care.

statement.kind: Three lists aligned into one

claims.role: It comes from one chain of causes
claims.t: All things are interwoven. What happens to me was spun together out of the oldest causes, and the same spinning made me. Even chance is not without that weaving.

Joint support is the spinning from the oldest causes, shared by 5.8 and 10.5. That the same spinning produced my existence is from 10.5 alone. The line on chance is from 1.17 alone, where the weaving is of things that providence governs.

support.quote: Whatever happens to you was being made ready for you beforehand, from all time, and the interweaving of causes was spinning together, from eternity, both your existence and the happening of this.

claims.t: If the world is random, I do not act at random myself. If the world is a jumble with nothing ruling it, I am glad that in such a rough sea I have within me a mind that rules. single.label: A warning
single.t: The complete whole is maimed if its connection is cut at any point. I cut it, as far as it lies with me, whenever I am discontented, and in a way I destroy it.
single.quote: the complete whole is maimed if you cut through the connection and continuity at any point at all: of its parts, and so too of its causes. And you do cut through it, as far as it lies with you, whenever you are discontented, and in a way you destroy it.

single.follows: Each time I am discontented I cut through the connection of the whole, as far as it lies with me, and in a way I destroy it.

decisions: Presents the section as one argument by cases. Marcus gives the cases in four passages and never sets out the whole argument in one place.

Acceptance is the widest common ground. Welcome and love are left to c3 because not every passage asks for them. “Find fault” is the wording of 9.38, where it sits in one arm of a disjunction, and 5.8 supports it through its warning about discontent.
articles.limit: The article joins two strands that the sources keep apart: confident statements that events are ordered for the good of the whole (5.8, 1.17, 7.6), and open disjunctions between providence, fate and atoms (9.26, 9.38, 12.11, 6.39). The opening commits only to acceptance and not finding fault. Welcome and holding dear rest on some passages only. The goodness claimed is first for the whole and is hedged in the sources. The rule that a part must not find fault comes from one branch of 9.38’s disjunction. In c4 the joint support from 9.26 is recurrence only. In c1 the opening sentence rests on 7.6 alone. c5 speaks only to the random branch and stays conditional throughout. The first-person wording is editorial: the sources mostly use second-person address or third-person description.

aside.7.22: A list of reminders about convention, death, pain and fame. Too many subjects to fuse with anything here.
aside.3.12: Questions to ask of any impression, tracing each thing to god, to the shared lot and chance, or to a kinsman. An exercise in examining impressions, nearer to judgment than to accepting what happens.
aside.4.8: What happens, happens justly. A stronger claim than claim 2, and only this passage makes it.

articles.title: The reason that governs the whole

claims.t: I think of the world as one living thing, with one substance and one soul. It is an order and not a stirred brew jumbled together. All things in it are spun together and wound together, and though spread out they feel with one another.
claims.shared: Wording unchanged. Only the oneness of the world is joint (4.33 and 6.23). “Living”, the one substance and the one soul are 4.33 alone. Only 4.22 decides for order. 6.8a merely names that option, so it is not used as proof.

support.follows: The world is one living thing with one soul.
gives: the world as one
living thing
with one substance and one soul

support.quote: all the things that come about, exist at once within the one and entire thing, the very thing we call the universe
support.follows: All the things that happen exist at once inside one whole thing, the thing we call the universe.
gives: the world as one

support.quote: or unity and order and providence
support.follows: Of the two possibilities for the world, the second is unity, order and providence.
support.note: Of the two possibilities for the world, the second is unity, order and providence.

claims.t: Reason governs the whole and has in itself no cause for doing anything bad. The mind of the whole is social. All things come about in accordance with that reason: they set out from it or they come as a consequence. Every kind of harm, like a thorn, like mud, is a by-product of revered and beautiful things.
claims.shared: Wording unchanged. The joint phrase is coming as a consequence (6.33 and 7.44). “In accordance with” is 6.1 alone, and setting out from the source is 6.33 alone, where the source is called the common ruling part. “Social” is 5.24 alone and describes the cosmos, not a human duty. Harm is still called harm and is a by-product, not something good or directly aimed at.

support.quote: the reason that governs it has in itself no cause for doing anything bad
support.follows: The reason that governs the world has no motive to do evil.
gives: Reason governs the whole and has in itself no cause for doing anything bad

support.quote: The mind of the whole is social.
support.follows: The whole has a mind, and that mind is social.
gives: The mind of the whole is social

support.quote: And all things come about and are carried through in accordance with it.
support.follows: Everything comes about and is carried through in accordance with the reason that governs.
gives: All things come about in accordance with that reason

support.quote: All things come from there: they have set out from that common ruling part, or they come as a consequence.

support.quote: The nature of the whole set out by impulse to make the universe. But now either everything that comes about comes about as a consequence

claims.t: What governs my life is akin to what is supreme in the whole. It uses everything else in me. The ruling part wakes itself and turns itself. What I find in myself I can expect in the whole. I consider how many things of body and soul come about in me at the same instant, and then the whole does not surprise me. I ask whether a kind of order can exist in me and disorder in the All.

The 6.7 saying stays in the third person because that passage does not say whose ruling part it means. The surprise removed in 6.23 is only at many things existing at once in one whole. 4.22 argues by a question, and the question form is kept.

support.quote: this is what is akin to that other

support.follows: In me too, what is supreme is what uses the other things, and my life is governed by it.

claims.t: I make a habit of looking at causes. In each thing I go to the quality of the cause, mark the cause off from the material and look at it. I see the power at work just as I see the power that presses downward and the power that rises upward. I think constantly of how the world does all things by one impulse and how all things are joint causes of all that comes about. I consider the source of all things.

The power is 10.26 alone and is not named reason or providence there, so the line does not name it either. The one impulse and the joint causes are 4.33 alone, and the source is 6.33 alone. The practice is stated as something I do, not a vow.

single.label: An instruction
single.t: Of the things in the universe, I honour what is supreme: what uses all things and directs all things. In the same way, of the things in me, I honour what is supreme.
single.quote: Of the things in the universe, honour what is supreme: this is what uses all things and directs all things. In the same way, of the things in you too, honour what is supreme
single.why: Single source 5.18: “Of the things in the universe, honour what is supreme: this is what uses all things and directs all things. In the same way, of the things in you too, honour what is supreme”. The duty is to honour. The restored clause says what the supreme thing does.
single.follows: I should honour what is supreme in the world, and likewise what is supreme in me.

single.label: A strong claim
single.t: Nothing is harmed by the reason that governs the whole.
single.quote: nothing is harmed by it

single.label: The second of two cases
single.t: If not everything comes about as a consequence, then even the most important things, the ones at which the ruling part of the universe directs a particular impulse, are irrational.
single.quote: or even the most important things, the ones at which the ruling part of the universe directs a particular impulse, are irrational

The condition negates the first limb exactly, which is that everything comes about as a consequence. The either/or form is kept, and the rejection of this limb is left unstated as in the source.
single.follows: If not everything follows as a consequence, then even the most important things, the ones the ruling part of the universe aims at in particular, are irrational.

single.label: The other case
single.t: If the world is a random compound and a jumble, why do I even want to spend my time in it?
single.quote: Now if it is the first, why do I even want to spend my time in a random compound and a jumble of that kind?
single.why: Single source 6.8: “Now if it is the first, why do I even want to spend my time in a random compound and a jumble of that kind?”. It is a question under the jumble hypothesis only, not a conclusion about how to act.
single.follows: If the world were mere confusion, there would be no reason to want to remain in it.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. In modern editions 4.22 is 4.27, 4.33 is 4.40, 5.18 is 5.21, 5.24 is 5.30, 6.7 is 6.8, 6.8 is 6.9 and 6.10, 6.23 is 6.25, 6.33 is 6.36, 7.44 is 7.75 and 9.23 is 9.25; 6.1 and 10.26 are the same.
First person replaces the impersonal original. “I judge” marks order as a decision, which only 4.22 states outright. “Akin” keeps the kinship of 5.18 and stops short of identity.
articles.limit: Only 4.22 decides for order. 6.8 leaves order or jumble open and 7.44 argues by an either/or, so the article states order as my judgement and keeps the conditionals. Kinship between my ruling part and the whole’s is likeness from 5.18 alone, not identity, and reading 6.7 as cosmic would be our interpretation. Treating the common ruling part of 6.33 as the governing reason of 6.1 is also our reading. The surprise removed in 6.23 is only at many things existing at once in one whole. Harms are by-products or consequences, never called good or denied. The power of 10.26 and the methods of 9.23 and 6.23 make no providential claim of their own. No rule for action or for other people is drawn from the cosmic order.

articles.title: What I was made for

claims.t: Each thing has come to be for something: a horse, a vine. The gods have work to do and fruit to bear. A human being and the universe bear fruit too, each in its own seasons.

The gods’ work comes from 8.17 and god’s fruit from 9.8, where the word is singular. The horse and vine are from 8.17 alone and the seasons from 9.8 alone.

claims.t: Am I for pleasure? I test whether that idea holds up. What I put before everything else is keeping my own soul rational and social, in its settled character and in what it does. I honour the rational soul for what it is and as part of a community, and reason has fruit, both shared and its own. From reason come other things of much the same kind as reason itself.
claims.shared: The pleasure question is from 8.17 alone and stays a test, not a verdict. The choice is carried by “before everything else”, which is from 6.13 alone. “Settled character” and “what it does” put 6.13’s condition and movement into plain words. “For what it is and as part of a community” renders “as such, and as civic”. The fourth sentence is the fused one, joining 6.13’s honour with 9.8’s fruit, shared and its own. The last sentence is from 9.8 alone and reads “from it” as “from reason”.

support.quote: See whether the idea holds up.

articles.limit: Joint support from 10.21 and 4.19 covers only the good and the timing of what the whole brings. The direct address to the universe is shared by 4.19 and 10.22. decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. In modern editions 8.38 is 8.40, 6.47 is 6.52, 7.13 is 7.16, 9.30 is the opening of 9.32, 8.47 is 8.49, 12.16 is 12.22, 4.9 is 4.11, 2.13 is 2.15 and 9.11 is 9.13; 7.2 is only the first part of the modern 7.2.

Pilot wording restored, 106 characters. “Acting on that much” is cut because no passage speaks of acting. “Facts” is our plain word for what impressions report in 8.47 and for things as they are in truth in 4.9. Leaving the rest undecided rests on 8.47’s unreported harm and on the freedom in 6.47, which stays a freedom in c2.
articles.limit: The sources do not agree on one remedy. Some withdraw the judgment (6.47, 12.16, 8.38), while others form the right one or see truly (7.2, 4.9). Only 8.47 holds both, so the opening, which joins judging by the facts with leaving the rest undecided, is our editorial reading, not Marcus’s statement. “Facts” and “criticism” are our plain words for what impressions report, for things as they are in truth, and for ill speech or abuse. “Everything is judgment” is accepted only so far as it is true. Nothing here denies the event, the body’s suffering or the child’s sickness, and nothing says that outside things are unreal or that the child is safe. The calm is a simile for a moment when the judgment is removed, not a promise that it lasts. 9.11 reports one day, and c1 states its throwing out as a practice on our reading.

support.quote: For the common nature was bringing you nothing that could not be borne.
support.follows: Whatever the common nature brought me, it was something that could be borne.
gives: I am fitted by nature to bear it

support.quote: Remember, though, that you are fitted by nature to bear everything that it rests with your own judgment to make bearable and endurable
support.follows: I am fitted by nature to bear everything that my own judgment can make bearable.
gives: I am fitted to bear whatever my own judgment can make bearable

support.quote: Nothing can happen to any human being that is not a human occurrence
support.follows: Only things of the human kind can happen to a human being.
gives: a human occurrence

support.quote: So if what happens to each is what is both usual and natural, why would you resent it?
support.follows: If what happens to each thing is usual and natural for it, there is no reason to resent it.
gives: both usual and natural
I do not resent it

support.quote: So if it happens to you in a way you are fitted by nature to bear, do not resent it, but bear it as you are fitted by nature to do.
support.follows: If what happens is something I am fitted by nature to bear, I should bear it and not resent it.
gives: I do not resent it

claims.t: What troubles me is not the thing outside me but my own judgment that it is bad. Unless I make that judgment I have not yet been harmed. It is in my power not to make it, or to wipe it out at once.
claims.shared: Restores “not yet” from 7.11 and “at once” from 8.45. The claim judges the event and does not deny that it happened. Wiping out the verdict is from 8.45 alone.

support.quote: If you are distressed because of something outside you, it is not that thing that troubles you but your own verdict about it, and it is in your power to wipe that out at once.
support.follows: When something outside distresses me, what troubles me is my verdict about it, and I can wipe that verdict out at once.
gives: What troubles me is not the thing outside me
but my own judgment that it is bad
to wipe it out at once

support.quote: What is bad for you does not have its existence in another’s ruling part, nor yet in any turn and alteration of what surrounds you.
support.follows: What is bad for me is not in another person’s mind and not in any change in my surroundings.
gives: What troubles me is not the thing outside me

support.quote: Things themselves do not touch the soul in any way at all
support.follows: Things themselves do not touch the soul at all.
gives: What troubles me is not the thing outside me

support.quote: In the place where you have what judges about bad things. So let that not judge, and all is well.
support.follows: What is bad for me lies in the part of me that judges things bad; if that part does not judge, all is well.
gives: but my own judgment that it is bad
It is in my power not to make it

support.quote: But I, unless I judge that what has happened is bad, have not yet been harmed.
support.follows: Unless I judge that what has happened is bad, I have not yet been harmed.
gives: Unless I make that judgment I have not yet been harmed

support.quote: Take away the judgment, and “I have been harmed” is taken away. Take away “I have been harmed”, and the harm is taken away.
support.follows: Without the judgment there is no thought “I have been harmed”, and without that thought there is no harm.
gives: Unless I make that judgment I have not yet been harmed

support.quote: And it is possible for me not to judge so.
support.follows: It is possible for me not to make that judgment.
gives: It is in my power not to make it

claims.role: The body’s pain, the mind’s calm
claims.t: Even if my body is cut, burned or torn apart, the pain is for the body and its senses to see to. Neither fire, nor iron, nor a tyrant touches what is my mind’s own. My mind can draw a line around itself and keep its own clear sky and calm. It does not add the judgment that this is bad.
claims.shared: Replaces the blanket “nothing from outside touches my mind” with 8.39’s narrower “what is the mind’s own”. Keeps “can”, because the sources assert a possibility. The fire and iron image is from 8.39 alone, the drawn line from 5.20 alone and the clear sky from 8.26.

support.quote: Even if what is nearest to it, the little body, is cut, is burned, festers, rots, still let the part that judges about these things keep quiet.
support.follows: Even if the body is cut, burned or rotting, the part that judges about these things should keep quiet.
gives: Even if my body is cut, burned or torn apart

support.quote: even if the wild beasts are tearing apart the little limbs of this lump of dough that has thickened around you
support.follows: I can live unforced and glad even while wild beasts tear apart the limbs of my body.
gives: Even if my body is cut, burned or torn apart

support.quote: Pain is either a bad thing for the body, and then let the body declare it so, or for the soul.
support.follows: If pain is a bad thing for the body, it is for the body to say so.
gives: the pain is for the body and its senses to see to

support.quote: Does pain, does pleasure touch you? That is for sensation to see to.
support.follows: Whether pain or pleasure touches me is a matter for sensation.
gives: the pain is for the body and its senses to see to

support.quote: let it draw a line around itself and confine those feelings within the parts of the body
support.follows: The ruling part should draw a line around itself and keep the body’s feelings within the parts of the body.
gives: draw a line around itself

support.quote: What is the mind’s own, however, no one else is in the habit of hindering: for neither fire, nor iron, nor a tyrant, nor slander, nor anything whatever touches it
support.follows: Nothing whatever, not fire, iron, a tyrant or slander, touches what is the mind’s own.
gives: Neither fire, nor iron, nor a tyrant touches what is my mind’s own

support.quote: For every verdict and impulse and desire and aversion is inside, and nothing climbs up to here.
support.follows: Every verdict, impulse, desire and aversion is inside, and nothing climbs up to that place.
support.note: Every verdict, impulse, desire and aversion is inside, and nothing climbs up to that place.

support.quote: For what, in all of this, prevents the mind from keeping itself in calm
support.follows: Nothing in all of this prevents the mind from keeping itself calm.
gives: keep its own clear sky and calm

support.quote: But it is possible for the soul to keep its own clear sky and calm, and not to judge that it is a bad thing.
support.follows: The soul can keep its own calm and can decline to judge that the thing is bad.
gives: keep its own clear sky and calm
does not add the judgment that this is bad

support.quote: but let the ruling part not add, from itself, the judgment that it is something good or bad
support.follows: The ruling part should not add, from itself, the judgment that the feeling is something good or bad.
gives: does not add the judgment that this is bad

claims.t: To be good and just is in my power everywhere. What is present and comes to hand is my material for virtue. Using it rightly makes me better, and to bear it nobly is good fortune.
claims.shared: Adds “everywhere”, material and right use to the opening. “Makes me better” is from 10.33 alone, where it is hedged with “if it must be said”. The good fortune is from 4.41 alone and lies in the bearing, not in the event.

support.quote: All of this is in your power: for who prevents you from being good and straightforward?
support.follows: Being good and straightforward is in my power, and no one prevents me from it.
gives: To be good and just is in my power everywhere

support.quote: Surely this that has happened does not prevent you from being just, great-hearted, self-controlled, sensible, not rash, not deceived, modest, free
support.follows: What has happened does not prevent me from being just, great-hearted, self-controlled, sensible and free.
gives: To be good and just is in my power everywhere

support.quote: Everywhere and without a break it is in your power to be well content, in reverence for the gods, with the present turn of events, to behave justly towards the people present
support.follows: Everywhere and at every moment I can be content with what is happening and behave justly towards the people present.
gives: To be good and just is in my power everywhere

support.quote: For one must judge to be an enjoyment everything that it is possible to do in accordance with one’s own nature. And it is possible everywhere.
support.follows: Acting in accordance with my own nature is possible everywhere, and I should count it an enjoyment.
gives: To be good and just is in my power everywhere

support.quote: For to me what is present is always material for rational and civic virtue
support.follows: Whatever is present is material for rational and civic virtue.
gives: What is present and comes to hand is my material for virtue

support.quote: that, for you, is doing the things that belong to the way a human being is made, with the material that is supplied and comes to hand
support.follows: My part is to do what belongs to a human being with the material that is supplied and comes to hand.
gives: What is present and comes to hand is my material for virtue

support.quote: the human being becomes both better and more praiseworthy by using rightly the things that befall them
support.follows: A human being becomes better and more praiseworthy by using rightly what befalls them.
gives: Using it rightly makes me better

support.quote: not “this is a misfortune”, but “to bear it nobly is good fortune.”
support.follows: The thing to say is not that this is a misfortune but that bearing it nobly is good fortune.
gives: to bear it nobly is good fortune

claims.t: At every impression of harm, and at every pain, I keep a rule ready. If the city I belong to by nature is not harmed, I have not been harmed. Pain is not shameful, and what does not make me worse does not harm me.
claims.shared: The practice of keeping rules ready is shared by three passages, and the city rule by two. The line on shame is from 7.35 alone and the “worse” test from 4.7 alone. 5.19 allows that the city can be harmed, so the rule is a test, not a guarantee.

support.quote: At every impression of having been harmed, apply this rule: if the city is not harmed by this, I have not been harmed either.
support.follows: Whenever I have the impression of being harmed, I should apply the rule that if the city is not harmed, I am not harmed.
gives: At every impression of harm
I keep a rule ready
If the city I belong to by nature is not harmed, I have not been harmed

support.quote: At every pain, have this ready to hand: that it is not shameful and does not make the mind at the helm any worse
support.follows: At every pain I should have ready the thought that pain is not shameful and does not make the governing mind worse.
gives: at every pain
I keep a rule ready
Pain is not shameful

support.quote: From now on, remember, at everything that leads you towards distress, to use this principle
support.follows: At everything that leads me towards distress, I should remember to use this principle: it is not a misfortune, but bearing it nobly is good fortune.
gives: I keep a rule ready

support.quote: nothing harms one who is by nature a citizen that does not harm the city
support.follows: Nothing harms a citizen that does not harm the city.
gives: If the city I belong to by nature is not harmed, I have not been harmed

support.quote: What does not make a human being worse than they were does not make their life worse either, and does not harm them from outside or from within.
support.follows: What does not make a person worse does not make their life worse and does not harm them.
gives: what does not make me worse does not harm me

claims.t: I do not take in all my hardships at one sweep of thought. Only the present weighs on me, and it shrinks when I mark it off by itself. I add no opinion to a pain and I remember its limits. Taken this way, neither the present task nor most pain is unbearable, and most pain is not everlasting.
claims.shared: Removes “whole life”, which 8.34a does not say and which now sits in the margin. The joint phrase gives the present task to 8.34 and pain to 7.35. Both halves of the Epicurean saying are narrowed to most pain, as Marcus frames it. The shrinking present is from 8.34 alone.

support.quote: it is neither the future nor the past that weighs on you, but always the present; and this shrinks if you mark it off by itself alone and show your mind up if it cannot hold out against the present stripped bare
support.follows: Only the present weighs on me, and it shrinks when I mark it off by itself, stripped bare.
gives: Only the present weighs on me
it shrinks when I mark it off by itself

support.quote: that it is neither unbearable nor everlasting, if you remember the limits and do not add to it by opinion
support.follows: Most pain is neither unbearable nor everlasting, if I remember its limits and do not add to it by opinion.
gives: I add no opinion to a pain and I remember its limits
neither the present task nor most pain is unbearable
most pain is not everlasting

support.quote: Do not take in at one sweep of thought what hardships and how many are likely to have come on you.
support.follows: I should not take in at one sweep all the hardships that are likely to have come on me.
gives: I do not take in all my hardships at one sweep of thought

support.quote: “What is there in this task that is unbearable and not to be endured?” For you will be ashamed to admit it.
support.follows: Asked what is unbearable in the task in front of me, I would be ashamed to name anything.
gives: neither the present task nor most pain is unbearable

single.label: Good and bad alike
single.t: What can happen equally to a bad man and a good one I judge neither bad nor good.
single.quote: That is, let it decide that what can happen equally to a bad man and a good one is neither bad nor good.
single.why: Single source, 4.32. Recast as what I judge and kept as the specific argument it is.
single.follows: What can happen equally to a bad man and a good one is neither bad nor good.

single.label: Help without alarm
single.t: When people come off worse in things that are neither good nor bad, I am not swept off wholesale by the impression. Even then I help as far as I am able and as far as is deserved. I do not form the impression that their loss is a harm, for that is a bad habit.
single.quote: Do not be swept off wholesale by the impression, but help as far as you are able and as far as is deserved, even if they are coming off worse in the middle things; do not, however, form the impression that it is a harm, for that is a bad habit.
single.why: Single source, 5.29, which breaks off incomplete. The occasion comes first so that “the impression” has a referent, and “Even then” keeps the source’s “even if”. “Things that are neither good nor bad” is our gloss on “the middle things”. Helping survives the denial of harm.
single.follows: I should help as far as I can, even when what others lose is neither good nor bad, but I should not form the impression that their loss is a harm.

single.label: In illness
single.t: In illness, if I am ill, and in any other circumstance, I do as Epicurus did in his illness. I do not stand away from philosophy, whatever befalls.
single.quote: So do the same as he did, in illness, if you are ill, and in any other circumstance. For not to stand away from philosophy in anything whatever that befalls
single.why: Single source, 9.41, truncated. Epicurus is a model for this conduct only, not an endorsement of his school.
single.follows: In illness, and in any other circumstance, I should do as Epicurus did and not stand away from philosophy, whatever befalls.

single.label: Pain unnoticed
single.t: Many things are the same as pain and go unnoticed as such, though I resent them: being drowsy, being overheated, having no appetite. When one of these displeases me, I say to myself: “You are giving in to pain.”
single.quote: many things that are the same as pain go unnoticed as such, though we resent them, such as being drowsy, being overheated and having no appetite. So when you are displeased at any of these, say to yourself: “You are giving in to pain.”
single.why: Single source, 7.35. Keeps the source’s three examples and its self-address.
single.follows: Drowsiness, heat and loss of appetite are forms of pain; being displeased at them is giving in to pain.

single.label: An unconditional impulse
single.t: If my impulse was without reservation and something came to stand in its way, that is already a bad thing for me as a rational being. If I accept the common lot, I have not yet been harmed or hindered.
single.quote: Did something come to stand in the way of your impulse? If your impulse was without reservation, then it is already a bad thing for you as a rational being. But if you accept the common lot, you have not yet been harmed or hindered.
single.why: Single source, 8.39, truncated. Removes the earlier explanatory gloss on “without reservation” and keeps the concession that an unreserved impulse really is thwarted.
single.follows: A blocked impulse is already bad for me if it was without reservation; if I accept the common lot I have not yet been harmed or hindered.

single.label: The feeling is natural
single.t: When the body’s feelings pass up into my mind, as in a unified body, I do not try to go against the sensation, which is natural.
single.quote: But when they pass up into the mind by the other shared feeling, as in a unified body, then one should not try to go against the sensation, which is natural
single.why: Single source, 5.20. It limits claim 3: the sensation is felt and not resisted, and only the added judgment is withheld.
single.follows: When bodily feelings reach the mind, one should not fight the sensation, which is natural.

single.label: Outdone by ignorance
single.t: The same things that happen to me happen to someone else, who stands firm and unhurt through not knowing what has happened or through showing off greatness of mind. It is a terrible thing if ignorance and the wish to please are stronger than wisdom.
single.quote: The same things happen to someone else, and either because they do not know that it has happened, or because they are showing off greatness of mind, they stand firm and remain unhurt. It is a terrible thing, then, that ignorance and the wish to please should be stronger than wisdom.
single.why: Single source, 5.16. “That happen to me” supplies the comparison the source takes from its preceding sentence. Kept in the third person as a warning, not turned into a vow.
single.follows: Others bear the same things out of ignorance or to show off; it is terrible if those are stronger than wisdom.

single.label: If I cannot bear it
single.t: If something happens that I am not fitted by nature to bear, I do not resent it. It will perish once it has used me up.
single.quote: And if in a way you are not fitted by nature to bear, do not resent it: for it will perish once it has used you up.
single.why: Single source, 10.3. It openly allows the unbearable case, which limits the opening.
single.follows: What I am not fitted to bear ends once it has used me up, so it too is not to be resented.

single.label: If I am blocked
single.t: If something stronger stands in the way of what seems sound to me, I am not distressed, for the cause of its not being done does not lie with me. If life is not worth living with this undone, I leave life kindly disposed, as the one who does it dies too, and gracious towards what stands in the way.
single.quote: “But something stronger stands in the way.” Then do not be distressed, for the cause of its not being done does not lie with you. “But life is not worth living if this is not done.” Then leave life kindly disposed, just as the one who is doing it dies too, and at the same time gracious towards the things that stand in the way.
single.why: Single source, 8.45. The condition is the objector’s own. The line governs the manner of leaving and sets no duty to leave.
single.follows: If something stronger blocks the act, the cause is not mine and I need not be distressed; if life is not worth living without it, I may leave life kindly.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. 8.45 is 8.46–47, 10.33 is 10.32–33, 7.39 is 7.68, 7.29 is 7.53–54, 4.32 is 4.39, 4.41 is 4.49b, 5.19 is 5.22–25, 7.35 is 7.64, 8.34 is 8.36, 5.16 is 5.17–19, 5.20 is 5.26, 7.11 is 7.14, 8.39 is 8.41a, 9.41 is 9.41a, 5.29 is 5.35–36a, 8.41 is 8.42–43, 8.26 is 8.28 and 4.7 is 4.7–9; 10.3 is 10.3 in both.

137 characters, three short sentences, no semicolon. The first sentence grants that the body can be hurt, so the second is heard as a judgement about the event and not a denial of it. Bearing is narrowed to the condition in 10.3, with 7.35 as second witness that opinion decides whether pain is unbearable. 7.35 speaks of most pains only. The broader wording of 5.16 and 8.45 stays in claim 1. No promise of indefinite endurance is made.
articles.limit: These lines judge what happens. They do not deny that it happens or that it is felt. Sensation is natural and reaches the mind, pain may be bad for the body, and a hindrance is bad for an animal nature. An impulse held without reservation really is thwarted. The opening claims only that I can bear what my judgment makes bearable. 5.16 and 8.45 say more broadly that nothing comes that cannot be borne, but 10.3 allows a case that uses a person up, and 8.45 and 10.33 contemplate leaving life. The Epicurean comfort covers most pains, not all. The city rule is a test and not a promise that the city cannot be harmed. Helping others remains. The passages argue in different ways and are not one system. 8.39, 9.41 and 5.29 are truncated, and the last line of 4.7 is too obscure to build on.

aside.8.41: Says what gladdens Marcus: a sound ruling part that turns away from nothing that happens and uses each thing according to its worth. The use of what happens is already in claim 4 from 10.33 and 7.39, and the passage’s first sentence, on not causing himself distress, is a different thought.

statement.t: What happens may hurt my body. It harms me only if I judge it bad. I can bear what my judgment makes bearable and still be good and just.

articles.title: Keeping the few names I have given myself

claims.t: I have named myself good, modest and truthful, and I take care never to bear other names. These are few things to keep. At every hour I do what is in hand with exact and unfeigned dignity, affection, freedom and justice. I keep myself simple, good and unpretentious, and I struggle to remain the kind of person philosophy wanted to make me.
claims.shared: The opaque boarding image is replaced by plain naming, and the image moves to the margin with its condition “if you can stay”. Fewness and keeping are the joint ground of 2.2 and 10.8. The three names are 10.8’s alone, the hourly work is 2.2’s alone, and the simple character and the struggle are 6.27’s alone. Each list stays with its own passage, and none is offered as a definition of the names.

support.quote: At every hour take firm care
support.follows: Care is to be taken at every hour, and firmly.
gives: At every hour

support.quote: to do what is in hand with exact and unfeigned dignity, affection, freedom and justice
support.follows: What is in hand is to be done with dignity, affection, freedom and justice, exactly and without feigning.
gives: I do what is in hand with exact and unfeigned dignity, affection, freedom and justice

support.quote: You see how few the things are
support.follows: The things that have to be mastered are few.
gives: These are few things to keep

support.quote: keep yourself simple, good, unspoiled, dignified, unpretentious, a friend of what is just, reverent towards the gods, kindly, warmly affectionate
support.follows: I should keep myself simple, good, dignified, unpretentious, just, reverent, kindly and affectionate.
gives: I keep myself simple, good and unpretentious

support.quote: Struggle to remain the kind of person philosophy wanted to make you.
support.follows: Remaining the person philosophy meant to make me takes a struggle.
gives: I struggle to remain the kind of person philosophy wanted to make me

support.quote: Having given yourself these names: good, modest, truthful, clear-minded, like-minded, high-minded, take care that you never come to bear other names
support.follows: Marcus has given himself six names and must take care that he does not end up bearing others.
gives: I have named myself good, modest and truthful
I take care never to bear other names

support.quote: if you keep yourself in these names
support.follows: A person can keep himself in these names.

support.quote: So put yourself aboard these few names, and if you can stay on them, stay
support.follows: The names are few; I should put myself aboard them and stay on them if I can.
gives: These are few things to keep

claims.t: The life I live depends on what I keep to. Once mastered, these things let me live a life that flows smoothly and is god-fearing. If I keep to these things, the gods will demand nothing more of me. If I keep myself in the names I have given myself, I will be a different person and enter a different life. The gods do not want to be flattered. They want all rational beings to become like them, the fig tree to do the work of a fig tree, the dog the work of a dog, the bee the work of a bee, and the human being the work of a human being.
claims.shared: The first sentence is the common proposition. In 2.2 mastering the few things lets a person live a smooth life, and in 10.8 keeping in the names brings a different life. The smooth life stays with 2.2 and the different life with 10.8. What the gods demand (2.2) and what they want (10.8) remain separate sentences with one witness each.

support.quote: once mastered, let a person live a life that flows smoothly and is god-fearing
support.follows: The few things, once mastered, let a person live a life that flows smoothly and is god-fearing.
gives: The life I live depends on what I keep to
Once mastered, these things let me live a life that flows smoothly and is god-fearing

support.quote: for the gods will demand nothing more of whoever keeps to these
support.follows: The gods will demand nothing more of anyone who keeps to these few things.
gives: If I keep to these things, the gods will demand nothing more of me

support.quote: if you keep yourself in these names, without craving to have others call you by them, you will be a different person and will enter a different life
support.follows: Whoever keeps himself in these names becomes a different person and enters a different life.
gives: The life I live depends on what I keep to
If I keep myself in the names I have given myself, I will be a different person and enter a different life

support.quote: what they want is not to be flattered, but for all rational beings to become like them, and for the fig tree to do the work of a fig tree, the dog the work of a dog, the bee the work of a bee, and the human being the work of a human being
support.follows: The gods do not want flattery; they want rational beings to become like them and each thing, the human being included, to do its own work.

They want all rational beings to become like them, the fig tree to do the work of a fig tree, the dog the work of a dog, the bee the work of a bee, and the human being the work of a human being

claims.t: I do not look to others to confirm what I am. I do not crave to have others call me by the names I have given myself. I need neither an oath nor any human being as witness. It is possible to live at a court and need neither bodyguards, nor clothes that mark one out, nor torches, statues and other such display.
claims.shared: The first sentence is the common proposition of 3.5 (no human witness) and 10.8 (no craving for others to use the names). The court sentence is a single-witness detail from 1.14 and stays a statement of what is possible, not a vow.

support.quote: it is possible to live at a court and need neither bodyguards, nor clothes that mark one out, nor torches and statues of this sort and other such display
support.follows: The ruler and father Marcus was placed under brought him to think that one can live at a court without guards, marked clothes or similar show.
gives: It is possible to live at a court and need neither bodyguards, nor clothes that mark one out, nor torches, statues and other such display

support.quote: needing neither an oath nor any human being as witness
support.follows: The man who has set himself in order needs no oath and no human witness.
gives: I do not look to others to confirm what I am
I need neither an oath nor any human being as witness

support.quote: without craving to have others call you by them
support.follows: The names are to be kept without craving that other people call me by them.
gives: I do not look to others to confirm what I am
I do not crave to have others call me by the names I have given myself

claims.t: As a Roman and a man, I carry out each action as the last of my life. I set myself in order, as someone would be who is waiting for the signal to withdraw from life, easily released. I want my last hour to come upon me with a conscience as good as that of Antoninus.
claims.shared: Waiting for the signal stays a simile for being in order, not a wish to die. The conscience is measured against Antoninus, as 6.28 says. The old line repeated the last-act thought and one instance is cut.

support.quote: so that your last hour may come upon you with a conscience as good as his
support.follows: Following Antoninus is meant to bring me to my last hour with a conscience as good as his.
gives: my last hour to come upon me with a conscience as good as that of Antoninus

support.quote: as a Roman and a man
support.follows: The care over what is in hand is to be taken as a Roman and a man.
gives: As a Roman and a man

support.quote: a living being that is male, old, engaged in public affairs, a Roman and a ruler, who has set himself in order
support.follows: The god within is to guard a being who is male, old, in public life, a Roman and a ruler, and who has set himself in order.
gives: As a Roman and a man
I set myself in order

support.quote: as someone would be who is waiting for the signal to withdraw from life, easily released
support.follows: The man described is to be like someone who waits for the signal to withdraw from life and is easily released.
gives: as someone would be who is waiting for the signal to withdraw from life, easily released

support.quote: carry out each action as the last of your life
support.follows: Each action is to be carried out as if it were the last of my life.
gives: I carry out each action as the last of my life

claims.t: I look back on how I have behaved towards my parents, my teachers, my friends and those close to me. They were good people, nearly all of them, and I was not carried away into any offence against any of them. I ask the same about my conduct towards the gods, my brothers, my wife, my children, those who brought me up and my household slaves. Does it hold of me up to now that I have done nothing wrong to anyone, nor said anything wrong?
claims.shared: The first sentence names only the people both passages list, and both passages look back on conduct towards them. The statement of no offence is 1.14’s and covers only those people. The standard from 5.25 stays a question “up to now” and is not a claim of innocence. The gods, brothers, wife, children, upbringers and household slaves are 5.25’s alone.

support.quote: How have you behaved up to now towards the gods, your parents, your brothers, your wife, your children, your teachers, those who brought you up, your friends, those close to you, your household slaves?
support.follows: Marcus asks himself how he has behaved up to now towards the gods, his family, teachers, friends, those close to him and his household.
gives: I look back on how I have behaved towards my parents, my teachers, my friends and those close to me
I ask the same about my conduct towards the gods, my brothers, my wife, my children, those who brought me up and my household slaves

support.quote: Does this hold of you up to now, towards all of them: “to have done nothing wrong to anyone, nor said anything wrong”?
support.follows: Marcus asks whether, towards all the people he has listed, he has done nothing wrong and said nothing wrong.
gives: Does it hold of me up to now that I have done nothing wrong to anyone, nor said anything wrong?

support.quote: that I had good grandfathers, good parents, a good sister, good teachers, good people close to me, relatives, friends, nearly all of them
support.follows: Marcus thanks the gods that nearly all his family, teachers, friends and those close to him were good.
gives: I look back on how I have behaved towards my parents, my teachers, my friends and those close to me
They were good people, nearly all of them

support.quote: I was not carried away into any offence against any of them
support.follows: Marcus was not carried away into any offence against his family, teachers, friends or those close to him.
gives: I look back on how I have behaved towards my parents, my teachers, my friends and those close to me
I was not carried away into any offence against any of them

claims.t: I can fall away from the person I mean to be. I take care that I am not turned into a Caesar, that I am not dyed, for it happens. My still falling short of the life according to nature is through my own fault and through not keeping to the reminders from the gods. If I lose my names, I go back to them quickly.
claims.shared: The first sentence is the common proposition. 6.27 says being dyed happens, 10.8 speaks of sensing a falling away, and 1.14 admits still falling short. “The person I mean to be” is our summary of the three different standards. The Caesar and the dye are 6.27’s alone, the own fault is 1.14’s alone, and the quick return is 10.8’s alone. The Caesar line remains a warning to take care.

support.quote: if you do lose these names, go back to them quickly
support.follows: The names can be lost; if they are, I should go back to them quickly.
gives: If I lose my names, I go back to them quickly

support.quote: Take care that you are not turned into a Caesar, that you are not dyed: for it happens.
support.follows: Being turned into a Caesar is something that happens, and care must be taken against it.
gives: I can fall away from the person I mean to be
I take care that I am not turned into a Caesar, that I am not dyed, for it happens

support.quote: if you sense that you are falling away and are not prevailing
support.follows: A person can sense that he is falling away from the names and not prevailing.
gives: I can fall away from the person I mean to be

support.quote: my still falling short of this is through my own fault and through not keeping to the reminders from the gods
support.follows: That Marcus still falls short of living according to nature is his own fault: he has not kept to the gods’ reminders.
gives: I can fall away from the person I mean to be
My still falling short of the life according to nature is through my own fault and through not keeping to the reminders from the gods

single.label: The one fruit
single.t: Life is short. There is one fruit of living on earth: a pious disposition and social actions.
single.quote: Life is short. There is one fruit of living on earth: a pious disposition and social actions.
single.why: Single source, 6.27. It stands as the speaker framed it. The gloss on social actions was editorial and is removed.
single.follows: Life is short, and the one thing to be had from it is a pious disposition and actions done for the community.

single.label: Leading without the show
single.t: I may draw myself in until I am very nearly a private person and not, on that account, be more lowly or more slack in what has to be done as a leader for the common good.
single.quote: one may draw oneself in until one is very nearly a private person and not, on that account, be more lowly or more slack in what has to be done as a leader for the common good
single.why: Single source, 1.14. “May” keeps it a permission learned at court, not a duty to withdraw.
single.follows: Marcus’s ruler and father showed him that one can live almost as a private person and be no lowlier or slacker in a leader’s work for the common good.

single.label: The trade I learned
single.t: I love the little trade I have learned, and I rest in it. I go through what is left of my life having entrusted everything that is mine to the gods with my whole soul, making myself neither the tyrant nor the slave of any human being.
single.quote: Love the little trade you have learned, and rest in it; and go through what is left of your life having entrusted everything that is yours to the gods with your whole soul, and making yourself neither the tyrant nor the slave of any human being.
single.why: Single source, 4.26. The trade is left unnamed, as in the source.
single.follows: I should love the trade I learned and rest in it, entrust what is mine to the gods, and be neither tyrant nor slave to anyone.

single.label: How not to act
single.t: I do not act unwillingly, or unsocially, or without examining, or while pulled the other way. I do not let elegance dress up my thought. I am not a person of many words or a busybody.
single.quote: Do not act unwillingly, or unsocially, or without examining, or while pulled the other way. Do not let elegance dress up your thought. Do not be a person of many words or a busybody.
single.why: Single source, 3.5. The source wording is kept in three plain sentences.
single.follows: Acting unwillingly, unsocially, unexamined or divided is ruled out, and so are dressed-up thought, many words and meddling.

single.label: Three further names
single.t: I remember what three of my names were to mean. “Clear-minded” was a discerning attention to each thing, and not letting things go unheeded. “Like-minded” was the willing acceptance of what the common nature assigns. “High-minded” was the lifting high of the part that has mind, above the smooth or rough movement of the flesh, above petty reputation, above death and everything of that kind.
single.quote: Remember that “clear-minded” was to mean for you a discerning attention to each thing, and not letting things go unheeded; “like-minded”, the willing acceptance of what the common nature assigns; and “high-minded”, the lifting high of the part that has mind, above the smooth or rough movement of the flesh, above petty reputation, above death and everything of that kind.
single.why: Single source, 10.8. The bracketed gloss “pleasure and pain” was editorial and is removed.
single.follows: The three names mean attention to each thing, willing acceptance of what nature assigns, and a mind lifted above the flesh, reputation and death.

single.label: Antoninus as my model
single.t: I do everything as a pupil of Antoninus: his vigour on behalf of what is done according to reason, his evenness everywhere, his piety, the calm of his face, his gentleness, his freedom from vanity and his ambition to grasp matters.
single.quote: Everything as a pupil of Antoninus: his vigour on behalf of what is done according to reason, his evenness everywhere, his piety, the calm of his face, his gentleness, his freedom from vanity, and his ambition to grasp matters
single.why: Single source, 6.28. “The emperor who adopted me” is removed, because the passages do not identify him so.
single.follows: Marcus is to do everything as a pupil of Antoninus, whose traits he lists, beginning with these seven.

single.label: What I have come through
single.t: I call to mind what I have passed through and what I have been strong enough to endure. I call to mind that the story of my life is now full and my service complete. I call to mind how many fine things I have seen, how many pleasures and pains I have looked down on, how many honours I have looked past, and to how many inconsiderate people I have been considerate.
single.quote: Call to mind, too, what things you have passed through and what things you have been strong enough to endure; and that the story of your life is now full and your service complete; and how many fine things you have seen; and how many pleasures and pains you have looked down on, how many honours you have looked past, and to how many inconsiderate people you have been considerate.
single.why: Single source, 5.25. Semicolons are removed. It stays a recollection to prompt me, not a verdict on my life.
single.follows: Marcus is to recall what he has endured, seen and looked past, and that his life’s story is full and his service complete.

single.label: Partly the gods’ kindness
single.t: I had a disposition from which I might well have offended those close to me. It is the gods’ kindness that no combination of circumstances came about that would have shown me up.
single.quote: although I had a disposition from which, if it had so happened, I might well have done something of the kind; but it is the gods’ kindness that no combination of circumstances came about that would have shown me up
single.why: Single source, 1.14. “Clean record” and “partly” were not in the source and are removed. “Those close to me” supplies the referent for “something of the kind”.
single.follows: Marcus had it in him to offend those close to him, and thanks the gods that no circumstances arose to bring it out.

single.label: The soul giving out
single.t: It is shameful if, in a life in which my body does not give out, my soul gives out first.
single.quote: It is shameful that, in a life in which your body does not give out, your soul should give out first.
single.why: Single source, 6.27. It is a separate remark in that passage and stands alone here.
single.follows: It is shameful for the soul to give out before the body does.

single.label: Like the beast-fighters
single.t: To go on being what I have been up to now, torn and soiled in a life like this, is the mark of someone thoroughly senseless and clinging to life. Such a person is like the half-eaten beast-fighters who, full of wounds and gore, still beg to be kept until tomorrow, to be thrown, just as they are, to the same claws and bites.
single.quote: For to go on being what you have been up to now, and to be torn and soiled in a life like this, is the mark of someone thoroughly senseless and clinging to life, someone like the half-eaten beast-fighters who, full of wounds and gore, still beg to be kept until tomorrow, to be thrown, just as they are, to the same claws and bites.
single.why: Single source, 10.8. The beast-fighters remain a comparison in the third person and are not made my identity.
single.follows: Going on unchanged in a life that tears and soils me is senseless clinging to life, like a mauled beast-fighter begging for one more day.

single.label: If I am not prevailing
single.t: If I sense that I am falling away and am not prevailing, I go away with a good heart to some corner where I will prevail.
single.quote: go away with a good heart to some corner where you will prevail
single.why: Single source, 10.8. The condition is kept so the withdrawal is not made a general rule. The further option of leaving life is held in the margin.
single.follows: Someone who is not prevailing should withdraw, in good heart, to a corner where he will prevail.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. In modern editions 2.2 is 2.5, 6.27 is 6.29 with the first part of 6.30, 6.28 is the rest of 6.30, 3.5 is the first part of 3.5, 5.25 is 5.31, 4.26 is 4.31 and 1.14 is 1.17; 10.8 is the same.

134 characters. “Such as good” tells a first hearer that the names are qualities of character. Only “good” is named because it stands in both 10.8 and 6.27. The naming itself is 10.8’s alone. 2.2 supplies fewness and keeping to the few things. The last act is a way of acting, not an expectation of death.
articles.limit: The names belong to 10.8 alone. 2.2 and 6.27 share only the fewness of what is required and overlapping but different lists of qualities, so the article joins them by theme and not as one canon. The opening names only “good”, the one quality that both 10.8 and 6.27 list. In the opening, the last-act wording is 2.2’s, and 6.28 and 3.5 witness only the shared last-hour frame. The boarding image and its condition “if you can stay” are held in the margin as 10.8’s alone. The first sentences of c2, c3, c5 and c6 are our summaries of what two passages share, and the sentences after them keep each passage’s own wording with its own witness. The gods play different parts in each passage and are not made one theology. “Service complete” (5.25) stands unresolved beside “struggle to remain” (6.27) and “still falling short” (1.14). The last-hour language is a frame for acting well and not a wish to die. The condition in 10.8i comes from the surrounding passage, and leaving life is held in the margin as 10.8’s alone. The ruler-father of 1.14 is not identified with Antoninus, and the little trade of 4.26 is not named.

statement.t: I have given myself a few names, such as good. I keep to them, do each act as the last of my life, and need no human being as witness.

parts.words: I have given myself a few names, such as good
I keep to them
do each act as the last of my life
need no human being as witness

statement.kind: A rule, the way it is carried out, and what it does not need
