statement.form: 134 characters. “Such as good” tells a first hearer that the names are qualities of character. Only “good” is named because it stands in both 10.8 and 6.27. The naming itself is 10.8’s alone. 2.2 supplies fewness and keeping to the few things. The last act is a way of acting, not an expectation of death.

empty.doubt: No passage in this section asks what holds if keeping these names is not enough, or if the gods ask something else.

articles.title: Living now as one about to die

claims.t: Before long I shall be no one and nowhere, as those before me already are. Soon I shall forget all, and all will forget me. I live only the present, an instant, and the present is what I lose.
claims.shared: Restores the two-way forgetting of 7.16, which the earlier line had halved. Adds from 12.19 alone that the present is what is lost. The named dead are generalised to ‘those before me’.

support.quote: in a little while you will be no one and nowhere, just as Hadrian is not, nor Augustus
support.follows: In a little while I shall be no one and nowhere, just as Hadrian and Augustus are not.
gives: Before long I shall be no one and nowhere
as those before me already are

support.quote: before long you will be no one and nowhere, and neither will any of the things you now see, nor any of the people now living
support.follows: Before long neither I, nor anything I now see, nor anyone now living will exist.
gives: Before long I shall be no one and nowhere

support.quote: How many a Chrysippus, how many a Socrates, how many an Epictetus has eternity already swallowed down.
support.follows: Eternity has already swallowed many a Chrysippus, many a Socrates and many an Epictetus.
gives: as those before me already are

support.quote: Your forgetting of all is near, and near is the forgetting of you by all.
support.follows: Soon I shall have forgotten everything, and soon everyone will have forgotten me.
gives: Soon I shall forget all, and all will forget me

support.quote: each person lives only this present, an instant. The rest has either been lived or is uncertain.
support.follows: A person lives only the present instant; the rest is either already lived or uncertain.
gives: I live only the present, an instant

support.quote: each person lives only the present, and this is what they lose
support.follows: A person lives only the present, and the present is what a person loses.
gives: I live only the present, an instant
the present is what I lose

claims.t: I live what is left as a surplus, like someone already at the end of life, and I do, say and think each thing knowing that I may leave life at this very moment. I no longer let what rules in me be a slave, pulled about on strings by unsocial impulse. I have in me something stronger and more divine than the things that produce the passions.
claims.shared: Semicolon removed. ‘Surplus’ is restored from 7.31 alone, and ‘slave’ from 1.16 alone. ‘Like’ keeps the dying person a comparison. The strings image is the jointly supported phrase.

support.quote: As someone who has died and has lived out their life up to now, one must live what is left, as a surplus, according to nature.
support.follows: I must count my life as lived and over, and live what remains as an extra, according to nature.
gives: I live what is left as a surplus
like someone already at the end of life

support.quote: as one already dying, despise the bits of flesh
support.follows: I am to despise my flesh, taking the stance of someone who is already dying.
gives: like someone already at the end of life

support.quote: Third, then, is the ruling part. Think of it this way: you are old. No longer let this be a slave, no longer let it be pulled about on strings by unsocial impulse
support.follows: I am old: I should no longer let my ruling part be a slave or be pulled about by unsocial impulse.
gives: I no longer let what rules in me be a slave
pulled about on strings
by unsocial impulse

support.quote: To do and say and think each thing in the knowledge that it is possible to leave life at this very moment.
support.follows: Everything I do, say and think should be done knowing that I could leave life right now.
gives: I do, say and think each thing knowing that I may leave life at this very moment

support.quote: you have in yourself something stronger and more divine than the things that produce the passions and that, in a word, pull you about on strings
support.follows: There is something in me stronger and more divine than the things that produce the passions and pull me about.
gives: pulled about on strings
something stronger and more divine than the things that produce the passions

claims.t: I leave the past behind, hand the future over to providence, and steer only the present. I steer it towards justice in what I do and towards being pleased with what is allotted to me. Until my time comes, it is enough to do good to people and bear with them, and I do not trouble myself about how long I shall be doing this.
claims.shared: ‘Until my time comes’ gives the waiting a referent a listener can hear, where 5.27 says ‘the right time for that’ and points back to a sentence outside this line. ‘How long I shall be doing this’ now names its action, following 6.21. The future is entrusted to providence on 12.1 alone. Reverence for the gods, holding back and the three hours of 6.21 are single-source details kept in the margin.

support.quote: if you leave all the past behind, hand the future over to providence, and steer only the present towards piety and justice
support.follows: I am to leave the past behind, entrust the future to providence, and steer only the present towards piety and justice.
gives: I leave the past behind, hand the future over to providence, and steer only the present
justice in what I do

support.quote: Piety, so that you love what is allotted, for nature brought it to you and you to it.
support.follows: Piety here means loving what is allotted to me, since nature brought it and me together.
gives: being pleased with what is allotted to me

support.quote: the person who is pleased with what is allotted from the whole and content with their own action being just and their disposition kind
support.follows: The good person is pleased with what the whole allots and content if their own action is just and their disposition kind.
gives: justice in what I do
being pleased with what is allotted to me

support.quote: In sum, life is short. The present must be turned to profit, with good reasoning and justice.
support.follows: Life is short; the present has to be put to good use, with good reasoning and justice.
gives: justice in what I do

support.quote: Freedom from disturbance about the things that happen from the cause outside; justice in the things done through the cause that comes from you.
support.follows: Two things are named: not being disturbed by what happens from outside, and justice in what comes from me.
gives: justice in what I do

support.quote: And until the right time for that is at hand, what is enough? What else but to revere the gods and speak well of them, to do good to human beings, to bear with them and to hold back
support.follows: Until the time of death comes, it is enough to revere the gods, do good to people, bear with them and hold back.
gives: Until my time comes
it is enough
to do good to people and bear with them

support.quote: do not trouble yourself about how long you will be doing this: for even three hours of this kind are enough
support.follows: How long I go on acting this way should not worry me; even three hours of it are enough.
gives: it is enough
I do not trouble myself about how long I shall be doing this

claims.t: I wait for death cheerfully, whether it is an extinguishing or a move elsewhere, and I do not chafe at the delay. The dissolving of the elements I am put together from is according to nature, and nothing that is according to nature is bad.
claims.shared: Text unchanged. 5.10a is removed from the cheerful waiting, because 5.10 speaks of comfort and patience and not of cheer, so only 2.15 and 5.27 carry that phrase. 5.10 still supports the patience and, with 2.15, the natural dissolution. The elements are from 2.15 alone, and the open alternative is from 5.27 alone.

support.quote: waiting for death with a cheerful mind, as nothing other than a dissolving of the elements of which every living thing is put together
support.follows: Philosophy includes waiting for death cheerfully, as nothing other than the coming apart of the elements a living thing is made of.
gives: I wait for death cheerfully
The dissolving of the elements I am put together from

support.quote: For it is according to nature, and nothing that is according to nature is bad.
support.follows: The change and dissolution of all is according to nature, and nothing according to nature is bad.
gives: is according to nature, and nothing that is according to nature is bad

support.quote: One must comfort oneself and wait for the natural dissolution, and not chafe at the delay
support.follows: I should comfort myself, wait for the dissolution that nature brings, and not be impatient that it is slow to come.
gives: I do not chafe at the delay
The dissolving of the elements I am put together from

support.quote: You wait cheerfully for what is either an extinguishing or a move elsewhere.
support.follows: I wait cheerfully for death, whichever it is: a going out like a flame or a move to another place.
gives: I wait for death cheerfully
whether it is an extinguishing or a move elsewhere

claims.t: I look at human affairs as if from high above, and I see how alike they are and how short-lived. The things people prize are empty and small, little dogs biting one another. A name is a noise and an echo, many will very quickly forget mine, and being remembered is of no account. Among these things I stand kindly, without sneering at them.
claims.shared: ‘Look at’ replaces ‘look down on’, so the height is a vantage and the contempt falls on prized things, not on people. The dogs and the echo are restored from 5.27 alone. The kindness is from 7.3 alone and closes the line as the limit on the contempt.

support.quote: To look down from above on countless herds and countless rites, on every kind of voyage in storms and in calms
support.follows: The exercise is to look down from above on the herds, rites and voyages of human life.
gives: I look at human affairs as if from high above

support.quote: if you were suddenly lifted high into the air and looked down on human affairs and their many turns, you will despise them
support.follows: Lifted high into the air and looking down on human affairs, I would despise them.
gives: I look at human affairs as if from high above

support.quote: Among these things, then, one must stand kindly and without snorting at them, and yet keep in view that each person is worth just as much as the things they have taken seriously are worth.
support.follows: I must stand among these things kindly and without contempt, and remember that people are worth what they take seriously.
gives: I stand kindly, without sneering at them

support.quote: The things highly prized in life are empty and rotten and small, little dogs biting one another, quarrelsome children laughing and then at once crying.
support.follows: What is highly prized in life is empty, rotten and small, like puppies biting or children quarrelling.
gives: The things people prize are empty and small
little dogs biting one another

support.quote: The empty seriousness of a procession, plays on a stage, flocks, herds, spear fights, a little bone thrown to little dogs
support.follows: A procession’s empty seriousness, plays and spear fights are listed beside a little bone thrown to little dogs.
gives: The things people prize are empty and small

support.quote: you will see the same things: how alike in kind, how short-lived
support.follows: However often I look from above, I see the same things, all alike and all short-lived.
gives: how alike they are and how short-lived

support.quote: neither being remembered is of any account, nor reputation, nor anything else at all
support.follows: Being remembered is worth nothing, and neither is reputation or anything else.
gives: being remembered is of no account

support.quote: the name is a noise and an echo
support.follows: A name left behind is only a noise and an echo.
gives: A name is a noise and an echo

support.quote: how many will very quickly forget it
support.follows: Many of those who know my name will very quickly forget it.
gives: many will very quickly forget mine

claims.t: What I fear is not that I shall some day stop living but that I may never begin to live according to nature. Only one thing troubles me, that I might do what the make-up of a human being does not want, or do it in a way or at a time it does not want.
claims.shared: 12.1 states the fear inside an ‘if’, and the line adopts it as a first-person stance. The wrong way and the wrong time are restored from 7.16 alone. The earlier gloss ‘living against nature’ is dropped as our wording, not his.

support.quote: what you fear is not some day ceasing to live but rather never beginning to live according to nature
support.follows: The thing to fear is not that life will stop one day, but never beginning to live according to nature.
gives: What I fear is not that I shall some day stop living but that I may never begin to live according to nature
Only one thing troubles me

support.quote: Only one thing troubles me: that I myself might do something that the constitution of a human being does not want, or in a way it does not want, or that it does not want now.
support.follows: One thing alone troubles Marcus: doing what a human being’s make-up does not want, or doing it in the wrong way or at the wrong time.
gives: Only one thing troubles me
that I might do what the make-up of a human being does not want
or do it in a way or at a time it does not want

single.label: Neither good nor bad
single.t: Death and life, good repute and ill repute, pain and pleasure, wealth and poverty all happen alike to good people and to bad. They are neither fine nor shameful, so I judge them neither good nor bad.
single.quote: Now death and life, good repute and ill repute, pain and pleasure, wealth and poverty, all these happen alike to the good and to the bad among human beings, and they are neither fine nor shameful. So they are neither good nor bad.
single.why: Single source, 2.8. The full list is restored. The verdict is strict indifference, which is weaker than the contempt of other passages and is not merged with it.
single.follows: What happens alike to good and bad people is neither honourable nor shameful, so death and life are neither good nor bad.

single.label: Those who stumble
single.t: It is proper to a human being to love even those who stumble. That love comes if it strikes me all at once that they are my kin, that they go wrong through ignorance and against their will, and that in a little while both of us will be dead.
single.quote: It is proper to a human being to love even those who stumble. This happens if it strikes you at the same moment that they are your kin, that they go wrong through ignorance and against their will, that in a little while both of you will be dead
single.why: Single source, 7.16. ‘All at once’ corrects the earlier ‘at the moment they stumble’. The supplied quote stops before the ground Marcus puts above all, which is kept in the margin.
single.follows: I can love those who go wrong if I recall at that moment that they are kin, that they err unwillingly, and that we shall both soon be dead.

single.label: Those who complained
single.t: At each thing that happens, I keep before my eyes the people to whom the same thing happened, who were vexed, found it strange and complained. Where are they now? Nowhere. Do I want to be like them?
single.quote: At each thing that happens, to keep before one’s eyes the people to whom the same things happened, and who then were vexed, found it strange, complained. So where are they now? Nowhere. Well then, do you too want to be like them?
single.why: Single source, 7.31. The closing question stays a question, as he framed it, and is not turned into a vow.
single.follows: When something happens I should picture those who complained of the same thing, who are now nowhere, and not wish to be like them.

single.label: Coming back to life
single.t: I can come back to life by seeing things again as I used to see them.
single.quote: You can come back to life. See things again as you used to see them: for in this lies the coming back to life.
single.why: Single source, 7.3. ‘Can’ is kept as a possibility, not a duty.
single.follows: Coming back to life is possible, and it consists in seeing things again as I used to see them.

single.label: Clinging to life
single.t: I ask what I am looking for. To breathe, to have sensation, to have impulse, to grow and then to stop, to use my voice, to think? Which of these seems worth longing for? If each of them is easy to despise, I go on to the last thing, following reason and god. To value breathing, sensing and the rest, and to be vexed that death will deprive me of them, conflicts with following reason and god.
single.quote: What are you looking for? To breathe? Or to have sensation? To have impulse? To grow? And then to stop? To use your voice? To think? Which of these seems to you worth longing for? But if each of them is easy to despise, go on to the last thing, following reason and god. But to value these things, to be vexed that by being dead a person will be deprived of them, conflicts with that.
single.why: Single source, 12.24. Parentheses removed. The despising stays conditional on ‘if’. Thinking is on the list of functions, while following reason is the goal.
single.follows: If breathing, sensing, speaking and thinking are each easy to despise, being vexed that death takes them conflicts with following reason and god.

single.label: With gods or without
single.t: If gods exist, going away from among human beings is nothing to fear, for they would not throw me into anything bad. If they do not exist, or do not care about human affairs, what is it to me to live in a universe empty of gods or empty of providence?
single.quote: if gods exist, it is nothing to fear, for they would not throw you into anything bad. And if either they do not exist or they do not care about human affairs, what is it to me to live in a universe empty of gods or empty of providence?
single.why: Single source, 2.8. The second branch stays a question, where the earlier line had asserted ‘worth nothing’. Marcus goes on to affirm the gods, which is noted in the margin.
single.follows: Leaving life is nothing to fear if gods exist; and if they do not, or do not care, there is nothing in such a universe to stay for.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. In modern editions 9.29 is 9.30–31, 7.31 is 7.56–59, 5.27 is 5.33, 2.8 is 2.11, 7.16 is 7.19–22, 12.15 is 12.19–21, 12.18 is 12.24, 4.21 is 4.25–26, 3.10 is 3.9–10, 8.4 is 8.4–5, 2.15 is 2.17, 7.3 is 7.2b–3, 6.21 is 6.22–23, 1.16 is 2.2, 5.10 is the second half of 5.10, 12.19 is 12.25–26 and 12.24 is 12.31; 12.1 is the same.
The existing opening stands verbatim at 130 characters. Each phrase has two passages behind it. The ‘so’ follows 4.21, which moves from the shortness of life to using the present with justice.
articles.limit: The article joins notes Marcus wrote separately, so the links between brevity, justice and cheerful waiting are editorial. The theology is left unsettled: providence in 12.1, chance or providence in 12.18, extinguishing or a move elsewhere in 5.27, and dissolution only in 2.15. Cheerful waiting rests on 2.15 and 5.27 alone, while 5.10 gives patience and consolation. In c6 the fear of 12.1 is conditional in the source, and ‘only one thing’ comes from 7.16 alone. Contempt is aimed at flesh, breath, fame and prized things, never at people or at the ruling part. Nothing here recommends hastening death or withdrawing from duty.

statement.t: Before long I shall be no one and nowhere, so I live the present justly, as one already at the end, and wait for death cheerfully.

parts.words: Before long I shall be no one and nowhere
so I live the present justly
as one already at the end
wait for death cheerfully

statement.kind: A ground, the conduct that answers it, and the stance towards the end
statement.form: The existing opening stands verbatim at 130 characters. Each phrase has two passages behind it. The ‘so’ follows 4.21, which moves from the shortness of life to using the present with justice.

articles.title: Coming back to my principles and keeping them ready

claims.t: Philosophy wants only what my nature wants. The good life lies in very few things, and I find it in doing what human nature asks. The work of philosophy is simple and modest. I make no show of obeying reason, I let go of reputation, and I do not look around to see whether anyone will know.
claims.shared: Adds where the good life is found and the modesty of the work. What 8.1 lets go is the reputation, not the practice. The godlike man recognised by no one (7.38) and the rest found in reason (5.9) are kept in the margin.

support.quote: philosophy wants only what your nature wants
support.follows: Philosophy asks for nothing beyond what my own nature asks for.
gives: Philosophy wants only what my nature wants

support.quote: living happily lies in very few things
support.follows: Very few things are needed for living happily.
gives: The good life lies in very few things

support.quote: nowhere found the good life: not in syllogisms, not in wealth, not in reputation, not in enjoyment, nowhere. Where is it, then? In doing what human nature asks for.
support.follows: The good life is not in argument, wealth, reputation or enjoyment; it is in doing what human nature asks for.
gives: The good life lies in very few things
I find it in doing what human nature asks

support.quote: Do what nature now demands.
support.follows: The thing to do is what nature demands at this moment.
gives: I find it in doing what human nature asks

support.quote: The work of philosophy is simple and modest
support.follows: What philosophy has to do is simple and modest.
gives: The work of philosophy is simple and modest

support.quote: it is very possible to become a godlike man and to be recognised by no one
support.follows: A man can become godlike without anyone recognising it.
support.note: A man can become godlike without anyone recognising it.

support.quote: Set out, if it is given to you, and do not look around to see whether anyone will know.
support.follows: I should start if I am given the chance, and not look around to see whether anyone will know of it.
gives: I do not look around to see whether anyone will know

support.quote: For in this way you will make no show of obeying reason, but will find rest in it.
support.follows: Coming to philosophy in the right way, I shall not display my obedience to reason; I shall rest in it.
gives: I make no show of obeying reason

support.quote: let go of what reputation you will have
support.follows: I should let go of the question of what reputation I shall have.
gives: I let go of reputation

claims.t: No other situation in life is so suited to philosophy as the one I am now in. The things I would run from are material for philosophy, exercises for a reason that has seen the things in life accurately. I stay until I have made them my own, as a strong stomach makes everything its own, as a bright fire makes flame and light out of whatever is thrown into it.
claims.shared: Narrowed. 8.1’s remark that the situation fights against a philosopher’s reputation concerns reputation, not practice, so it moves to the margin and is not set against 11.6. Neither passage names the situation or the things. Linking them is our reading. The stomach and fire images are 10.32’s alone.

support.quote: winning the reputation of a philosopher is no longer easy for you; and your situation fights against it too
support.follows: Being known as a philosopher is no longer easy for Marcus, and his situation works against it as well.
support.note: Being known as a philosopher is no longer easy for Marcus, and his situation works against it as well.

support.quote: there is no other situation in life so suited to philosophy as this one in which you now happen to be
support.follows: No situation in life is better suited to philosophy than the one I happen to be in now.
gives: No other situation in life is so suited to philosophy as the one I am now in
material for philosophy

support.quote: What material, what a subject, you are running away from! For what are all these things but exercises for a reason that has seen the things in life accurately and as a student of nature?
support.follows: What I am running away from is material: exercises for a reason that has looked exactly at the things in life.
gives: The things I would run from
material for philosophy
exercises for a reason that has seen the things in life accurately

support.quote: Stay, then, until you have made these things too your own, as a strong stomach makes everything its own, as a bright fire makes flame and light out of whatever you throw into it.
support.follows: I should stay until I have made these things my own, as a strong stomach does with food and a bright fire with whatever is thrown into it.
gives: I stay until I have made them my own
as a strong stomach makes everything its own
as a bright fire makes flame and light out of whatever is thrown into it

claims.t: Being good is my craft, and I do it well from principles that my impulses and actions come from. I keep them always at hand, as doctors keep their instruments and blades for emergencies. I use them like the all-in fighter, not the gladiator: the gladiator puts his sword down and picks it up, but the fighter always has his hand and needs only to clench it. One thought I keep to hand is this: when I have done something as a social being, I have been benefited.
claims.shared: 11.4 puts the need for theory as a question, so the line says ‘from principles’ without ‘only’. The doctor image is 3.14’s and the fighter image is 12.6’s. Both make the point of readiness, not combativeness. The social saying is 11.4’s alone.

support.quote: What is your craft? To be good. And how does that come about well, except from points of theory
support.follows: My craft is to be good, and it is done well only from points of theory.
gives: Being good is my craft
I do it well from principles

support.quote: How, then, will you do these things? If you have principles from which your impulses and actions come.
support.follows: I shall do what is asked of me if I have principles from which my impulses and actions come.
gives: I do it well from principles
that my impulses and actions come from

support.quote: As doctors always have their instruments and blades at hand for emergency treatments, so have your principles ready
support.follows: I should have my principles ready in the way doctors always keep their instruments at hand for emergencies.
gives: I keep them always at hand
as doctors keep their instruments and blades for emergencies

support.quote: in the use of principles one must be like the all-in fighter, not the gladiator. For the gladiator puts down the sword he uses and picks it up; but the other always has his hand, and needs only to clench it.
support.follows: Principles should be used like a fighter’s own hand, which is always there, and not like a sword that is put down and picked up.
gives: I keep them always at hand
like the all-in fighter, not the gladiator
the gladiator puts his sword down and picks it up, but the fighter always has his hand and needs only to clench it

support.quote: I have done something as a social being: then I have been benefited. See that this always comes to hand, and never stop.
support.follows: The thought that acting as a social being is itself my benefit should always be at hand.
gives: One thought I keep to hand is this
when I have done something as a social being, I have been benefited

claims.t: Whatever comes up in my life, I look at it bare, whole and taken apart. I see what it is in its substance, what it is put together from and what it will be broken up into. I ask how long it lasts and what it is worth to the whole and to the human being. Where a thing gives the impression of being very trustworthy, I strip off the story it prides itself on and see its cheapness plainly. I train myself to watch how all things change into one another. Nothing so produces greatness of mind as this testing and this watching.
claims.shared: Text unchanged. The anchor is split so that 12.6b supports only looking at a thing bare, while ‘whole and taken apart’ rests on 3.11a alone. The stripping is confined to things that impress as trustworthy, as 6.11 frames it, and sits beside 3.11’s question of worth, so no general contempt follows. Greatness of mind is promised for two different exercises, testing (3.11) and watching change (10.11), and both are named.

support.quote: always to make a definition or outline of the thing that comes up in an impression, so as to see it as it is in its substance, bare, whole and entire, and taken apart, and to say to oneself its own name and the names of the things from which it was put together and into which it will be broken up
support.follows: I should define each thing that comes up, see it bare and in its parts, and name what it was made from and what it will break up into.
gives: Whatever comes up in my life
I look at it bare
whole and taken apart
what it is in its substance
what it is put together from
what it will be broken up into

support.quote: the recognition, in each case, of what the thing is in its substance, what place it has in the universe, how long it is in its nature to last, what it is put together from
support.follows: Marcus asks when he will enjoy recognising, case by case, what a thing is, how long it lasts and what it is made of.
gives: what it is in its substance
what it is put together from
how long it lasts

support.quote: so one must do through the whole of life, and where things give the impression of being very trustworthy, strip them bare, see their cheapness plainly, and strip off the story on which they pride themselves
support.follows: All through life, where things look very trustworthy, I should strip them bare, see how cheap they are and take away their story.
gives: Whatever comes up in my life
Where a thing gives the impression of being very trustworthy, I strip off the story it prides itself on and see its cheapness plainly

support.quote: To look at what is causal, bare of its husks.
support.follows: One thing to keep in mind is to look at what is causal with its husks taken off.
gives: I look at it bare

support.quote: How all things change into one another: get yourself a method for contemplating it, attend to it constantly, and train yourself in this field. For nothing so produces greatness of mind.
support.follows: I should get a method for contemplating how all things change into one another and train in it; nothing does more for greatness of mind.
gives: I train myself to watch how all things change into one another
Nothing so produces greatness of mind
this testing and this watching

support.quote: nothing so produces greatness of mind as being able to test methodically and truly each of the things that come up in life
support.follows: Nothing makes the mind greater than being able to test, by method and truly, each thing that comes up in life.
gives: Whatever comes up in my life
Nothing so produces greatness of mind
this testing and this watching

support.quote: what it is worth to the whole, and what to the human being
support.follows: Of each thing I should ask what it is worth to the whole and what it is worth to a human being.
gives: what it is worth to the whole and to the human being

claims.t: When acting from right principles does not come to me time after time, I do not give up. Knocked aside, I come back, glad if most of what I do is more in keeping with a human being. I can no longer have lived my whole life as a philosopher, and I am content to live the rest of it as my nature wants. Having given up hope of being a logician and a student of nature, I still hold to being free, modest, social and obedient to god. I do not hope for Plato’s republic, and I am content if the smallest thing goes forward.
claims.shared: Adds the measures of enough: ‘most’ and not perfection (5.9), the rest of life (8.1), the virtues still open (7.38), the smallest advance (9.28). The concession about logic and the study of nature is 7.38’s alone and does not dismiss either.

support.quote: Do not be disgusted, do not give up, do not lose patience, if doing each thing from right principles does not come to you time after time
support.follows: If I do not manage to act from right principles every time, that is no reason for disgust, for giving up or for impatience.
gives: When acting from right principles does not come to me time after time
I do not give up

support.quote: you can no longer have lived your whole life, or at least your life since youth, as a philosopher, but to many others, and to you yourself, it has become plain that you are far from philosophy
support.follows: Marcus can no longer have lived his whole life as a philosopher, and he and many others can see that he is far from philosophy.
gives: I can no longer have lived my whole life as a philosopher

support.quote: because you have given up hope of being a logician and a student of nature, do not for that reason give up on being free, modest, social and obedient to god
support.follows: Having lost hope of being a logician or a student of nature is no reason to give up on being free, modest, social and obedient to god.
gives: I do not give up
Having given up hope of being a logician and a student of nature
I still hold to being free, modest, social and obedient to god

support.quote: when you have been knocked aside, come back again, and be glad if most of what you do is more in keeping with a human being
support.follows: Knocked aside, I should come back, and be glad if most of what I do is more fitting for a human being.
gives: Knocked aside, I come back
glad if most of what I do is more in keeping with a human being

support.quote: be content if you live at least the rest of your life, however much it may be, as your nature wants
support.follows: It is enough to live what is left of my life, however much that is, as my nature wants.
gives: I am content to live the rest of it as my nature wants

support.quote: Do not hope for Plato’s republic, but be content if the smallest thing goes forward
support.follows: I should not hope for a perfect state, and should be content if the smallest thing moves forward.
gives: I do not hope for Plato’s republic
I am content if the smallest thing goes forward

single.label: What the principles say
single.t: My principles are about what is good and what is bad: nothing is good for a human being that does not make them just, self-controlled, brave and free, and nothing is bad that does not make them the opposite.
single.quote: What principles? Those about good things and bad: that nothing is a good thing for a human being which does not make them just, self-controlled, brave, free, and nothing is a bad thing which does not make them the opposite of these.
single.why: Single source, quote 8.1g. Only 8.1 states the content of the principles, so it stands alone. Original wording kept.
single.follows: The principles are about good and bad: only what makes a person just, self-controlled, brave and free is good, and only what does the opposite is bad.

single.label: As to a remedy
single.t: I love what I come back to. I do not come back to philosophy as to a schoolboy’s minder, but as people with sore eyes go to the little sponge and the egg, as another goes to a poultice, as to a medicinal wash.
single.quote: love what you are coming back to. And do not come back to philosophy as to a schoolboy’s minder, but as people with sore eyes go to the little sponge and the egg, as another goes to a poultice, as to a medicinal wash.
single.why: Single source, quote 5.9c. Restores the source’s own images, including the wash, and drops the added gloss on the minder. The medical image here is about relief, not readiness.
single.follows: I should love what I return to, and return to philosophy as a sick person goes to a remedy, not as a boy to the slave who keeps him in order.

single.label: How principles fade
single.t: Farce, war, panic, numbness, slavery. Day by day my sacred principles are wiped out, all those I picture without study of nature and let go by.
single.quote: Farce, war, panic, numbness, slavery: day by day those sacred principles of yours will be wiped out, all those that you picture without study of nature and let go by.
single.why: Single source, quote 10.9b. Kept as a warning, not a vow. The principles at risk are only those held without study of nature.
single.follows: After naming farce, war, panic, numbness and slavery, Marcus says that principles pictured without study of nature will be wiped out day by day.

single.label: Hard, not impossible
single.t: If something is hard for me to carry out, I do not judge it impossible for a human being. If it is possible for a human being and proper to them, I count it within my own reach too.
single.quote: If something is hard for you yourself to carry out, do not judge it impossible for a human being; but if something is possible for a human being and proper to them, consider it within your own reach too.
single.why: Single source, quote 6.18a. Original wording kept. The inference depends on ‘and proper’, so it does not cover everything merely possible.
single.follows: What is hard for me is not for that reason impossible for a human being, and what a human being can properly do is within my reach too.

single.label: If I cannot be sure
single.t: Even to the Stoics, things seem hard to grasp. Every assent of mine can shift, for where is the person who does not shift? So I pass on to the objects themselves and see how short-lived they are, and how cheap.
single.quote: to the Stoics themselves, at least, they seem hard to grasp. And every assent of ours can shift: for where is the person who does not shift? Pass on, then, to the objects themselves: how short-lived they are, how cheap
single.why: Single source, quote 5.9f. Drops the added ‘truth of things’. This part of 5.9 breaks off before its counter-turn, so the line is a step in a doubt and not a final verdict on the world.
single.follows: The Stoics themselves find things hard to grasp and no one’s assent is fixed; Marcus then turns to the objects and finds them short-lived and cheap.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. In modern editions 5.9 is 5.9 with the first part of 5.10, 12.6 is 12.7 to 12.9, 6.11 is 6.13, 9.28 is 9.29, 10.32 is 10.31, 7.38 is 7.67, 11.4 is 11.4 and 11.5, 11.6 is 11.7, 3.14 is 3.13 and 6.18 is 6.19; 8.1, 10.9, 3.11 and 10.11 keep their numbers.
Keeps the warranted original and splits it into two sentences for reading aloud. Every phrase rests on two different passages.
articles.limit: The passages do not settle how much theory or study of nature the principles need: 10.9, 11.4, 3.14 and 10.32 tie them to it, while 7.38 and 8.1 concede a limit. Only 8.1 states what the principles are. That the present situation of 11.6 and the things of 10.32 are the same material is our reading, since neither passage names them. The stripping of things in 6.11 and 5.9 does not amount to contempt for the world, since 3.11 also asks what each thing is worth and 5.9 breaks off. 5.12 and 10.38 remain aside because they do not speak of keeping or returning to principles.

aside.5.12: A test of what most people call good, made with a line of comedy. Its list of true goods is close to 8.1’s, but its subject is which things are good, not how I keep to philosophy or come back to it.
aside.10.38: Says that what moves a person is hidden inside and that the body is its tool. Nothing in it is about principles, their use or falling short; it belongs with the passages on the ruling part and the body.

statement.t: When I fall short of philosophy I do not give up. I do what nature asks, keep my principles at hand and look at each thing stripped bare.

parts.words: When I fall short of philosophy
I do not give up
I do what nature asks
keep my principles at hand
look at each thing stripped bare

statement.kind: A rule for failure and the three things I come back to
statement.form: Keeps the warranted original and splits it into two sentences for reading aloud. Every phrase rests on two different passages.

articles.title: The retreat within

claims.t: I do not need a country place, a seashore or a mountain. Where I am is just like them, and at any hour I am free to retreat into myself. No retreat is quieter than my own soul. Ease in my soul is nothing other than good order. My ruling part is content with itself when it acts justly, and by that very fact it has calm.
claims.shared: “Ease in my soul” names the place so the definition is clear when heard. “At any hour” and “free” are 4.3 only, and 7.20a supports only the turn inward. The definition of ease is 4.3 only. The tie between calm and just action is 7.20 only. “Free to” keeps this a permission, not a duty.

support.quote: People look for retreats for themselves: country places, seashores, mountains. You too are in the habit of longing very much for such things. But all of this is the mark of someone with no training at all, when you are free, at whatever hour you wish, to retreat into yourself.
support.follows: Longing for a retreat in the country, by the sea or in the mountains is untrained, since I can retreat into myself whenever I wish.
gives: I do not need a country place, a seashore or a mountain
at any hour I am free
to retreat into myself

support.quote: Let it always be clear that the country place over there is just like this, and how everything here is the same as on the top of the mountain or on the seashore or wherever you like.
support.follows: The place where I am is no different from a country place, a mountain top or a seashore.
gives: I do not need a country place, a seashore or a mountain
Where I am is just like them

support.quote: Draw in upon yourself.
support.follows: Marcus tells himself to draw in upon himself.
gives: to retreat into myself

support.quote: nowhere that a person retreats to is quieter or freer from business than their own soul
support.follows: No place a person can retreat to is quieter or freer from business than their own soul.
gives: No retreat is quieter than my own soul
Ease in my soul is nothing other than good order

support.quote: they are at once in complete ease; and by ease I mean nothing other than good order
support.follows: Whoever has the right things within and looks into them is at once at ease; by ease Marcus means nothing but good order.
gives: Ease in my soul is nothing other than good order

support.quote: It is the nature of the rational ruling part to be content with itself when it acts justly and by that very fact has calm.
support.follows: When the rational ruling part acts justly, it is content with itself and, by that very fact, calm.
gives: My ruling part is content with itself when it acts justly, and by that very fact it has calm

claims.t: I do not wear away what is left of my life on thoughts about other people, unless those thoughts serve the common benefit. I do not guess at what a neighbour is doing, saying or thinking. I look only at what I am doing and keep watch over what is within me. The praise of the many is a clapping of tongues, and I set no store by it.
claims.shared: The common-benefit exception is 3.4 only and is attached to the thoughts it qualifies. The clapping image is 6.15 only. In 3.4c the praise set aside comes from people who do not live in agreement with nature, so the margin keeps the good opinion that 3.4 still values.

support.quote: Do not wear away what is left of your life in impressions about other people, when you are not referring them to something of common benefit
support.follows: I should not use up what is left of my life on impressions of other people, unless they serve some common benefit.
gives: I do not wear away what is left of my life on thoughts about other people
unless those thoughts serve the common benefit

support.quote: forming impressions of what so-and-so is doing, and for what purpose, and what they are saying, and what they have in mind, and what they are contriving, and all such things as make you wander away from watching over your own ruling part
support.follows: Picturing what others do, say, mean and plot draws me away from watching over my own ruling part.
gives: I do not guess at what a neighbour is doing, saying or thinking
keep watch over what is within me

support.quote: looks by guesswork for what is in the souls of their neighbours, but does not notice that it is enough to keep only to the guardian spirit within them and to serve it truly
support.follows: Guessing at what is in other people’s souls is wretched; it is enough to keep to the guardian spirit within me and serve it.
gives: I do not guess at what a neighbour is doing, saying or thinking
keep watch over what is within me

support.quote: How much leisure a person gains who does not look at what their neighbour said or did or thought, but only at what they themselves are doing
support.follows: Whoever looks only at what they are doing, not at what a neighbour said, did or thought, gains much leisure.
gives: I do not guess at what a neighbour is doing, saying or thinking
I look only at what I am doing

support.quote: So he sets no store either by praise that comes from such people, who are not even pleased with themselves.
support.follows: The good man sets no store by praise from people who do not live by nature and are not even pleased with themselves.
gives: I set no store by it

support.quote: Being clapped? No. Then not being clapped by tongues either; for the praises of the many are a clapping of tongues. So you have let petty fame go as well.
support.follows: Applause has no value, and the praise of the many is only applause by tongues, so petty fame has no value either.
gives: The praise of the many is a clapping of tongues
I set no store by it

claims.t: The things I chase or flee in turmoil do not come to me. They stand outside, unmoving, and in a way I go to them. My turmoil comes only from my own judgment about them. When I let that judgment be quiet, they stay still, and I am seen neither chasing nor fleeing.
claims.shared: The scope stays with the things that cause turmoil and keeps the hedge “in a way” from 11.10. This is not a ban on all pursuit. The line judges how events disturb me and does not deny that they occur.

support.quote: The things whose pursuit and avoidance throw you into turmoil do not come to you, but in a way you yourself go to them.
support.follows: The things I chase or flee do not come to me; in a way I go to them.
gives: The things I chase or flee in turmoil do not come to me
They stand outside, unmoving
in a way I go to them

support.quote: things do not touch the soul but stand outside it, unmoving, and disturbances come only from the judgment within
support.follows: Things stay outside the soul and do not touch it; every disturbance comes from the judgment within.
gives: They stand outside, unmoving
My turmoil comes only from my own judgment about them

support.quote: At least let your judgment about them be quiet, and they will stay still, and you will be seen neither pursuing nor avoiding.
support.follows: If my judgment about these things is quiet, they stay where they are, and I neither pursue nor avoid them.
gives: My turmoil comes only from my own judgment about them
When I let that judgment be quiet, they stay still
I am seen neither chasing nor fleeing

claims.t: Of body, breath and mind, only my mind is properly mine. The other two are mine so far as I must take care of them. I keep my mind apart from body and breath, and from whatever they attach to me unchosen. Once my mind has taken itself back and knows its own power, it does not mix with the breath, smooth or rough. I ask whether my ruling part can be melted into the flesh, so that it turns as the flesh turns.
claims.shared: The threefold division and the care owed to body and breath are 12.2 only. The image of melting into the flesh is a question in 10.24, so it stays a question and does not become a vow. In 12.2 the separation is the condition of a promise. Here it is stated as a practice.

support.quote: There are three things of which you are made up: a little body, a little breath, mind. Of these the other two are yours so far as you must take care of them, but only the third is properly yours.
support.follows: Of body, breath and mind, only the mind is properly mine; body and breath are mine to care for.
gives: Of body, breath and mind, only my mind is properly mine
The other two are mine so far as I must take care of them

support.quote: So if you separate from yourself, that is, from your thought, all that others do or say, or all that you yourself have done or said, and all that troubles you as something to come, and all that attaches to you, without your choosing it, from the little body that surrounds you or the little breath born with you
support.follows: Marcus tells himself to separate from his thought, among other things, all that comes to him unchosen from his body and breath.
gives: I keep my mind apart from body and breath
from whatever they attach to me unchosen

support.quote: the mind does not mix with the breath, whether that moves smoothly or roughly, once the mind has taken itself back and come to know its own power
support.follows: Once the mind has drawn back and knows its own power, it does not mix with the breath, whether that moves smoothly or roughly.
gives: I keep my mind apart from body and breath
Once my mind has taken itself back and knows its own power, it does not mix with the breath, smooth or rough

support.quote: Can it be melted into the bit of flesh and blended with it, so that it turns as the flesh turns?
support.follows: Marcus asks, with misgiving, whether his ruling part has been melted into the flesh, so that it turns as the flesh turns.
gives: I ask whether my ruling part can be melted into the flesh, so that it turns as the flesh turns

claims.t: I keep to what is present. I practise living only what I am living, that is, the present. I do not think of absent things as already here, and I reckon up the best of what is here. I ask my soul whether it will be content with its present state and take pleasure in all that is present.
claims.shared: 10.1 is an unanswered question to the soul, so the old “I am content” claimed an achievement the source does not. It is restored as a question. “Already here” follows 7.20, which does not say “already mine”.

support.quote: practise living only what you are living, that is, the present
support.follows: Marcus tells himself to practise living only what he is living now, the present.
gives: I keep to what is present
I practise living only what I am living, that is, the present

support.quote: Not to think of absent things as already there, but to reckon up the best of the things that are present
support.follows: I should not treat absent things as already there, but count up the best of what is present.
gives: I keep to what is present
I do not think of absent things as already here
I reckon up the best of what is here

support.quote: But will you be content with your present state and take pleasure in all that is present
support.follows: Marcus asks his soul whether it will ever be content with its present state and take pleasure in all that is present.
gives: I ask my soul whether it will be content with its present state and take pleasure in all that is present

claims.t: I guard against drifting in what I do, as people drift who have no target for their impulses and impressions. I have no need of guessing when I am free to look at what has to be done. When I see it clearly, I go that way with good will and without turning back. I run straight along the line, not looking round and not thrown this way and that.
claims.shared: 2.4 is a warning about people with no target, so the line guards against their drifting and does not vow a target. The lack of a target now clearly belongs to those people, not to me. The runner image is 4.15 only. The case where I do not see clearly is 10.13 only and stays in the margin.

support.quote: But now there is the other kind of drifting to guard against as well. For people play the fool through their actions too: those who are worn out by life and have no target at which to direct every impulse and, in general, every impression.
support.follows: People with no target for their impulses play the fool in what they do, and this drifting has to be guarded against.
gives: I guard against drifting in what I do
as people drift who have no target for their impulses and impressions

support.quote: What need is there of guessing, when you are free to look at what has to be done, and, if you see it clearly, to go that way with good will and without turning back
support.follows: Instead of guessing, I can look at what has to be done and, if I see it clearly, go that way without turning back.
gives: I have no need of guessing when I am free to look at what has to be done
When I see it clearly, I go that way with good will
without turning back

support.quote: not to look round at a dark character, but to run straight along the line, not thrown this way and that
support.follows: I should not look round at a bad character but run straight along my line, not thrown from side to side.
gives: without turning back
I run straight along the line
not looking round
not thrown this way and that

single.label: Renewing the retreat
single.t: I retreat into myself continually and renew myself. I keep short, elementary truths ready, enough to wash away all distress and to send me back without resentment at what I return to.
single.quote: So give yourself this retreat continually, and renew yourself. And let the things be short and elementary which, as soon as they meet you, will be enough to wash away all distress and to send you back without resentment at the things you are returning to.
single.why: Single source, 4.3f: “So give yourself this retreat continually, and renew yourself. And let the things be short and elementary”. It adds that the retreat is repeated, brief and ends in a return. “A few” is dropped because the source does not say it.
single.follows: The retreat should be taken continually, with a few short truths that wash away distress and send me back without resentment.

single.label: A test for my thoughts
single.t: I accustom myself to form only thoughts that I could name at once and frankly if someone suddenly asked, “What are you thinking now?”
single.quote: And you must accustom yourself to form only those impressions about which, if someone suddenly asked, “What are you thinking now?”, you would answer at once and frankly, “This, and this”
single.why: Single source, 3.4d: “you must accustom yourself to form only those impressions about which, if someone suddenly asked”. The question is kept in the speaker’s framing as a test of my own thoughts.
single.follows: I should form only impressions I could name at once and frankly if someone suddenly asked what I was thinking.

single.label: Three questions
single.t: I ask what my ruling part is to me, what kind of thing I am making it now, and what I am using it for now.
single.quote: What is my ruling part to me, and what kind of thing am I making it now, and what am I using it for now?
single.why: Single source, 10.24c: “What is my ruling part to me, and what kind of thing am I making it now, and what am I using it for now?” The gloss “my mind” is removed because 10.24 goes on to ask whether the ruling part can be empty of mind.
single.follows: Marcus asks himself what his ruling part is to him, what he is making of it now and what he is using it for.

single.label: Serving what is within
single.t: I serve the guardian spirit within me by keeping it clean of passion, of aimlessness, and of discontent with what comes from the gods and from people.
single.quote: To serve it is to keep it clean of passion and aimlessness and discontent with what comes from the gods and from people.
single.why: Single source, 2.11b: “To serve it is to keep it clean of passion and aimlessness and discontent with what comes from the gods and from people.” The guardian spirit is 2.11’s own term and is not merged with mind or ruling part. The pilot wording stands.
single.follows: Serving the guardian spirit within means keeping it free of passion, aimlessness and discontent with what gods and people send.

single.label: Valuing other things
single.t: If I go on valuing many things besides my own mind, I will be neither free nor sufficient to myself nor without passion. Then I am bound to envy, to suspect those who can take those things away, and to plot against those who have them. Respect for my own mind, and the value I set on it, makes me pleasing to myself.
single.quote: Will you not stop valuing many other things as well? Then you will be neither free nor sufficient to yourself nor without passion. For you are bound to envy, to be jealous, to look with suspicion on those who can take those things away, to plot against those who have what you value. In short, anyone who is in need of any of those things is bound to be in confusion, and, what is more, to find much fault even with the gods. But respect for your own mind, and the value you set on it, will make you pleasing to yourself
single.why: Single source, 6.15b: “Then you will be neither free nor sufficient to yourself nor without passion.” It is a warning stated as a consequence, not a vow. “Besides my own mind” is our gloss on the source’s “many other things”, taken from its closing contrast.
single.follows: Valuing many outside things leaves me unfree, envious and confused; respect for my own mind makes me pleasing to myself.

single.label: Not prizing what I have too much
single.t: Glad as I am of what is present, I guard against prizing it so much that I would be troubled if it were ever absent.
single.quote: be on your guard that through being so glad of them you do not accustom yourself to prize them so much that, if ever they are not present, you will be troubled.
single.why: Single source, 7.20d: “be on your guard that through being so glad of them you do not accustom yourself to prize them so much”. It is the counterweight to c5 and keeps the gladness.
single.follows: Being glad of what I have, I should not get used to prizing it so much that losing it would trouble me.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. In modern editions 2.11 is 2.12–13, 7.20 is 7.27–28, 10.24 is 10.23–24, 6.15 is 6.16, 2.4 is 2.7, 10.13 is 10.12, 11.10 is 11.11, 4.15 is 4.18 and 12.2 is 12.2–3; 4.3, 3.4 and 10.1 are the same.

Every phrase rests on two passages. “At any hour” is in 4.3 only, so it moves to c1. “What is within me” replaces “my own mind” because 3.4 speaks of the ruling part and 2.11 of the guardian spirit, and the sources do not equate them.
articles.limit: This article describes a brief, repeatable return to oneself that sends me back to people and to work. It is not permanent solitude, a ban on all thought about others, or contempt for the body or for present goods. “Soul”, “mind”, “ruling part” and “guardian spirit” are each source’s own terms, and the passages do not equate them. Several sources are conditional or interrogative (4.3, 10.1, 12.2), so the lines state practices and questions, not attainments. In c4 the keeping apart is a condition in 12.2, and what 12.2 separates from the mind is what body and breath attach unchosen. In c2 the praise set aside in 3.4 is that of people who do not live in agreement with nature, and “the many” comes from 6.15. Rendering the sources in the first person, treating “impressions” as thoughts, and glossing the “many other things” of 6.15 as things besides my own mind are our editorial reading and not primary evidence.

statement.t: I can retreat into myself wherever I am, and I watch what is within me, not what others say or do.

parts.words: I can retreat into myself
wherever I am
I watch what is within me
not what others say or do

statement.kind: A place, how I keep to it, and the way back
statement.form: Every phrase rests on two passages. “At any hour” is in 4.3 only, so it moves to c1. “What is within me” replaces “my own mind” because 3.4 speaks of the ruling part and 2.11 of the guardian spirit, and the sources do not equate them.

empty.doubt: No passage in this section asks what still holds if I cannot retreat into myself, or if my mind is not my own.

articles.title: Whether anything is better than virtue

claims.t: I find nothing in human life better than justice, truth, self-control and courage. My own good lies in a just disposition and just action, and my desire stops there. I hold everything else smaller and cheaper, and I live neither pursuing nor fleeing.
claims.shared: Names the four virtues and adds 5.28’s limit on desire. “Smaller and cheaper” is 3.7 alone. The joint anchors are the good that is my own (3.7 with 5.28) and living without fleeing (3.8 with 3.13). “Pursuing” is 3.8’s word, where 3.13 says “waiting for nothing”. The finding stays a judgement reached under 3.7’s conditional.

support.quote: But if nothing appears better than the spirit itself that is seated in you
support.follows: If nothing appears better than the spirit seated within me, that spirit is the best thing I have.
gives: I find nothing in human life better than justice, truth, self-control and courage

support.quote: whoever has preferred their own mind and spirit, and the rites of its virtue
support.follows: Whoever has preferred their own mind and spirit and its virtue does not make a tragedy of things and does not groan.
support.note: Whoever has preferred their own mind and spirit and its virtue does not make a tragedy of things and does not groan.

support.quote: If you find in human life anything better than justice, truth, self-control, courage
support.follows: Justice, truth, self-control and courage are the standard that anything better in human life would have to beat.
gives: I find nothing in human life better than justice, truth, self-control and courage

support.quote: that good which is proper to you and is yours
support.follows: There is a good that belongs to me as my own, and I am to honour it above everything else.
gives: My own good lies in a just disposition and just action, and my desire stops there

support.quote: to have its good in a just disposition and just action, and to have its desire stop there
support.follows: A rational being’s good lies in being just and acting justly, and its desire should go no further than that.
gives: My own good lies in a just disposition and just action, and my desire stops there

support.quote: if you find everything else smaller and cheaper than this, give room to nothing else
support.follows: If everything else looks smaller and cheaper than the spirit within, nothing else should be given room.
gives: I hold everything else smaller and cheaper

support.quote: Greatest of all, they will live neither pursuing nor fleeing.
support.follows: Whoever prefers their own mind and spirit lives without chasing things and without running from them.
gives: I live neither pursuing nor fleeing

support.quote: waiting for nothing and fleeing nothing
support.follows: Living well comes from joining several things, among them waiting for nothing and running from nothing.
gives: I live neither pursuing nor fleeing

claims.t: No one can prevent me from living well, for that power is in my own soul. No one prevents me from doing and saying what is in keeping with the nature of which I am a part. No one can stop me from making sure that each action does its own part. Nothing from outside stands in the way, at least not in the way of my acting justly, with self-control and with good sense.
claims.shared: “At least not” keeps 8.30’s limit: only virtuous action is unhinderable. The soul’s power is from 11.15 alone. The concession that other activity may be blocked is kept in the margin.

support.quote: you will live well. And there is no one who can prevent this.
support.follows: Whoever does the present work by right reason and keeps their spirit pure will live well, and no one can prevent it.
gives: No one can prevent me from living well

support.quote: To live life through in the finest way: this power is in the soul
support.follows: The power to live in the finest way lies in the soul itself.
gives: that power is in my own soul

support.quote: there is no one who prevents you from always doing and saying what is in keeping with the nature of which you are a part
support.follows: No one can stop me from always doing and saying what fits the nature of the whole I am part of.
gives: No one prevents me from doing and saying what is in keeping with the nature of which I am a part

support.quote: No one will prevent you from living according to the reason of your own nature.
support.follows: No one can stop me from living by the reason of my own nature.
gives: No one can prevent me from living well
No one prevents me from doing and saying what is in keeping with the nature of which I am a part

support.quote: And no one at all can prevent you from making sure that it does its own part.
support.follows: No one can stop each of my actions from doing its own part as far as it can.
gives: No one can stop me from making sure that each action does its own part

support.quote: “But something from outside will stand in the way.” Nothing will, at least not in the way of acting justly, with self-control and with good sense.
support.follows: Nothing outside me can stop me from acting justly, with self-control and with good sense.
gives: Nothing from outside stands in the way, at least not in the way of my acting justly, with self-control and with good sense

claims.t: In what I say and do, I do what is necessary and what reason requires of a being made by nature for life among fellow citizens, in the way reason requires it. Most of what I say and do is not necessary. I strip away what is not necessary, impressions as well as actions, and I am less troubled. I run to the short road, the one according to nature, and say and do everything in the soundest way. That purpose frees me from toil, from hanging back, and from all contriving and affectation.
claims.shared: The second sentence now names whose words and acts are meant and what is stripped away. The necessary (4.20) and the short road (4.43) stand side by side and are not equated. The joint anchor is saying and doing. “Short” means sound, not less effort.

support.quote: For most of what we say and do is not necessary, and if a person strips it away they will have more leisure and be less troubled.
support.follows: Most of what we say and do is unnecessary, and stripping it away gives more leisure and less trouble.
gives: In what I say and do
Most of what I say and do is not necessary
I strip away what is not necessary, impressions as well as actions, and I am less troubled

support.quote: Might it not be better to do what is necessary, and whatever the reason of a living being that is civic by nature requires, and in the way it requires?
support.follows: Doing what is necessary, as reason requires of a being made for civic life, may be better than simply doing few things.
gives: I do what is necessary and what reason requires of a being made by nature for life among fellow citizens, in the way reason requires it

support.quote: And one must strip away not only the actions that are not necessary but impressions too
support.follows: Needless impressions should be stripped away as well as needless actions.
gives: I strip away what is not necessary, impressions as well as actions, and I am less troubled

support.quote: Always run to the short road. And the short road is the one according to nature, so that you say and do everything in the soundest way.
support.follows: The short road is the road of nature, and taking it lets me say and do everything in the soundest way.
gives: In what I say and do
I run to the short road, the one according to nature, and say and do everything in the soundest way

support.quote: For a purpose of this kind frees you from toil and from hanging back, and from all contriving and affectation.
support.follows: Keeping to that road frees one from toil, from hanging back, and from contriving and affectation.
gives: That purpose frees me from toil, from hanging back, and from all contriving and affectation

claims.role: Benefit to the rational or the animal in me
claims.t: When something is said to benefit me, I ask whether it benefits me as a rational being or as an animal. If as a rational being, I keep to it. If as an animal, I say so. I take up all that my nature as an animal asks for, unless my nature as a rational animal would be put in a worse state. What is rational is by that very fact also civic, and I let nothing take up a position against the rational and civic good.
claims.shared: Animal nature’s demands are affirmed and only capped, as 10.2 has it. The candour clause is 3.7 alone, and the cap and “by that very fact” are 10.2 alone. The joint point, anchored on “the rational and civic good”, is that the rational and the civic go together.

support.quote: “But the better is what benefits.” If it benefits you as a rational being, keep to that. But if as an animal, say so
support.follows: If something benefits me as a rational being I should keep to it; if only as an animal, I should admit that.
gives: When something is said to benefit me
I ask whether it benefits me as a rational being or as an animal
If as a rational being, I keep to it
If as an animal, I say so

support.quote: Next you must watch what your nature as an animal asks for, and take up all of this, unless your nature as a rational animal is going to be put in a worse state.
support.follows: What my animal nature asks for is to be taken up, unless it would make my rational nature worse.
gives: I take up all that my nature as an animal asks for, unless my nature as a rational animal would be put in a worse state

support.quote: should take up a position against the rational and civic good
support.follows: The good of a rational being is also a civic good, and nothing of another kind may be set against it.
gives: I let nothing take up a position against
the rational and civic good

support.quote: And what is rational is by that very fact also civic.
support.follows: Whatever is rational is, for that very reason, also civic.
gives: What is rational is by that very fact also civic
the rational and civic good

claims.t: I put my life together one action at a time. I judge and act step by step, as along a road. I carry through what lies before me as I would gently count off the letters of a name. I join one good to another so as to leave not even the shortest gap.
claims.shared: Step by step is shared by 5.28 and 6.24. The road is 5.28 alone, the letters 6.24 alone, the gapless joining 12.22 alone and the assembled life 8.30 alone. Each image is kept because it explains the method, and the letters stay a comparison.

support.quote: You must put your life together one action at a time
support.follows: A life is to be built one action at a time.
gives: I put my life together one action at a time

support.quote: if indeed you can also judge and act step by step, as along a road
support.follows: Life goes well for whoever can judge and act step by step, as one goes along a road.
gives: I judge and act step by step
as along a road

support.quote: carry through step by step what lies before you
support.follows: Whatever lies before me is to be carried through step by step.
gives: I judge and act step by step
I carry through what lies before me

support.quote: Will you not gently go on counting off each of the letters?
support.follows: Asked how a name is written, one calmly counts off its letters one by one.
gives: as I would gently count off the letters of a name

support.quote: joining one good to another so as to leave not even the shortest gap
support.follows: Once I do what is just and say what is true, what is left is to enjoy living, linking one good to the next.
gives: I join one good to another so as to leave not even the shortest gap

claims.t: I simply and freely choose the better and hold on to it. Once I tip and turn aside towards anything else, I am pulled about. Praise from the many, offices, wealth and the enjoyment of pleasures seem to fit for a little while, then suddenly take control and carry me off course. I never value as a benefit to myself anything that will one day force me to break faith, to abandon my self-respect, to hate someone, to suspect, to curse, to play a part, or to desire something that needs walls and curtains.
claims.shared: The choice comes first so that “anything else” has a clear referent. The warning about rival goods stays a warning. The joint anchor is narrowed to the compelling: 3.7 says such things take control and 3.8 says they force. Valuing as a benefit and the full list, with its walls and curtains, are 3.8 alone.

support.quote: Once you have tipped and turned aside towards anything else, you will no longer be able, without being pulled about, to honour above all else
support.follows: Once I lean towards anything else, I can no longer honour my own good above all without being pulled about.
gives: Once I tip and turn aside towards anything else, I am pulled about

support.quote: Never value as a benefit to yourself anything that will one day force you to break faith, to abandon your self-respect, to hate someone, to suspect, to curse, to play a part, to desire something that needs walls and curtains.
support.follows: Nothing that will one day force me to break faith, hate, suspect or pretend should count as a benefit to me.
gives: I never value as a benefit to myself
anything that will one day force me
to break faith, to abandon my self-respect, to hate someone, to suspect, to curse, to play a part, or to desire something that needs walls and curtains

support.quote: such as praise from the many, or offices, or wealth, or the enjoyment of pleasures
support.follows: Praise from the many, offices, wealth and pleasures are things of another kind than the rational and civic good.
gives: Praise from the many, offices, wealth and the enjoyment of pleasures

support.quote: All these, even if for a little while they seem to fit, suddenly take control and carry you off course.
support.follows: Such things may seem to fit for a while, but then they suddenly take control and carry one off course.
gives: seem to fit for a little while, then suddenly take control and carry me off course
anything that will one day force me

support.quote: But you, I say, simply and freely choose the better and hold on to it.
support.follows: I should choose the better, simply and freely, and hold on to it.
gives: I simply and freely choose the better and hold on to it

single.label: If I find better
single.t: If I see anything better than justice, truth, self-control, courage and a mind content with its own right action and with what fate allots, I turn to it with my whole soul and enjoy what is found to be best.
single.quote: if, I say, you see anything better than this, turn to it with your whole soul and enjoy what is found to be best
single.why: Single source 3.7, quote 3.7b: “if, I say, you see anything better than this, turn to it with your whole soul and enjoy what is found to be best”. “This” is spelled out from the same passage so the line reads alone. It stays an open conditional test and is not a vow to search.
single.follows: If something better than justice and a mind content with itself is ever seen, one should turn to it wholeheartedly.

single.label: Keeping it pure
single.t: I keep my own spirit standing pure, as if I had to give it back this very moment.
single.quote: keep your own spirit standing pure, as if you had to give it back this very moment
single.why: Single source 3.13, quote 3.13a: “keep your own spirit standing pure, as if you had to give it back this very moment”. “Standing” is restored from the source. Readiness to give the spirit back is not made the article’s common theme.
single.follows: I should keep my spirit pure as though I had to hand it back right now.

single.label: Wiping out a verdict
single.t: Things do not put a judgment about themselves into me. They stay still, and I produce the verdicts about them and write them in myself. It is in my power not to write them, and if one escapes my notice, to wipe it out at once.
single.quote: none of them puts a judgment about itself into us, nor comes to us, but the things stay still, and it is we who produce the verdicts about them and, as it were, write them in ourselves, when it is in our power not to write them, and in our power, even if one of them somehow escapes our notice, to wipe it out at once
single.why: Single source 11.15, quote 11.15b: “none of them puts a judgment about itself into us, nor comes to us, but the things stay still, and it is we who produce the verdicts about them and, as it were, write them in ourselves, when it is in our power not to write them, and in our power, even if one of them somehow escapes our notice, to wipe it out at once”. The semicolon is removed and “stay still” restored. The line concerns my verdict about a thing and does not deny the thing.
single.follows: Things do not judge themselves in me; I write the verdicts, and I can refuse to write them or wipe one out at once.

single.label: When things go against nature
single.t: When things are contrary to nature, I look for what there is for me that is according to my own nature and hurry towards that, even if it brings no reputation.
single.quote: if they are contrary to nature, look for what there is for you that is according to your own nature and hurry towards that, even if it brings no reputation
single.why: Single source 11.15, quote 11.15c: “if they are contrary to nature, look for what there is for you that is according to your own nature and hurry towards that, even if it brings no reputation”. In the source “they” are the indifferent things. The companion case, rejoicing in what accords with nature, is in the margin.
single.follows: When things are contrary to nature, I should seek what accords with my own nature and go for it, even if it brings no fame.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. In modern editions 3.7 is 3.6, 3.8 is 3.7, 3.13 is 3.12, 11.15 is 11.16, 12.22 is 12.29, 2.6 is 2.9, 8.30 is 8.32, 4.20 is 4.24, 4.43 is 4.51, 5.28 is 5.34, 6.53 is 6.58, 6.24 is 6.26; 10.2 and 10.6 are the same.
“I find” keeps 3.7’s open test, which a flat “nothing is better” would close. The freedom claimed covers living by the spirit, not outward success.
