articles.limit: The claim that nothing is better than the spirit and its virtue is a finding under 3.7’s open test, not a closed dogma. What no one can prevent is just, truthful, rational and civic action and judgement, not outward success or events matching my wishes. 8.30 concedes that other activity may be blocked. 3.13’s promise of living well holds only when all its parts are joined, and 11.15 places the power in the soul on condition of indifference to indifferent things. Shortness of life and readiness to depart appear only in 3.8, 3.13 and 11.15, so they are not made common doctrine. The single-source lines speak for their own passages only. In the fused claims, single-witness details such as the road, the letters, the walls and curtains, “smaller and cheaper” and “by that very fact” are anchored to their one passage and are not joint doctrine.

aside.10.6: Its subject is that I am a part of the whole and kin to those of my own kind, and so welcome what the whole allots and do nothing unsocial; Articles 1 and 3 say this, and it does not speak of what is best or of what no one can prevent.

statement.t: I find nothing better than the spirit within me and its virtue, and no one can prevent me from living by it.

parts.words: I find nothing better than the spirit within me and its virtue
no one can prevent me from living by it

statement.kind: What is best, and why it is safe
statement.form: “I find” keeps 3.7’s open test, which a flat “nothing is better” would close. The freedom claimed covers living by the spirit, not outward success.

articles.title: Living with the gods

claims.role: With the gods at every moment
claims.t: On every occasion I experience the power of the gods and show them my own soul. To live with the gods is to show them a soul content with what is allotted and doing all that the spirit wants. Zeus gave me that spirit as protector and leader, a fragment of himself.
claims.shared: The first sentence joins 12.21’s ‘on every occasion’ with 5.21’s ‘constantly shows’. Living with the gods stays a definition, as 5.21 frames it, and is not a boast of achievement. Both conditions, contentment and action, are kept. The fragment image is 5.21 alone.

support.quote: the one who lives with the gods is the one who constantly shows them their own soul, content with what is allotted and doing all that the spirit wants, the spirit that Zeus has given to each person as protector and leader, a fragment of himself
support.follows: To live with the gods is to show them, constantly, a soul content with its lot that does all that the spirit given by Zeus wants.
gives: On every occasion I experience the power of the gods and show them my own soul
To live with the gods is to show them a soul content with what is allotted and doing all that the spirit wants
Zeus gave me that spirit as protector and leader, a fragment of himself

support.quote: from what I experience of their power on every occasion
support.follows: Marcus experiences the power of the gods on every occasion.
gives: On every occasion I experience the power of the gods and show them my own soul

claims.t: I have never seen my own soul, yet I honour it. I revere the gods, and I hold reason in reverence.
claims.shared: The unseen but honoured soul is what this claim adds to the opening, and it is 12.21 alone. The second sentence joins 12.21’s reverence for the gods with 4.13’s reverence for reason without saying the two are the same thing.

support.quote: that you revere them as you do
support.follows: Those who question Marcus take it as a fact that he reveres the gods.
gives: I revere the gods, and I hold reason in reverence

support.quote: reverence for reason
support.follows: Reason is something to be revered.
gives: I revere the gods, and I hold reason in reverence

support.quote: I have not seen my own soul either, and yet I honour it
support.follows: Marcus has never seen his own soul, and he honours it all the same.
gives: I have never seen my own soul, yet I honour it

claims.t: I keep in mind two reminders from other schools. The Pythagoreans say to turn the eyes to the sky at dawn, and so be reminded of those that always complete their own work along the same lines and in the same way. The Epicureans laid down a rule to remind oneself constantly of one of the people of old who practised virtue.
claims.shared: Both are reported practices of other schools, so the line keeps them as reports and claims only that I keep them in mind. The semicolon is removed. The sky practice is 11.25 alone, and the exemplar rule is 11.24 alone and has no gods in it.

support.quote: The Pythagoreans: to turn our eyes to the sky at dawn, so that we are reminded of those that always complete their own work along the same lines and in the same way
support.follows: The Pythagoreans’ instruction is to look at the sky at dawn, as a reminder of those in the sky that always complete their own work in the same way.
gives: I keep in mind two reminders from other schools
The Pythagoreans say to turn the eyes to the sky at dawn, and so be reminded of those that always complete their own work along the same lines and in the same way

support.quote: In the writings of the Epicureans a rule was laid down: to remind oneself constantly of one of the people of old who practised virtue
support.follows: The Epicureans had a written rule: keep reminding yourself of one of the people of old who practised virtue.
gives: I keep in mind two reminders from other schools
The Epicureans laid down a rule to remind oneself constantly of one of the people of old who practised virtue

single.label: What the spirit is
single.t: The spirit in me is my own mind and reason.
single.quote: this spirit is each person’s mind and reason
single.why: Single source, 5.21. Narrowed to what the quote says, which is that the spirit is a person’s mind and reason. Zeus’s gift and the role of leader belong to c1.
single.follows: The spirit Zeus gives each person as protector and leader is that person’s own mind and reason.

single.label: Seen with the eye
single.t: The gods are visible even to the eye.
single.quote: they are visible even to the eye
single.why: Single source, 12.21. This is the first of two separate answers. The passage does not say which visible things the gods are.
single.follows: Marcus’s first answer to those who ask where he has seen the gods is that they can be seen with the eye.

single.label: Known by their power
single.t: From what I experience of the gods’ power, I both grasp that they exist and stand in awe of them.
single.quote: from that I both grasp that they exist and stand in awe of them
single.why: Single source, 12.21. ‘What I experience of the gods’ power’ spells out the quote’s ‘from that’ as the passage itself does, so the line can stand alone. The ground is experienced power producing awe, not sight of the gods and not a proof.
single.follows: Marcus’s ground for holding that the gods exist, and for his awe of them, is what he has just named: his experience of their power.

single.label: What the sky shows
single.t: The stars remind me of their order, their purity and their nakedness. For a star has no veil.
single.quote: and of their order, their purity and their nakedness. For a star has no veil.
single.why: Single source, 11.25, from a reported Pythagorean practice. The stars are named from the quote’s own image so that ‘their’ has a referent. The image stands in the third person as given, and the line does not call the stars gods.
single.follows: Those in the sky are also a reminder of order, purity and nakedness, since a star has nothing hung in front of it.

single.label: From beast to god
single.t: If I turn back to the principles, within ten days I will seem a god to the very people to whom I now seem a beast and an ape.
single.quote: Within ten days you will seem a god to the very people to whom you now seem a beast and an ape, if you turn back to the principles
single.why: Single source, 4.13. It is conditional and concerns how I seem to the same onlookers, not what I become. It is not a vow, and their opinion is not the aim.
single.follows: Whoever turns back to the principles will soon seem a god to the same people who now take him for a beast and an ape.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. In modern editions 12.21 is 12.28, 5.21 is 5.27, 4.13 is 4.16, 11.25 is 11.27 and 11.24 is 11.26.

Each phrase rests on two passages. Reverence for the gods is 12.21 and reverence for reason is 4.13. The reminders are the Pythagorean one of work always done the same way and the Epicurean one of virtue. ‘Live with the gods’ is left to c1 because only 5.21 says it.
articles.limit: The article joins reverence for the gods and reason (12.21, 5.21, 4.13) with reminder practices that Marcus only reports from other schools (11.25, 11.24). The first-person form suggests more adoption of those practices than the sources state. 4.13’s ‘seem a god’ is about reputation and is kept apart from 5.21’s living with the gods. 12.21 offers experience of the gods’ power and awe, not a demonstration.

statement.t: I revere the gods and reason, and I keep before me reminders of steady work and of virtue.

parts.words: I revere the gods and reason
I keep before me reminders of steady work and of virtue

statement.kind: A way of living with the gods, what I revere, and two exercises of reminding
statement.form: Each phrase rests on two passages. Reverence for the gods is 12.21 and reverence for reason is 4.13. The reminders are the Pythagorean one of work always done the same way and the Epicurean one of virtue. ‘Live with the gods’ is left to c1 because only 5.21 says it.

empty.doubt: No passage in this section asks what still holds if there are no gods; 12.21 answers those who ask where Marcus has seen them by giving his grounds for holding that they exist, and those grounds stand under “Why”.

articles.title: Blaming no one for what is not up to me

claims.role: What counts as good or bad
claims.t: I judge only what is up to me to be good or bad. It is better to use what is up to me in freedom than to let what is not up to me make a difference to me, in slavery and degradation. That difference leads us into many wrongs.
claims.shared: Adds the judgement of good and bad and the contrast of freedom with slavery, which the opening lacks. Freedom and slavery come from 9.40 alone, and the many wrongs from 6.36 alone.

support.quote: if we judge only the things that are up to us to be good and bad
support.follows: Marcus proposes that we count only the things that are up to us as good or bad.
gives: I judge only what is up to me to be good or bad

support.quote: And indeed we do many wrongs because of the difference these things make to us.
support.follows: When things outside our choice make a difference to us, that leads us into many wrongs.
gives: what is not up to me make a difference to me
That difference leads us into many wrongs

support.quote: is it not better to use what is up to you in freedom than to let what is not up to you make a difference to you, in slavery and degradation?
support.follows: It is better to use freely what is up to me than to let what is not up to me make a difference to me, which is slavery.
gives: use what is up to me in freedom
what is not up to me make a difference to me
in slavery and degradation

claims.t: No one is to be blamed, neither the gods nor people. People go wrong only unwillingly. I do not accuse a god or take an enemy’s stand against a person. I am not angry with things, for they do not care at all.
claims.shared: Things are removed from the no-blame list because 7.25 speaks of anger, not blame. That line is a quoted verse with a single witness. Human error is affirmed and only its willingness denied, from 12.9 alone. In 6.36 the absence of cause is conditional on judging rightly.

support.quote: No one is to be blamed.
support.follows: No one, and nothing, is to be blamed for what goes wrong.
gives: No one is to be blamed

support.quote: The gods are not to be blamed
support.follows: The gods are not to be blamed.
gives: neither the gods nor people

support.quote: Nor are people, for they go wrong in nothing except unwillingly.
support.follows: People are not to be blamed either, since whatever they go wrong in, they go wrong in unwillingly.
gives: neither the gods nor people
People go wrong only unwillingly

support.quote: So no one is to be blamed.
support.follows: Since neither the gods nor people are to be blamed, no one is.
gives: No one is to be blamed

support.quote: no cause is left either for accusing a god or for taking an enemy’s stand against a person
support.follows: Once only what is up to us counts as good or bad, there is no cause to accuse a god or to stand against a person as an enemy.
gives: neither the gods nor people
I do not accuse a god or take an enemy’s stand against a person

support.quote: For one must not be angry with things, for they do not care at all.
support.follows: One must not be angry with things, because they do not care at all.
gives: I am not angry with things, for they do not care at all

claims.role: When the gods seem to neglect us
claims.t: The gods go wrong in nothing, willingly or unwillingly. If the gods have neglected me and my children, this too has its reason. Suppose the gods seem to have overlooked some very good people. If the lot of those people ought to have been otherwise, the gods would have made it otherwise. The gods would not let anything in the order of things be neglected unjustly and against reason.
claims.shared: Both cases of neglect stay conditional. The neglect line is a quoted verse in 7.25, where the speaker has two children. “The lot of those people” names what might have been otherwise without asserting extinction, which this claim’s quotes do not carry and which stays in the margin.

support.quote: for they go wrong in nothing, willingly or unwillingly
support.follows: The gods go wrong in nothing, neither on purpose nor against their will.
gives: The gods go wrong in nothing, willingly or unwillingly

support.quote: But if I and my two children have been neglected by the gods, this too has its reason.
support.follows: Even if the gods have neglected me and my children, there is a reason for that too.
gives: If the gods have neglected me and my children
this too has its reason

support.quote: overlooked this one thing only: that some people, and very good ones
support.follows: It looks as if the gods, who arranged everything well, overlooked one thing: what becomes of very good people after death.
gives: the gods seem to have overlooked some very good people

support.quote: they would not have let anything in the order of things be neglected unjustly and against reason
support.follows: If the gods are best and most just, nothing in the order of things has been neglected unjustly or against reason.
gives: this too has its reason
The gods would not let anything in the order of things be neglected unjustly and against reason

support.quote: be sure that if it ought to have been otherwise, they would have made it otherwise
support.follows: If things ought to have been otherwise, the gods would have made them otherwise.
gives: If the lot of those people ought to have been otherwise, the gods would have made it otherwise

claims.t: If a wrong is up to me, I ask why I do it. It is ridiculous to flee the vice of others, which is impossible, and not to flee my own vice, which is possible. If a wrong is up to another, I set that person right if I can. If I cannot, I set right at least the thing itself. If I can do neither, blaming serves no end.
claims.shared: Text unchanged. The joint anchor now covers only what both passages say, that my own wrong is within my power. The ridicule and the fleeing are from 7.41 alone, and the order of setting right is from 8.15 alone.

support.quote: If it is up to you, why do you do it?
support.follows: If what is going wrong is up to me, I have no reason to go on doing it.
gives: If a wrong is up to me, I ask why I do it
my own vice, which is possible

support.quote: It is ridiculous not to flee one’s own vice, which is in fact possible, but to flee that of others, which is impossible.
support.follows: I can get clear of my own vice and cannot get clear of other people’s, so it is ridiculous to try the second and not the first.
gives: It is ridiculous to flee the vice of others, which is impossible
not to flee
my own vice, which is possible

support.quote: If it is up to another, whom or what do you blame?
support.follows: If what is going wrong is up to someone else, there is no one and nothing for me to blame.
gives: If a wrong is up to another

support.quote: For if you can, set the other right. If you cannot do that, set right at least the thing itself. And if not even that, what end does blaming still serve for you?
support.follows: I should correct the other person if I can, or else the thing itself; if I can do neither, blaming serves no end.
gives: I set that person right if I can
I set right at least the thing itself
blaming serves no end

claims.t: When I set up as good or bad something that is not mine to choose, I make a case against the gods. Then I blame the gods when I meet such a bad thing or miss such a good one, and I hate the people who are the cause. When I pry into what the gods have allowed, I am arguing a case of justice with god. Enough of the grumbling. Towards the gods too, now at last, I become simpler and better.
claims.shared: Describes the lapse, with “Then” tying the blame to the misjudgement so it is not heard as a vow. “What the gods have allowed” gives the prying an object. In 12.4 that object is specifically the fate of good people after death. Hatred of people is from 6.36 alone. 9.35 stands beside the lapse without being called its cure, and “simpler” is left undefined.

support.quote: Whatever you set up for yourself as good or bad among the things that are not yours to choose, it must follow that when you meet with such a bad thing or miss such a good one, you blame the gods, and hate people too: those who are the cause
support.follows: Whoever counts things outside their choice as good or bad will blame the gods and hate people when they meet or miss those things.
gives: I set up as good or bad something that is not mine to choose
I make a case against the gods
I blame the gods when I meet such a bad thing or miss such a good one
I hate the people who are the cause

support.quote: For you see for yourself that in prying into this you are arguing a case of justice with god.
support.follows: Prying into why the good do not come to be again after death is arguing a case of justice with god.
gives: I make a case against the gods
When I pry into what the gods have allowed
I am arguing a case of justice with god

support.quote: Enough of the wretched life, the grumbling, the aping.
support.follows: Marcus tells himself to have done with a wretched life of grumbling and putting on an act.
gives: Enough of the grumbling

support.quote: But towards the gods too, now at last, become simpler and better.
support.follows: It is time to become simpler and better towards the gods as well.
gives: Towards the gods too, now at last, I become simpler and better

single.label: Turning prayers round
single.t: I turn my prayers round and watch what happens. Another prays, “How may I not lose my little child?” I pray, “How may I not be afraid of losing it?”
single.quote: Another: “How may I not lose my little child?” You: “How may I not be afraid of losing it?” In short, turn your prayers round like this and watch what happens.
single.why: Single source, 9.40. Restores the paired prayers and “watch what happens”. Prayer is redirected, not abolished, and no result is promised.
single.follows: I should pray not to be afraid of losing my child, instead of praying not to lose it, and see what happens.

single.label: Looking at what troubles me
single.t: When I am troubled, I ask what is new in the thing that troubles me. I look at the cause, and I look at the material. Beyond these there is nothing.
single.quote: Why are you troubled? What in this is new? What puts you beside yourself? The cause? Look at it. Or the material? Look at it. Beyond these there is nothing.
single.why: Single source, 9.35. Keeps the source’s terms cause and material and its closing sentence.
single.follows: When something troubles me, I should look at its cause and at what it is made of, since there is nothing more to it.

single.label: Not joining in
single.t: I do not join in the wailing, and I do not let my pulse race.
single.quote: No joining in the wailing, no racing pulse.
single.why: Single source, 7.25. This is the only line of that passage in Marcus’s own voice. The added “When others lament” is dropped as unneeded.
single.follows: I should not join others in lamenting, and I should not let myself grow agitated.

single.label: Giving up on bad people
single.t: When I am ready to give up on bad people, I remember the gods. The gods, who are immortal, are not vexed at having to put up with so many bad people for so long, and the gods care for those people in every kind of way. I am about to come to an end, and I am one of the bad ones myself.
single.quote: The gods, who are immortal, are not vexed that through so long a time they will certainly always have to put up with bad people of such a kind and in such numbers. More than that, they care for them in every kind of way. But you, who are about to come to an end any moment now, do you give up, and that when you are one of the bad ones?
single.why: Single source, 7.41. Kept as a rebuke to giving up, not turned into a vow. Blame is not mentioned in the source.
single.follows: If the immortal gods bear with bad people and care for them, I, who will soon die and am bad myself, have no ground to give up on them.

single.label: Either way
single.t: Blaming the atoms is madness, and blaming the gods is madness.
single.quote: The atoms or the gods? Both are madness.
single.why: Single source, 8.15. Names blaming as the madness and leaves the choice between atoms and gods undecided, as in the source.
single.follows: Whether things come about by the atoms or by the gods, blaming either is madness.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. In modern editions 6.36 is 6.41, 12.4 is 12.5, 8.15 is 8.17, 7.25 is 7.38 to 7.43, 7.41 is 7.70 to 7.71, 9.35 is 9.37a and 12.9 is 12.11b to 12.12; 9.40 is the same.

Replaces the double negative with a positive statement of what externals cannot settle, my judgement of good and bad. The words good or bad are from 6.36. 9.40 supports the same point only as not letting what is not up to me make a difference. The refusal of blame is flat in 8.15 and 12.9 and conditional on right judgement in 6.36. The first sentence of c1 now overlaps the opening, though c1 still adds freedom, slavery and the many wrongs.
articles.limit: The passages agree in refusing blame, but on different grounds: misplaced valuation in 6.36, aimlessness in 8.15, divine inerrancy and unwilling human error in 12.9, the justice presupposed by questioning in 12.4. The article does not merge these into one argument. The opening’s words good or bad come from 6.36, and 9.40 supports them only as the difference that what is not up to me should not make. The article does not settle whether the gods govern or can act, nor whether the dead are extinguished. The lines from 7.25 are quoted verses, and “simpler” in 9.35 is left undefined. In c5 the prying of 12.4 is stated generally, though the passage concerns good people after death. 7.41 does not mention blame. Not blaming does not deny that people do wrong, and it does not replace setting things right. Only the opening was reviewed here, and its repair leaves the first sentence of c1 overlapping it.

statement.t: I judge only what is up to me to be good or bad, and I blame no one, neither the gods nor people.

parts.words: I judge only what is up to me to be good or bad
I blame no one
neither the gods nor people

statement.kind: A ground and the conduct that follows from it
statement.form: Replaces the double negative with a positive statement of what externals cannot settle, my judgement of good and bad. The words good or bad are from 6.36. 9.40 supports the same point only as not letting what is not up to me make a difference. The refusal of blame is flat in 8.15 and 12.9 and conditional on right judgement in 6.36. The first sentence of c1 now overlaps the opening, though c1 still adds freedom, slavery and the many wrongs.

articles.title: Happiness and unhappiness are my own doing

claims.t: I look for my happiness and my unhappiness in my own soul. Happiness is a good spirit, or a good ruling part. If I do not keep track of the movements of my own soul, I am bound to be unhappy. Hardly anyone has been seen to be unhappy through not attending to what goes on in another person’s soul.
claims.shared: Restores the ‘or’ of 7.14 and the empirical hedge of 2.5. The last sentence is a comparison from 2.5 alone and does not forbid concern for others.

support.quote: Happiness is a good spirit, or a good ruling part.
support.follows: Happiness is having a good spirit, or a good ruling part.
gives: I look for my happiness and my unhappiness in my own soul
Happiness is a good spirit, or a good ruling part

support.quote: But those who do not keep track of the movements of their own soul are bound to be unhappy.
support.follows: People who do not keep track of what moves in their own soul are certain to be unhappy.
gives: I look for my happiness and my unhappiness in my own soul
If I do not keep track of the movements of my own soul, I am bound to be unhappy

support.quote: Hardly anyone has been seen to be unhappy through not attending to what goes on in another person’s soul.
support.follows: Hardly anyone has been seen to be unhappy because they did not attend to what goes on in another person’s soul.
gives: Hardly anyone has been seen to be unhappy through not attending to what goes on in another person’s soul

claims.t: I look to myself for what I need. I am a beggar when I am in need of another and do not have from myself everything useful for life. I endured countless things because I was not content with my ruling part doing what it is made to do. I tell the impression, “Go away as you came, for I do not need you.”
claims.shared: Text unchanged and anchors corrected. The first sentence rests jointly on 4.24c and 9.24a. The beggar is a warning image from 4.24 alone. The endurance is Marcus’s own past in 9.24. ‘I do not need you’ is said only to an impression in 7.14, and the anchor now covers the act of telling it.

support.quote: You have endured countless things because you were not content with your ruling part doing the kind of things it is made to do.
support.follows: Marcus tells himself that he endured countless things because he was not content with his ruling part doing what it is made to do.
gives: I look to myself for what I need
I endured countless things because I was not content with my ruling part doing what it is made to do

support.quote: A beggar is whoever is in need of another and does not have from themselves everything that is useful for life.
support.follows: Whoever needs another and does not have from themselves everything useful for life is a beggar.
gives: I look to myself for what I need
I am a beggar when I am in need of another and do not have from myself everything useful for life

support.quote: So what are you doing here, impression? Go away, by the gods, as you came, for I do not need you.
support.follows: Marcus asks an impression what it is doing here and tells it to go away as it came, because he does not need it.
gives: I tell the impression, “Go away as you came, for I do not need you

claims.role: Not wanting what happens is deserting
claims.t: When I resent an event, I do not want the event itself to have happened. Displeased with an event, I stand apart and separate myself from the reason of the common nature. The common nature brings forth each event, and the same nature brought me forth too. Distressed, angry or afraid, I do not want an appointed thing to have happened, to be happening or to be going to happen. The law is the master that governs all things and deals out all that falls to each. Whoever flees a master is a runaway slave, so in distress, anger or fear I am a runaway slave from the law.
claims.shared: Only the first sentence is joint. It says the refusal is aimed at the event itself, which keeps it distinct from any choice about what to do next. Standing apart from the common nature, and its ground that the same nature brought me forth, are 4.24 alone. The three passions, the three tenses, law as master and the runaway slave are 10.25 alone. The chain is now stated in steps so the slave image explains itself. The abscess image moves to the margin as a quotation. No remedy is added.

support.quote: An abscess standing apart from the universe is whoever stands apart and separates themselves from the reason of the common nature by being displeased with what happens
support.follows: Whoever is displeased with what happens separates themselves from the reason of the common nature, as an abscess stands apart.
gives: When I resent an event, I do not want the event itself to have happened
Displeased with an event, I stand apart and separate myself from the reason of the common nature

support.quote: for that nature brings this forth, the same one that brought you forth too
support.follows: The nature that brings this event is the same nature that brought you into being.
gives: The common nature brings forth each event, and the same nature brought me forth too

support.quote: Whoever flees from their master is a runaway slave. And the law is master
support.follows: Someone who flees from their master is a runaway slave, and the law is master.

Whoever flees a master is a runaway slave, so in distress, anger or fear I am a runaway slave from the law

support.quote: But whoever is distressed or angry or afraid also does not want one of the things appointed by the one who governs all things to have happened, or to be happening, or to be going to happen
support.follows: Whoever is distressed, angry or afraid does not want something that the one who governs all things appointed, past, present or to come.

Distressed, angry or afraid, I do not want an appointed thing to have happened, to be happening or to be going to happen

support.quote: and the one who governs all things is law, as the one who deals out all that falls to each
support.follows: The one who governs all things is law: the one who deals out all that falls to each.
gives: The law is the master that governs all things and deals out all that falls to each

support.quote: So whoever is afraid or distressed or angry is a runaway slave.
support.follows: Whoever is afraid, distressed or angry is therefore a runaway slave.
gives: Whoever flees a master is a runaway slave, so in distress, anger or fear I am a runaway slave from the law

single.label: Sending an impression away
single.t: When an impression comes out of old habit, I am not angry with it. I tell the impression only to go away.
single.quote: But you have come out of old habit. I am not angry with you. Only go away.
single.why: Quote: “But you have come out of old habit. I am not angry with you. Only go away.” Single source, 7.14. Keeps the calm tone, and the second sentence now names the impression so it reads alone.
single.follows: The impression has come out of old habit; Marcus is not angry with it and only tells it to go away.

single.label: An exile by my own act
single.t: I am an exile when I exile myself from the reason that belongs to citizens.
single.quote: An exile is whoever exiles themselves from the reason that belongs to citizens.
single.why: Quote: “An exile is whoever exiles themselves from the reason that belongs to citizens.” Single source, 4.24. The original stands verbatim because the image is precise and warranted.
single.follows: A person becomes an exile by exiling themselves from the reason that belongs to citizens.

single.label: Blind by my own act
single.t: I am blind when I shut the eye of my own mind.
single.quote: Blind is whoever shuts the eye of the mind.
single.why: Quote: “Blind is whoever shuts the eye of the mind.” Single source, 4.24. The original stands verbatim.
single.follows: To be blind, in the sense meant here, is to shut the eye of the mind.

single.label: Breaking off
single.t: Of my discontent with my ruling part I say: enough.
single.quote: But enough.
single.why: Quote: “But enough.” Single source, 9.24. Removes the invented ‘catching myself going over’ and keeps the curt tone. The passage names no method.
single.follows: Marcus breaks off with two words: but enough.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. In modern editions 4.24 is 4.29 without its first sentence, 2.5 is 2.8, 7.14 is 7.17 and 9.24 is 9.26; 10.25 is the same.

135 characters. ‘The part of me that rules’ puts the ruling part of 7.14 and 9.24 in plain words. ‘Resent an event that has happened’ shows the fault is a refusal of the event itself, joining 4.24’s displeasure with 10.25’s not wanting a thing to have happened. Nature (4.24) and law (10.25) are named side by side in place of ‘order’ and are not merged. The opening narrows to past events. Fear and the future stay in c3.
articles.limit: Only 4.24 and 10.25 speak of a source that sends events, and in different terms: the common nature that also brought me forth, and law as the one who deals out what falls to each. The opening names them side by side and does not claim they are one thing. 2.5, 7.14 and 9.24 say nothing of fate, so the opening’s second sentence is not their doctrine. ‘Resent’ is our word for 4.24’s displeasure and for 10.25’s distress and anger. The opening narrows to events that have happened, while c3 keeps fear and the present and future from 10.25. The passages judge the refusal of an event. They say nothing about what to do next and prescribe no remedy, so the article neither forbids nor directs later action. ‘The part of me that rules’ is our plain wording for the ruling part, and no passage says what its proper work is. The beggar image must be read with 4.24’s civic reason and one soul of rational beings. ‘I look to myself for what I need’ in c2 is inferred from the beggar warning and the 9.24 reproach, not stated by either. No passage gives a method beyond dismissing an impression and saying ‘enough’, and what ‘enough’ refers to in 9.24 is our reading.

statement.t: My happiness lies in the part of me that rules. When I resent an event that has happened, I desert the nature and the law that sent it.

parts.words: My happiness lies in the part of me that rules
When I resent an event that has happened
I desert the nature and the law that sent it

statement.kind: A ground, what follows from it, and the failure named
statement.form: 135 characters. ‘The part of me that rules’ puts the ruling part of 7.14 and 9.24 in plain words. ‘Resent an event that has happened’ shows the fault is a refusal of the event itself, joining 4.24’s displeasure with 10.25’s not wanting a thing to have happened. Nature (4.24) and law (10.25) are named side by side in place of ‘order’ and are not merged. The opening narrows to past events. Fear and the future stay in c3.

empty.doubt: No passage in this section considers what would still hold if my happiness were not decided in my own soul, so Marcus gives nothing under this label.

articles.title: Ready to leave

claims.t: My time is short. Any moment now I will be dead, and very soon I will leave all these things behind.
claims.shared: Adds to the opening what is left behind. “All this” became “all these things” so the reference is clear. The 10.17 sentence was folded into the joint first phrase to avoid saying shortness twice.

support.quote: having taken in that very soon they will have to leave all these things behind as they go from among people
support.follows: The person described has understood that very soon they must leave all this behind and go from among people.
gives: My time is short
very soon I will leave all these things behind

support.quote: Any moment now you will be dead
support.follows: Marcus tells himself that he will be dead any moment now.
gives: My time is short
Any moment now I will be dead

support.quote: What is left now is little.
support.follows: Marcus tells himself that little is left now.
gives: My time is short

claims.t: Dying is one of the acts of my life and nothing much. When I leave life, I leave as one who suffers nothing bad. If my mind is disciplined and cleansed, fate does not overtake my life while it is unfinished. I am then not like a tragic actor who leaves before playing the drama through.
claims.shared: The actor is now a comparison, as in 3.9, and is no longer confused with the role-playing actor of 5.23. “When I leave life” is anchored to 5.23d. “Nothing much” has joint support from 5.23 and 6.2. The completeness claim stays conditional on the cleansed mind and is 3.9 alone. “Suffers nothing bad” is 5.23 alone and judges the leaving without denying it.

support.quote: as one who is suffering nothing bad
support.follows: If one has to go out of life, one goes as someone who is suffering nothing bad.
gives: I leave as one who suffers nothing bad

support.quote: There is smoke, and I leave. Why do you think it anything much?
support.follows: When there is smoke, Marcus leaves, and he asks why one should think leaving any great matter.
gives: nothing much
When I leave life

support.quote: Let it make no difference to you whether you do what is fitting while shivering or warm, and whether drowsy or having slept enough, and whether spoken ill of or praised, and whether dying or doing some other kind of act.
support.follows: Whether I am cold or warm, praised or spoken ill of, dying or doing something else, it should make no difference to doing what is fitting.
gives: nothing much

support.quote: For this too is one of the acts of life, the one in which we die.
support.follows: Dying is one of the acts of life.
gives: Dying is one of the acts of my life

support.quote: In the mind of someone who has been disciplined and thoroughly cleansed you would find nothing full of pus
support.follows: A mind that has been disciplined and cleansed has nothing festering in it.
gives: If my mind is disciplined and cleansed

support.quote: Nor does fate overtake their life while it is unfinished, as one might say of a tragic actor who leaves before finishing and playing the drama through.
support.follows: Whenever death comes to such a person, their life is not left unfinished, like a play an actor walks out of.
gives: fate does not overtake my life while it is unfinished
not like a tragic actor who leaves before playing the drama through

claims.t: I do not play a part. I keep nothing affected in me and nothing lurking in a hole. The finer thing is to go from among people without ever having tasted lying, pretence, luxury or vanity.
claims.shared: “Go from among people” is the wording of 9.2 and cannot be heard as abandoning anyone. The first phrase has joint support from 7.40, 3.9 and 9.2. The “lurking in a hole” image is 3.9 alone. “Finer” keeps the ranking in 9.2, which is 9.2 alone, and does not claim the ideal as achieved.

support.quote: It would have been the mark of a finer man to go from among people without having tasted lying, or any pretence or luxury or vanity.
support.follows: It would have been finer to leave life without ever having tasted lying, pretence, luxury or vanity.
gives: I do not play a part
The finer thing is to go from among people without ever having tasted lying, pretence, luxury or vanity

support.quote: nor to play a part
support.follows: A perfect character does not play a part.
gives: I do not play a part

support.quote: nothing slavish, nothing affected, nothing tied to anything, nothing split off, nothing liable to be called to account, nothing lurking in a hole
support.follows: In a cleansed mind there is nothing slavish, affected or hidden, and nothing that has to answer for itself.
gives: I do not play a part
nothing affected in me and nothing lurking in a hole

claims.t: I live as on a mountain, for it makes no difference whether there or here. The life I have in mind I can live here, in the universe as in a city, according to nature. If I am not allowed to live so, death is better than living another way.
claims.shared: Restores the mountain and city images, which are 10.17 alone and mean indifference of place, not retreat. The last sentence is conditional and makes no promise about other people. It does not settle whether I leave (5.23) or am killed (10.17).

support.quote: As you have in mind to live once you have gone out, so you can live here.
support.follows: The life one plans to live after leaving can be lived here already.
gives: it makes no difference whether there or here
The life I have in mind I can live here

support.quote: Live as on a mountain. For it makes no difference whether there or here, if a person, wherever they are, lives in the universe as in a city.
support.follows: One can live as on a mountain anywhere, since the place makes no difference to someone whose city is the universe.
gives: I live as on a mountain
it makes no difference whether there or here
in the universe as in a city

support.quote: Let human beings see, let them study, a true human being living according to nature.
support.follows: Marcus asks that people see and study a true human being living according to nature.
gives: according to nature

support.quote: And I want what accords with the nature of the rational and social living being.
support.follows: What Marcus wants is what fits the nature of a rational and social creature.
gives: according to nature

support.quote: But if they do not allow it, then go out of life as well
support.follows: If others do not let one live that way, one should go out of life.
gives: If I am not allowed to live so

support.quote: If they do not bear it, let them kill that person. For that is better than to live that way.
support.follows: If people cannot bear a person who lives by nature, being killed by them is better than living that way.
gives: If I am not allowed to live so
death is better than living another way

single.label: Free while I stay
single.t: As long as nothing leads me out of life, I stay, free, and no one will prevent me from doing what I want.
single.quote: But as long as nothing of that kind leads me out, I stay, free, and no one will prevent me from doing what I want.
single.why: Existing wording kept, since no pilot wording was supplied. It rests on 5.23 alone. “Nothing of that kind” refers to the smoke and is given as “nothing leads me out of life” so the line reads clearly alone. Staying free is the default. “What I want” is limited by the next sentence of 5.23, which is kept in the margin.
single.follows: Until something like the smoke leads Marcus out, he stays, free, and no one stops him from doing what he wants.

single.label: Every day as the last
single.t: Perfection of character is to live through every day as the last, neither feverish nor numb.
single.quote: Perfection of character has this: to live through every day as the last, and neither to be feverish nor to go numb
single.why: Rests on 7.40 alone. Kept as the speaker’s definition of perfection so the ideal is not claimed as attained. The third negative, playing a part, sits in c3.
single.follows: A perfect character lives each day as the last, without agitation and without numbness.

single.label: The next best course
single.t: To breathe my last having at least grown sick of vice is the next best course. Have I chosen to stay sitting beside vice? Does experience not yet persuade me to flee the plague? Corruption of the mind is a plague far worse than any unhealthy change of the air.
single.quote: But at any rate to breathe one’s last having at least grown sick of these things is the next best course. Or have you chosen to stay sitting beside vice, and does not even experience yet persuade you to flee from the plague? For the corruption of the mind is a plague, far more so than any such unhealthy mixture and change of this air that is poured around.
single.why: Rests on 9.2 alone. The reproachful questions stay questions, where the earlier line turned them into a vow. “These things” is given as “vice”, the quote’s own word. The plague is moral corruption, not death.
single.follows: Having tasted these vices, the next best course is to die sick of them, since staying with vice is staying with a worse plague.

single.label: The piglet at the sacrifice
single.t: I picture everyone who is pained or displeased at anything whatever as like the piglet that is being sacrificed and kicks and squeals. Like it too is the one who laments on a little bed, alone, in silence.
single.quote: Picture everyone who is pained or displeased at anything whatever as like the piglet that is being sacrificed and kicks and squeals. Like it too is the one who laments on their little bed, alone, in silence.
single.why: Rests on 10.28 alone. Kept as a picturing exercise in the third person, so the comparison stays a comparison. It does not say the pain is unreal.
single.follows: Whoever is pained or displeased at what happens is like a sacrificial piglet kicking, even when they lament in silence.

single.label: Three cases
single.t: Either I live here, and by now I am used to it. Or I am going out from here, and that is what I wanted. Or I am dying, and I have completed my service. Besides these there is nothing, so let me be cheerful.
single.quote: Either you live here, and by now you are used to it; or you are going out from here, and that is what you wanted; or you are dying, and you have completed your service. Besides these there is nothing. So be cheerful.
single.why: Rests on 10.23 alone. Semicolons removed. Leaving “here” and dying remain separate cases, and “here” is left unspecified as in the source. The ending stays a self-exhortation.
single.follows: Whether one lives on here, goes away or dies, there is no fourth case, and in each one can be cheerful.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. In modern editions 10.12 is 10.11b, 4.30 is 4.37, 3.9 is 3.8, 10.23 is 10.22, 10.17 is 10.15, 7.40 is 7.69 and 5.23 is 5.28b–29; 9.2, 6.2 and 10.28 are the same.

Semicolon removed and “may die” dropped, since the sources say death is near, not merely possible. Every phrase rests on two passages. The line states a resolve: 4.30 and 9.2 show the speaker still falling short.
articles.limit: These lines state a resolve and an ideal, not an achievement: 4.30 and 9.2 are self-reproach, and 3.9 and 10.12 describe an ideal figure. Leaving life in 5.23 and being killed in 10.17 are conditional on being prevented from living rightly, and they differ in agency. Neither supports seeking death. The actor of 3.9 is an unfinished drama and is not the role-playing actor of 5.23 and 7.40. “What I want” in 5.23 means what accords with the nature of a rational and social being. The first-person wording and the fusion of passages are our editorial interpretation.

statement.t: Death is near. I live without pretence, here as anywhere, and dying is nothing much to me.

parts.words: Death is near
I live without pretence
here as anywhere
dying is nothing much to me

statement.kind: A fact faced, and how to live under it
statement.form: Semicolon removed and “may die” dropped, since the sources say death is near, not merely possible. Every phrase rests on two passages. The line states a resolve: 4.30 and 9.2 show the speaker still falling short.

articles.title: Content wherever I am put

claims.t: A good lot is one I assign myself: good turnings of the soul, good impulses, good actions. In whatever place I am, the divinity within me is content if its state and the way it acts follow from its own make-up. It is enough that my present judgement has a firm grasp of what is there and that my present action serves other people.
claims.shared: Gives the reason behind the opening: the lot is self-assigned (5.30 only), contentment is conditional (8.43 only), and present judgement and present social action are enough (9.5, with 8.22 for the social aim). “It is enough that my present judgement” removes the misleading “for the present”. The pilot’s “refused” and “I do not wait for somewhere better” go beyond the quotes and stay out.

support.quote: For there too I will have the divinity within me gracious
support.follows: Even in the place I am thrown to, the divinity within me will be gracious.
gives: In whatever place I am
the divinity within me is content

support.quote: wherever caught, a person whose lot is good
support.follows: The words describe a person whose lot is good wherever that person is caught.
gives: In whatever place I am

support.quote: “whose lot is good” means having assigned yourself a good lot
support.follows: To have a good lot is to have assigned a good lot to yourself.
gives: A good lot is one I assign myself

support.quote: good lots are good turnings of the soul, good impulses, good actions
support.follows: A good lot consists of good turnings of the soul, good impulses and good actions.
gives: good turnings of the soul, good impulses, good actions

support.quote: content if the state it is in and the way it acts follow from its own make-up
support.follows: The divinity within me is content if its state and its way of acting follow from the way it is made.
gives: the divinity within me is content
if its state and the way it acts follow from its own make-up

support.quote: It is enough that the present judgment should have a firm grasp of what is there
support.follows: Three present things are enough, and the first is a judgment with a firm grasp of what is there.
gives: It is enough that my present judgement has a firm grasp of what is there

support.quote: the present action should be social
support.follows: Marcus requires the action at hand to be social.
gives: my present action serves other people

support.quote: I do it, referring it to the doing of good to human beings.
support.follows: Marcus directs action to the good of human beings.
gives: my present action serves other people

claims.t: What I do, I do for the good of other people. What happens to me, I accept, whatever it is, as something that comes from the gods.
claims.shared: Pilot wording stands unchanged. Doing and undergoing stay distinct, as in 8.22. “Whatever it is” comes from 12.8 only, and “from the gods” from 8.22 only. 12.8 says god and 9.5 says the external cause, and the line does not equate them.

support.quote: Am I doing something? I do it, referring it to the doing of good to human beings.
support.follows: Whatever I am doing, I do it with the good of other people as its aim.
gives: What I do, I do for the good of other people

support.quote: the present action should be social
support.follows: What I am doing at this moment should be a social action.
gives: What I do, I do for the good of other people

support.quote: Is something happening to me? I accept it, referring it to the gods and to the spring of all things, from which everything that comes about is wound together.
support.follows: When something happens to me, I accept it and trace it back to the gods and to the one source of everything that comes about.
gives: What happens to me, I accept
as something that comes from the gods

support.quote: to accept everything god assigns to them, whatever it is
support.follows: A human being is able to accept everything god assigns, whatever it turns out to be.
gives: What happens to me, I accept
whatever it is

support.quote: the present disposition should be well pleased with everything that happens from the external cause
support.follows: My disposition at this moment should be well pleased with everything that comes from the cause outside me.

claims.role: Words that hand over the choice
claims.t: I leave three things to a will that is not mine: what I am given, what is taken back and where I am put. To nature, which gives everything and takes everything back, I say: “Give what you want. Take back what you want.” I say these words in obedience to nature and good will towards it, not in bold defiance.
claims.shared: The joint proposition is that the choice is left to another’s will: “what you want” in 10.16 and “wherever you want” in 8.43. The will in 8.43 is unnamed and is not identified with nature. The words to nature and their tone are from 10.16 only, where a third person speaks them, so the first-person form is editorial. The throwing image is kept in the margin.

support.quote: To nature, which gives everything and takes everything back
support.follows: Nature gives everything and takes everything back.
gives: what I am given, what is taken back
To nature, which gives everything and takes everything back

support.quote: “Give what you want. Take back what you want.”
support.follows: The educated and modest person tells nature to give what it wants and to take back what it wants.
gives: I leave three things to a will that is not mine
what I am given, what is taken back
Give what you want. Take back what you want.

support.quote: Pick me up and throw me wherever you want.
support.follows: The speaker tells someone unnamed to pick him up and throw him wherever they want.

support.quote: not in bold defiance, but only in obedience to it and good will towards it
support.follows: The words are said in obedience to nature and good will towards it, not to defy it.

not in bold defiance

single.label: A great power
single.t: To do nothing but what god is going to praise is in my power, as it is in every human being’s, and it is a great power.
single.quote: How great a power a human being has: to do nothing other than what god is going to praise
single.why: Single source, 12.8. Pilot wording kept. It states a capacity, not a command and not a claim of achievement.
single.follows: A human being has the power to do only what god is going to praise, and it is a great power.

single.label: Taking, letting go
single.t: I take without conceit, and I let go readily.
single.quote: To take without conceit, and to let go readily.
single.why: Single source, 8.31. The maxim names no object and no giver, so none is added.
single.follows: Whatever is taken should be taken without conceit and let go readily.

single.label: When I am troubled
single.t: When an impression troubles me or is out of place, I can push it away and wipe it out, and at once be completely calm. This is easy.
single.quote: How easy it is to push away and wipe out every impression that is troublesome or out of place, and at once to be in a complete calm.
single.why: Single source, 5.2. Pilot wording kept. The ease applies to impressions that are troublesome or out of place, not to events or to acceptance.
single.follows: A troublesome or out-of-place impression is easy to push away and wipe out, and complete calm follows at once.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. In modern editions 12.8 is the first part of 12.11, 8.43 is the first part of 8.45, 9.5 is 9.6, 10.16 is 10.14, 8.22 is 8.23, 5.30 is the end of 5.36 and 8.31 is 8.33; 5.2 is the same.

Pilot wording restored, with “even somewhere I would not have chosen” cut because no quotation states it and the line must stay within 140 characters. “Put” replaces the throwing scenario. “Can” and “depends on” keep the condition in 8.43 and promise no success. “My life” renders “lot” in 5.30 in plain words and is editorial.
articles.limit: The outside source is called god, the gods and the spring, nature, or the external cause, and the passages do not equate these. The will addressed in 8.43 is unnamed, and “a will that is not mine” in c3 does not identify it with nature. The lot is assigned by god in 12.8 but self-assigned in 5.30, and the article leaves that unreconciled. “My life” in the opening is an editorial rendering of “lot”. Contentment in 8.43 is conditional, and the power in 12.8 is a capacity, not an achievement. The sufficiency in 9.5 has three parts. c1 states judgement and action, and the third, a disposition well pleased with what comes from the external cause, is carried only as acceptance in c2 and in the margin. The words to nature in 10.16 belong to a third person of a certain character, and their tone qualifier applies only to those words. Ease in 5.2 covers impressions only. No passage says acceptance is easy, that the place is one I would have refused, or why what is assigned should be welcomed.

statement.t: Wherever I am put, my life can still be good. Whether it is good depends on two things I govern there: the state of my mind and how I act.

parts.words: Wherever I am put
my life can still be good

the state of my mind and how I act

statement.kind: A ground, the rule it supports, and words to say
statement.form: Pilot wording restored, with “even somewhere I would not have chosen” cut because no quotation states it and the line must stay within 140 characters. “Put” replaces the throwing scenario. “Can” and “depends on” keep the condition in 8.43 and promise no success. “My life” renders “lot” in 5.30 in plain words and is editorial.

articles.title: When someone offends me

claims.t: People do wrong against their will, in ignorance of what is good and bad. With a disposition like theirs, what are they to do? To require that bad people do no wrong is to demand the impossible, like wanting the fig tree to bear no sap in its figs, or babies not to cry.
claims.shared: Adds ignorance of good and bad and the impossibility of the demand. The semicolon is removed, and 12.12’s question replaces the flat “can do nothing else”. The fig tree and babies come from 12.12 alone. The line judges my demand and does not say wrongdoers bear no fault.

support.quote: “Every soul,” he says, “is deprived of truth against its will.” So too, then, of justice and self-control and kindness and everything of that kind. It is most necessary to remember this continually, for you will be gentler towards everyone.
support.follows: No soul loses truth, justice, self-control or kindness willingly, and keeping this in mind makes me gentler towards everyone.
gives: People do wrong against their will

support.quote: and if not rightly, then plainly they do them against their will and in ignorance.
support.follows: If what they do is not right, they do it against their will and without knowing better.
gives: People do wrong against their will
in ignorance of what is good and bad

support.quote: All these things have come upon them through ignorance of what is good and bad.
support.follows: The faults of the people I will meet come from not knowing what is good and what is bad.
gives: in ignorance of what is good and bad

support.quote: For what are they to do, having a disposition like that?
support.follows: Someone with that disposition cannot be expected to act otherwise.
gives: With a disposition like theirs, what are they to do?

support.quote: whoever does not want the bad person to do wrong is like someone who does not want the fig tree to bear sap in its figs, or babies to cry, or the horse to neigh, or any of the other things that have to be.
support.follows: Wanting a bad person not to do wrong is like wanting a fig tree to have no sap: both wish away something that has to be.
gives: like wanting the fig tree to bear no sap in its figs, or babies not to cry

support.quote: that to require bad people not to do wrong is madness, for it aims at the impossible.
support.follows: Requiring bad people not to do wrong is madness, because it asks for the impossible.
gives: To require that bad people do no wrong is to demand the impossible

support.quote: “Is it possible, then, for there to be no shameless people in the universe?” It is not possible. Then do not demand the impossible.
support.follows: There cannot be a world without shameless people, so I should not demand one.
gives: To require that bad people do no wrong is to demand the impossible

claims.t: No one who wrongs me can harm me, because no one can wrap me in what is shameful. What is bad for me exists only in my own mind. The one who does the wrong is the one harmed: they have condemned themselves, as if tearing at their own face.
claims.shared: Explains why no harm reaches me and where harm falls instead. The wrapping image is from 1.15 alone, and the location of harm in the mind from 9.43 alone. Applying the torn face to the wrongdoer is our reading of 12.12’s “this”.

support.quote: can neither be harmed by any of them, for no one will wrap me in what is shameful
support.follows: None of the people I will meet can harm me, because none of them can wrap me in what is shameful.
gives: No one who wrongs me can harm me
no one can wrap me in what is shameful

support.quote: And what harm have you in fact suffered? For you will find that none of those you are provoked at has done anything of a kind that was going to make your mind worse; and it is there that what is bad for you, and what harms you, has its whole existence.
support.follows: No one who provokes me has made my mind worse, and only there can anything be bad for me or harm me.
gives: No one who wrongs me can harm me
What is bad for me exists only in my own mind

support.quote: I shall certainly not be harmed; it is you who are being harmed, child.

claims.role: Teaching them, or bearing with them
claims.t: When someone is mistaken, I teach them kindly if I can and show them what they fail to see, without reproach or any show of putting up with them. If I cannot, I bear with them. Kindness was given to me for this, and gentleness as an antidote to the unfeeling person.
claims.shared: Adds the manner of teaching and the fallback. Teaching stays conditional and no success is promised. The antidote image is from 9.43 alone. 10.4’s withdrawal of self-blame goes to the margin.

claims.t: If someone despises me, blames me or hates me, that is for them to see to. My part is to be found doing and saying nothing that deserves to be despised. When I look into the springs of their judgment, I do not need their testimony. I need not be torn apart over what they think of me.
claims.shared: Covers contempt and hatred rather than wrongs. “Testimony” and “springs of their judgment” are from 7.34 alone, and “torn apart” from 9.25 alone. Independence of their opinion is not ill will, as c3 keeps.

claims.t: When someone wrongs me, I consider at once what they judged to be good or bad. I see what sort of person they are and what compulsions their principles have laid on them. claims.t: To be indignant at people and to turn away from them is against nature, and so is a scowl on the face. Anger and harshness are both weakness. In anger I have been wounded and have given in. If I become estranged from one who is by nature kin and friend, I desert my post as surely as if I had abandoned my own action from fright.

support.quote: So to work against one another is against nature; and to be indignant and to turn away is to work against one another.
support.follows: Working against one another is against nature, and being indignant and turning away is a way of working against.

claims.t: When someone seems to have done wrong, I ask how I know that it is a wrong. I have not grasped it for certain, because many things are done with some further purpose in view. If the thing was done rightly, I should not be annoyed.

single.label: A false belief is strong
single.t: To people with jaundice honey appears bitter, to those bitten by a mad dog water appears frightening, and to small children their little ball appears beautiful. Why, then, am I angry? A false belief has no less power than the bile or the poison.
single.quote: To people with jaundice honey appears bitter, and to those bitten by a mad dog water appears frightening, and to small children their little ball appears beautiful. Why, then, am I angry? Or do you think that a false belief has less power than the bile has over the person with jaundice and the poison over the one bitten by a mad dog?
single.why: Single source, 6.52. All three images are restored, with “appears” in place of “tastes” and the question kept as a question. It addresses anger only and says nothing about teaching.
single.follows: A false belief rules a person as bile rules the jaundiced, so it makes no sense for me to be angry at them.

single.label: Reason answering reason
single.t: I have reason too, so I stir the other person’s rational disposition with my own: I show them, I remind them. If they listen, I will cure them, and there is no need of anger.
single.quote: Well then, you have reason too: stir a rational disposition with a rational disposition; show them, remind them. For if they listen, you will cure them, and there is no need of anger.
single.why: Single source, 5.22. The cure depends on their listening, and the passage does not say what follows if they do not.
single.follows: I have reason as they do, so I can show and remind them; if they listen, they are cured and anger is not needed.

single.label: Each morning
single.t: At dawn I say to myself beforehand: I shall meet a meddler, an ungrateful person, an insolent one, a deceitful one, an envious one, an unsocial one.
single.quote: At dawn, say to yourself beforehand: I shall meet a meddler, an ungrateful person, an insolent one, a deceitful one, an envious one, an unsocial one.
single.why: Single source, 1.15. It stays close to the source wording as a premeditation and makes no claim about what any particular person will do.
single.follows: Each morning I should expect to meet difficult people, naming beforehand the kinds I will meet.

single.label: Taking away the verdict
single.t: It is not other people’s actions that trouble me, for those are in their ruling parts. It is my own judgments. If I take away the verdict that this is something terrible, and am willing to let it go, the anger is gone.
single.quote: Seventh: that it is not their actions that trouble us, for those are in their ruling parts, but our own judgments. At any rate, take away the verdict that this is something terrible, and be willing to let it go, and the anger is gone.
single.why: Single source, 11.16, seventh heading. The verdict is removed, not the event. The difficult reasoning that follows in the source is not pressed.
single.follows: My anger comes from my judgment, not from their act; when I drop the verdict that it is terrible, the anger goes.

single.label: Training partners
single.t: In the gymnasium someone scratches us, butts us and lands a blow, yet we do not mark them down, take offence or suspect them of plotting. We are on our guard, but not as against an enemy: we step aside kindly. I let the same happen in the rest of life and overlook many things in those who are, as it were, my training partners.
single.quote: In the gymnasium someone has scratched us with their nails, and butted us with their head and landed a blow; but we do not mark them down, nor take offence, nor suspect them afterwards of plotting against us. We are on our guard, certainly, yet not as against an enemy, nor with suspicion, but with a kindly stepping aside. Let something like this happen in the other parts of life too: let us overlook many things in those who are, as it were, our training partners.
single.why: Single source, 6.19. The gymnasium image is restored and “as it were” is kept, so the comparison does not become an identity. Staying on guard is preserved.
single.follows: As in the gymnasium, I should be careful without being suspicious, step aside kindly, and let many things pass.

single.label: Indignation is cruel
single.t: It is cruel not to let people go after what appears to them to suit them and to be good for them. Whenever I am indignant that they do wrong, I am in a way refusing them this.
single.quote: How cruel it is not to let people go after the things that appear to them to suit them and to be good for them. And yet in a way you do not allow them to do this, whenever you are indignant that they do wrong.
single.why: Single source, 6.25. “In a way” is kept. The point is against indignation, not against correcting them.
single.follows: Being indignant at people’s wrongs is cruel, because it refuses them the pursuit of what looks good to them.

single.label: Blaming the ungrateful
single.t: Whenever I blame someone as faithless or ungrateful, I turn to myself. Plainly the wrong is mine. Either I trusted that a person with such a disposition would keep faith, or I did a favour without treating it as something that ended there. I did not take the whole fruit at once from the act itself.
single.quote: Above all, whenever you blame someone as faithless or ungrateful, turn to yourself. For plainly the wrong is yours, whether you trusted that a person with such a disposition would keep faith, or whether, in doing a favour, you did not do it as something that ended there, nor so as to have received the whole fruit at once from the act itself.
single.why: Single source, 9.43. The overlong sentence is split and the source’s plain assertion restored. The self-blame is limited to charges of faithlessness or ingratitude, and to misplaced trust or wanting a return. It is not a general rule of blaming myself.
single.follows: If I blame someone for ingratitude, the fault is mine, for trusting them or for wanting a return for a favour.

single.label: Not becoming like them
single.t: I watch that I never come to feel towards the inhuman anything like what the inhuman feel towards human beings.
single.quote: See that you never come to feel towards the inhuman anything like what the inhuman feel towards human beings.
single.why: Single source, 7.36. It is kept as a warning to watch for, not a vow of success. It concerns my own feeling only and gives no reason.
single.follows: However inhuman someone is, I must not come to feel towards them what they feel towards others.

single.label: Life is short
single.t: Whenever I am extremely indignant or take something hard, I remember that human life is a moment long, and in a little while we are all laid out.
single.quote: Sixth: that, whenever you are extremely indignant or even take it hard, human life is a moment long, and in a little while we are all laid out.
single.why: Single source, 11.16, sixth heading. It stays close to the source and keeps the image of being laid out.
single.follows: Whenever I am deeply indignant, I should remember that a human life lasts a moment and that soon we will all be dead.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. In modern editions 9.43 is 9.42, 7.34 is 7.62–63, 11.16 is 11.17–18, 7.19 is 7.26, 1.15 is 2.1, 12.12 is 12.16, 9.25 is 9.27, 11.12 is 11.13, 6.19 is 6.20, 6.25 is 6.27, 7.18 is 7.24–25, 9.9 is 9.11, 11.8 is 11.8b–9, 5.22 is 5.28a, 7.36 is 7.65, 6.52 is 6.57 and 8.56 is 8.59; 10.30 and 10.4 are the same.

The opening is 130 characters and states the distinction itself: “wrongs me” grants the wrong, and the denial covers only damage to my character. 9.43 says no one provoking me has done anything to make my mind worse, and 1.15 says no one will wrap me in what is shameful. “A worse person” is our joint wording for the two. That harm exists only in the mind is left to c2. Teaching stays conditional. “Bear with them” is 8.56’s wording and “kindly” is 9.9’s fallback.
articles.limit: This is an editorial synthesis of separate notes, not a single doctrine stated by the author. Teaching is always conditional and no success is promised. The opening grants that people do wrong me and denies only that the wrong can make me a worse person. “A worse person” is our wording for 9.43’s mind made worse and 1.15’s being wrapped in what is shameful. Where c2 says no one “can harm me”, it means the same harm to the mind and does not deny that wrongs or injuries occur. The impossibility of a world without wrongdoers addresses my own demand and anger. It does not say that wrongdoers bear no fault or that nothing should be resisted or corrected. Kindness here is not approval: the sources also keep guard, refuse flattery and hold to right action. In c3 the people wished well are those 9.25 names, who blame or hate me, and joining them to 9.9’s people who cannot be taught is our editing. The gods’ help is towards ordinary things those people care about and does not endorse those things. Self-blame in 9.43d is limited to charges of faithlessness or ingratitude, and 10.4 withdraws self-blame when teaching fails. 7.18’s scowl and 7.36 touch the theme only obliquely. Reading 12.12’s torn face as the wrongdoer’s self-harm is our interpretation.

aside.11.14: About counterfeit frankness, a “wolf’s friendship”, and how real goodness shows in the eyes. It does not speak of meeting someone who wrongs me.

claims.t: Now it rests with me that my soul holds no wickedness, no craving and no disturbance. I keep my ruling part in my own power, and no one can rob me of the power to choose.

claims.t: People may kill, butcher and curse. Nothing they do captures or stains a mind that is gathered into itself, free of passions, clean and just. That mind is a citadel, and I have nothing better fortified to flee to. I guard myself at every hour so as to be free.
claims.shared: Text unchanged and anchor corrected. The outrages are admitted and only their effect on a mind in this state is judged. “Captures” rests on 8.46. “Stains” takes its word from the spring in 8.50b and its application to the mind from 8.50a, where the mind stays clean. The citadel is from 8.46 alone, and the spring itself stays in the margin as a comparison.

support.quote: Remember that the ruling part becomes unconquerable when, gathered into itself, it is content with itself
support.follows: The ruling part cannot be conquered when it is gathered into itself and content with itself.

support.quote: This is why the mind free of passions is a citadel, for a human being has nothing better fortified to flee to, where they would from then on be beyond capture.
support.follows: A mind free of passions is a fortress: whoever flees to it cannot be captured.
gives: Nothing they do captures or stains a mind
free of passions

support.follows: A clear spring quickly washes away mud or dung thrown into it and is not stained by them.
gives: Nothing they do captures or stains a mind

support.quote: If you guard yourself at every hour so as to be free
support.follows: The mind stays an ever-flowing spring if I guard myself at every hour so as to be free.
gives: I guard myself at every hour so as to be free

claims.t: I wipe out an impression by speaking to myself, and I keep doing it. I guard without a break against four turns my ruling part takes, and whenever I catch one I wipe it away, saying a sentence over it.
claims.shared: Adds the method to the opening: wiping is done in words and without a break. The four turns are from 11.17 alone and are kept apart from impressions in general.

support.quote: Wipe out the impression.
support.follows: An impression can be wiped out, and Marcus tells himself to do it.
gives: I wipe out an impression

support.follows: Four turns of the ruling part are to be watched for and wiped away when caught, with a sentence said over each.

claims.t: I can stop an impulse. I keep watch on my impulses to act, so that each is held with a reservation and is social. At each impulse I give what is just. I see what kind of thing each thing is, and my impulse goes by that thing’s worth. I quench desire and keep away from it altogether.
claims.shared: Plain sentences replace the list, and justice keeps its own sentence from 4.18. Worth is jointly supported by 11.31 and 8.27, and desire by 9.6 and 11.31. Stopping an impulse (9.6) stands beside directing impulses and is not harmonised with them. The reservation and “altogether” are Epictetus’s words in 11.31. This claim’s quotes do not say what the reservation permits when an act is blocked, so that point is carried by the opening and c6 from 6.45, not asserted here.

support.quote: To stop an impulse.
support.follows: An impulse can be stopped, and one is to stop it.

support.quote: in the field of the impulses keep up attention, so that they are with a reservation, so that they are social, so that they are according to worth
support.follows: Impulses must be watched so that each carries a reservation, serves the community and matches the worth of its object.

support.follows: One is to keep away from desire entirely.
gives: I quench desire and keep away from it altogether

claims.t: I do no act at random or in a slovenly way, but by a rule that goes to make up the art. I do not roam or wander among impressions, and at every impression I keep the sure grasp.
claims.shared: 4.2 leaves the art unnamed, so “art of living” is removed. The gloss “so clear that it cannot be false” was editorial and is cut. The sure grasp is from 4.18 alone.

support.quote: Let no act be done at random, or otherwise than according to a rule that goes to make up the art.
support.follows: Every act should follow a rule that belongs to the art, and none should be done at random.
gives: I do no act at random or in a slovenly way
by a rule that goes to make up the art

support.quote: Not to be slovenly in actions
support.follows: My actions should not be slovenly.

support.quote: not to wander in impressions
support.follows: I should not let myself wander from one impression to another.

support.quote: at every impression to keep the sure grasp
