claims.role: When I am kept from something
claims.t: When someone uses force and stands in my way, I change over to being content and free of distress. I use the hindrance for another virtue that is still possible. When it is not possible to read, it is possible to hold back insolence and to get the better of pleasures and pains. I remember that my impulse was with a reservation, and that I was not desiring what is impossible.
claims.shared: The trigger is restored to force standing in the way, as in 6.45. The reading example is from 8.7 alone, where the loss is conceded as real. No claim is made that outcomes are attained.

support.quote: If, however, someone uses force and stands in the way, change over to being content and free of distress, and use the hindrance for another virtue
support.follows: When someone forcibly blocks what I set out to do, I should be content and use the hindrance to practise another virtue.
gives: When someone uses force and stands in my way, I change over to being content and free of distress
I use the hindrance for another virtue that is still possible

support.quote: remember that your impulse was with a reservation, and that you were not desiring what is impossible
support.follows: When blocked, I am to remember that my impulse had a reservation and that I was not desiring the impossible.
gives: I remember that my impulse was with a reservation, and that I was not desiring what is impossible

support.quote: It is not possible to read. But it is possible to hold back insolence. But it is possible to get the better of pleasures and pains.
support.follows: Reading may not be possible, but holding back insolence and getting the better of pleasures and pains still are.
gives: I use the hindrance for another virtue that is still possible

single.label: What is at stake
single.t: The contest is not about just anything. It is about being mad or not.
single.quote: is not about just anything, but about being mad or not
single.why: Single source: Epictetus as quoted in 11.31, kept in his third-person framing. The original’s list of what the contest governs was not in the quote.
single.follows: Epictetus says the contest is about being mad or not, not about some ordinary matter.

single.label: Another’s wrong
single.t: The wrong another person did, I leave where the wrong came to be.
single.quote: The wrong that person did, leave it there, where the wrong came to be.
single.why: Single source, 7.21. Keeps the image of place and does not interpret it as “with them”.
single.follows: A wrong stays with the one who did it, and I should leave it there.

single.label: The ungrateful
single.t: It is possible for me not to be angry with the insensitive and the ungrateful and, more than that, to care for them.
single.quote: But it is possible not to be angry with the insensitive and the ungrateful, and more than that, to care for them.
single.why: Single source, 8.7. Kept as a possibility, not turned into a vow.
single.follows: It is possible not to be angry with the insensitive and ungrateful, and even to care for them.

single.label: Three sentences
single.t: Over three turns of my mind I say, one for each: “This imagining is not necessary.” “This one dissolves community.” “This thing you are about to say is not from yourself.”
single.quote: “This imagining is not necessary.” “This one dissolves community.” “This thing you are about to say is not from yourself.”
single.why: Single source, 11.17. The three formulas stand verbatim as self-address, and the fourth turn is treated separately.
single.follows: Each of three turns has its sentence: this imagining is not needed, this breaks community, these words are not my own.

single.label: Beaten by the body
single.t: One turn of my mind I reproach myself for: the more divine part in me beaten and lying down under the less worthy, mortal portion, the body, and under its rough or smooth movements.
single.quote: The fourth is the one for which you will reproach yourself: that this is the mark of the more divine part in you being beaten and lying down under the less worthy and mortal portion, that of the body, and under its rough or smooth movements.
single.why: Single source, 11.17. Framed as self-reproach, not a vow. “Rough or smooth” is kept rather than glossed as pain and pleasure.
single.follows: When the more divine part gives way to the body and its movements, it has been beaten, and that is a cause for self-reproach.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. In modern editions 7.21 is 7.29–31a, 11.17 is 11.19, 8.27 is 8.29, 6.45 is 6.50, 8.46 is 8.48, 8.49 is 8.51a, 11.31 is 11.36–38, 4.18 is 4.22, 8.50 is 8.51b, 8.7 is 8.8 and 9.6 is 9.7; 4.2 is the same.

The unsupported word “first” is removed. The sources speak of wiping out an impression. The reservation in 6.45 and 11.31 qualifies my impulse to act, and 6.45 shows someone standing in the way. “Without insisting” is our plain gloss of the reservation.
articles.limit: “Wipe out” is not uniform across the sources: 4.18 keeps a sure grasp of impressions, 8.27 pairs wiping with seeing each thing’s worth, and 11.17 targets four named turns, so the opening’s “set an impression aside” must not be read as erasing every impression. Stopping an impulse (9.6) and directing impulses (4.18, 6.45, 11.31) are left side by side. The reservation rests on 6.45 and 11.31 only. In the opening, “without insisting that nothing must stand in my way” is our plain gloss of the reservation, drawn from 6.45, where someone stands in the way and the impulse was not a desire for the impossible. What the reservation permits when an act is blocked is stated only in c6 and the 6.45 margin, because c4’s quotes do not say it. The sayings on choice, the art of assent, desire and madness are Epictetus’s as quoted by Marcus. The mind’s security is conditional on hourly guarding and a passion-free, just state, and it does not deny that the outrages happen. In c2 the word “stains” is carried over from the spring comparison in 8.50, and the spring itself is kept in the margin as a comparison. Joining the unnamed “art” of 4.2 to Epictetus’s art of assent would be our interpretation, so it is not made.

statement.t: I can set an impression aside. I can decide what to do without insisting that nothing must stand in my way.

parts.words: I can set an impression aside
I can decide what to do without insisting that nothing must stand in my way

statement.kind: A power and its daily exercise
statement.form: The unsupported word “first” is removed. The sources speak of wiping out an impression. The reservation in 6.45 and 11.31 qualifies my impulse to act, and 6.45 shows someone standing in the way. “Without insisting” is our plain gloss of the reservation.

empty.doubt: No passage in this section asks what holds if wiping out impressions and checking impulses were not in my power.

articles.title: Good whatever others say, and open to being set right

claims.t: Whatever anyone does or says, I must be good, as an emerald must be emerald and have its own colour. When I act well and am spoken ill of, I do not let the blame or the talk that comes afterwards pull me away.
claims.shared: Keeps the emerald as a comparison, not an identity. The joint phrase rests on 7.24 and 5.3. “Kingly” is a quoted saying in 7.24 alone and goes to the margin. The critics are not called wrong.

support.quote: Whatever anyone does or says, I must be good; just as if gold or emerald or purple were always saying this: “Whatever anyone does or says, I must be emerald and have my own colour.”
support.follows: Whatever anyone else does or says, I must still be good, as an emerald must still be an emerald and have its own colour.
gives: Whatever anyone does or says, I must be good
as an emerald must be emerald and have its own colour

support.quote: “It is kingly to act well and yet be spoken ill of.”
support.follows: To act well and still be spoken ill of befits a king.
gives: When I act well and am spoken ill of

support.quote: Judge yourself worthy of every word and deed that accords with nature, and do not let the blame or the talk that comes afterwards from some people pull you away
support.follows: When I say or do what accords with nature, the blame and talk that come afterwards from some people should not pull me away from it.
gives: When I act well and am spoken ill of
I do not let the blame or the talk that comes afterwards pull me away

claims.t: My mind must shape and order itself. I stand upright, not set upright, as the headland stands while the waves break against it without pause. I need no service from outside and no quiet that others provide.
claims.shared: Standing is the joint point of 3.6 and 4.40. The waves are left unidentified, as in the source. Self-ordering is 7.24 alone and independence of service and quiet is 3.6 alone. No semicolon and no added “anything else”.

support.quote: while the mind itself is not shaped and put in order by itself
support.follows: The mind ought to shape itself and put itself in order; it is shameful when it does not.
gives: My mind must shape and order itself

support.quote: So one must be upright, not set upright.
support.follows: One must stand straight of oneself, not be straightened or propped up by something else.
gives: I stand
upright, not set upright

support.quote: And let there be cheerfulness within, and no need of service from outside, and no need of the quiet that others provide.
support.follows: Cheerfulness should come from within, without needing help from outside or a quiet that others provide.
gives: I need no service from outside and no quiet that others provide

support.quote: To be like the headland against which the waves break without pause; but it stands, and around it the water that had swelled up is put to sleep.
support.follows: I should be like a headland: the waves break on it without pause, it stands, and the swell around it grows calm.
gives: I stand
as the headland stands while the waves break against it without pause

claims.role: Changing my mind for the truth
claims.t: When someone sets me right and makes it plain that I am not judging or acting rightly, I gladly change my mind. The change is no less free, because the judgment is still my own. What moves me must be just or of common benefit, not what appeared pleasant or well thought of. I am looking for the truth, by which no one was ever harmed.
claims.shared: Adds to the opening the condition of actual demonstration, the freedom of yielding and the test for what may move me. “Gladly” is 6.20 alone and the test of just or common benefit is 4.10 alone. “No less free” does not make yielding better than holding firm.

support.quote: The second is to change one’s mind, if it turns out that someone is at hand who sets one right and leads one away from some mistaken notion.
support.follows: I should be ready to change my mind when someone is at hand to set me right and lead me away from a mistaken notion.
gives: When someone sets me right
I gladly change my mind

support.quote: But the leading away must always come from something persuasive, as being just or of common benefit, and what is preferred must be of that kind only, not because it appeared pleasant or well thought of.
support.follows: I should change only when persuaded by what is just or of common benefit, never because the new view is pleasant or well regarded.
gives: What moves me must be just or of common benefit, not what appeared pleasant or well thought of

support.quote: Remember that to change your mind, too, and to follow the one who sets you right is no less free.
support.follows: Changing my mind and following the one who sets me right is no less free.
gives: When someone sets me right
I gladly change my mind
The change is no less free

support.quote: For the activity is yours, carried through according to your own impulse and judgment, and indeed according to your own mind.
support.follows: When I follow someone who corrects me, the act is still mine, done by my own impulse, judgment and mind.
gives: because the judgment is still my own

support.quote: If anyone can refute me and make it plain to me that I am not judging or acting rightly, I will gladly change.
support.follows: If anyone shows me plainly that I am judging or acting wrongly, I will change, and gladly.
gives: makes it plain that I am not judging or acting rightly
I gladly change my mind

support.quote: For I am looking for the truth, by which no one was ever harmed; the one who is harmed is the one who persists in their own delusion and ignorance.
support.follows: What I want is the truth, which harms no one; the one harmed is the one who holds on to delusion and ignorance.
gives: I am looking for the truth, by which no one was ever harmed

claims.t: I court approval when I flatter, try to please and show off, and I could have been rid of these long ago. The mind that says “Let everyone praise whatever I do” is a diseased eye that wants the green things.
claims.shared: “Court approval” is our editorial label for what 5.5 and 10.35 share. “Rid of these long ago” is 5.5 alone and covers only the 5.5 faults. The eye image is 10.35 alone and stays in the third person as framed. 10.35’s wider scope is noted in the margin.

support.quote: to flatter, to blame your poor body, to try to please, to show off
support.follows: Flattering, trying to please and showing off are among the faults no lack of talent forces on me.
gives: I court approval
when I flatter, try to please and show off

support.quote: you could have been rid of these long ago
support.follows: I could have got rid of these faults long ago; nothing in my nature kept me from it.
gives: I could have been rid of these long ago

support.quote: “Let everyone praise whatever I do,” is an eye that looks for the green things
support.follows: A mind that says “Let everyone praise whatever I do” is like an eye that looks only for the green things.
gives: I court approval
The mind that says “Let everyone praise whatever I do”
is a diseased eye that wants the green things

support.quote: The healthy eye must see everything that can be seen, and not say, “I want the green things”; for that belongs to someone whose eyes are diseased.
support.follows: A healthy eye takes in everything there is to see; wanting only the green things is a sign of diseased eyes.
gives: is a diseased eye that wants the green things

claims.t: I accustom myself to stay with what another person is saying, without inattention, and as far as possible to be in the soul of the one who speaks. I enter into each person’s ruling part, and I allow every other person to enter into my own.
claims.shared: Entering another’s mind is common to 6.48 and 8.58. The limit “as far as possible” is 6.48 alone and the reciprocal opening of my own mind is 8.58 alone. Attention is not agreement. The added gloss on “ruling part” is dropped.

support.quote: Accustom yourself to be with what another person is saying, without inattention, and, as far as possible, be in the soul of the one who speaks.
support.follows: I should train myself to follow what another person says closely and, as far as I can, be inside the soul of the one speaking.
gives: I accustom myself to stay with what another person is saying, without inattention
as far as possible
to be in the soul of the one who speaks

support.quote: To enter into each person’s ruling part, and also to allow every other person to enter into one’s own ruling part.
support.follows: I should enter into each person’s ruling part and let every other person enter into mine.
gives: to be in the soul of the one who speaks
I enter into each person’s ruling part
I allow every other person to enter into my own

single.label: Their impulse is their own
single.t: Some people blame or talk about what I have done. They have a ruling part of their own and act on an impulse of their own, and I do not look round at their blame or their talk.
single.quote: For those people have a ruling part of their own and act on an impulse of their own. You, for your part, do not look round at those things
single.why: Single source, 5.3. “Those things” is replaced by its referent, the blame and talk. The critics are left to their own judgment, not called wrong.
single.follows: Other people judge and act from their own minds and impulses, and I need not keep looking at what moves them.

single.label: One road
single.t: I go the straight road right through, following my own nature and the common nature, and the road of these two is one.
single.quote: go the straight road right through, following your own nature and the common nature; and the road of these two is one.
single.why: Single source, 5.3. The road image is kept nearly verbatim because it carries the idea.
single.follows: I should go straight on following my own nature and the common nature, and the two take one road.

single.label: Being, not discussing
single.t: I no longer discuss at all what the good man is like. My task is to be one.
single.quote: No longer to discuss at all what the good man is like, but to be one.
single.why: Single source, 10.18. “No longer” is kept, so the discussion is ended, not disowned. The semicolon is removed.
single.follows: The time for discussing what a good man is has ended; what is left is to be one.

single.label: What is in my power
single.t: I offer what is wholly in my power: being genuine, dignity, bearing hard work, not loving pleasure, not complaining of my lot, needing little, kindness, freedom, plainness, no idle talk, greatness. Lack of natural gift is no excuse for withholding these.
single.quote: Offer those, then, which are wholly in your power: being genuine, dignity, bearing hard work, not loving pleasure, not complaining of your lot, needing little, kindness, freedom, plainness, no idle talk, greatness. Do you not see how many things you are already able to offer, for which lack of natural gift or unfitness is no excuse, and yet you still stay down below of your own will?
single.why: Single source, 5.5. The full list is restored instead of “and more”. The admitted slowness that must still be worked on is in the margin.
single.follows: These qualities depend on no natural gift, so I can show them now and have no excuse for lacking them.

single.label: Fitting and true
single.t: If it is not fitting, I do not do it. If it is not true, I do not say it.
single.quote: If it is not fitting, do not do it; if it is not true, do not say it.
single.why: Single source, 12.13. The reason clause breaks off in the source, so none is supplied.
single.follows: Before acting I ask whether the act is fitting, and before speaking whether the words are true.

single.label: A practice · speaking
single.t: Both in the senate and to anyone at all, I speak with decorum, not over-distinctly, and I use sound speech.
single.quote: To speak, both in the senate and to anyone at all, with decorum, not over-distinctly; to use sound speech.
single.why: Single source, 8.28. It concerns manner of speech for every audience. The source’s wording is kept and the earlier gloss “too careful or studied” is removed as interpretation.
single.follows: Whether in the senate or with anyone, I should speak with decorum, not with an over-careful delivery, and say what is sound.

single.label: A practice · bearing
single.t: My body too must be firmly set, not thrown about in movement or in posture. What my mind gives my face, keeping it composed and graceful, I require of my whole body as well. All this I keep up without affectation.
single.quote: The body too must be firmly set, and not thrown about, either in movement or in posture. For what the mind provides in the face, keeping it composed and graceful, something of that kind must be required in the whole body as well. But all this must be kept up without affectation.
single.why: Single source, 7.32. “Without affectation” is kept as the governing limit, so this is not advice to cultivate a look.
single.follows: My body should be steady and composed, as my face is when my mind governs it, and none of it should be put on.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. In modern editions 7.12 is 7.15, 4.10 is 4.12, 8.28 is 8.30, 6.48 is 6.53, 12.13 is 12.17, 7.32 is 7.60, 3.6 is 3.5, 8.14 is 8.16, 7.24 is 7.36 and 7.37, 4.40 is 4.49, 8.36 is 8.38, 10.18 is 10.16, 8.58 is 8.61 and 6.20 is 6.21; 5.3, 5.5 and 10.35 are the same.

Joins the two shared threads: goodness independent of talk, and openness to correction. “Only” and “gladly” are dropped because each rests on one passage, and the criteria for yielding are left to c3.
articles.limit: No passage says critics are generally wrong or that I should withdraw from people. The only tests given for telling correction from mere blame are in 4.10 and 6.20: what is plainly shown to be true, just or of common benefit. Four points are editorial interpretation, not primary evidence: reading the headland’s waves as opinion, using “court approval” to link 5.5 and 10.35, taking “those things” in 5.3 to mean the blame and talk when it may mean the critics’ own ruling part and impulse, and restating the 7.24 reproach as “my mind must” in c2. 8.36 is too obscure and 12.13 too truncated to carry any claim beyond their bare words.

aside.8.36: Obscure: the speaker is not named, and the Greek as given does not settle whether it means judging together with the wisest men or by the wisest standards.
