articles.title: Keeping to one’s craft

claims.t: I attend only to what I am doing now. If sailors spoke ill of me while I steered, or the sick while I treated them, I would still attend to nothing but how I myself might keep those on board safe or make those under treatment healthy.
claims.shared: Keeps the existing structure and the helmsman and doctor image. The hypothetical stays a hypothetical. It adds the end the attention serves, which is the safety and health of those in my charge. It does not say the criticism is false. The image is from 6.50 alone.

support.quote: To be occupied only with what is being done now
support.follows: My attention is to stay on what is being done now.
gives: I attend only to what I am doing now

support.quote: If the sailors were speaking ill of me while I was steering, or the sick while I was their doctor, would I be attending to anything other than how I myself might bring about what keeps those on board safe, or what makes those under treatment healthy?
support.follows: If the sailors or the sick spoke ill of me while I steered or treated them, I would still attend only to keeping those on board safe or making the sick well.
gives: I attend only to what I am doing now
If sailors spoke ill of me while I steered, or the sick while I treated them
I would still attend to nothing but how I myself might keep those on board safe or make those under treatment healthy

single.label: Up to a point
single.t: Craftsmen in the manual trades adapt to laymen up to a point, but they hold on to the reason of their craft and will not agree to abandon it.
single.quote: Do you not see how craftsmen in the manual trades adapt themselves to laymen up to a point, but all the same hold on to the reason of their craft and will not agree to abandon it?
single.why: Single source, 6.32, left in the third person as the speaker framed it. Restores “reason of their craft” in place of the editorial gloss “rule”. Keeps “up to a point”: accommodation is permitted and only abandonment is refused.
single.follows: Craftsmen fit in with people outside the craft up to a point, but they keep to the craft’s own rule and refuse to give it up.

single.label: My own reason
single.t: It would be shocking if the master builder and the doctor respected the reason of their craft more than I respect my own reason, the reason a human being shares with the gods.
single.quote: Is it not shocking if the master builder and the doctor are to have more respect for the reason of their own craft than a human being has for their own reason, which a human being shares with the gods?
single.why: Single source, 6.32. The last clause is recast so its referent is clear when heard alone: the reason is the one a human being shares with the gods, as the source says. This detail appears in no other passage. The original is a rhetorical question, kept here as a judgement and not as a rule.
single.follows: A human being’s own reason, shared with the gods, deserves at least the respect a builder or a doctor has for the reason of a craft.

single.label: The instrument
single.t: In what I am doing, I keep my mind on the instrument through which I act.
single.quote: and with the instrument through which you act
single.why: Single source, 9.42. “Also” is dropped so the line reads alone. The instrument is not identified in the source and is not identified here as reason, body or tool.
single.follows: I am to be occupied also with the instrument through which I act.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. 6.32 is 6.35 in modern editions and 6.50 is 6.55; 9.42 is the end of 9.41, the last words of one sentence and the sentence after it.

Narrowed to the thought the passages share. The first phrase rests on 9.42 and 6.50, the second on 6.32 and 6.50. The doctor comparison, the gods and “speak ill” are left to their own lines so that no single-source detail becomes joint doctrine. “Turn me from it” does not refuse accommodation, which 6.32 allows.
articles.limit: The opening turns the precept of 9.42, two rhetorical questions and one hypothetical into a first-person practice. It is not a doctrine of ignoring other people: 6.32 allows adapting to laymen up to a point, and the stated aim in 6.50 is the good of the very people who speak ill. Passage 9.42 supports only exclusive attention to the present action together with its unidentified instrument, and its lost opening cannot be used. Only 6.32 speaks of reason and the gods, and it says the sharing of a human being.

statement.t: I keep my attention on the work in hand, and I do not let other people turn me from it.

parts.words: I keep my attention on the work in hand
I do not let other people turn me from it

statement.kind: A likeness, and a rule of attention with its test
statement.form: Narrowed to the thought the passages share. The first phrase rests on 9.42 and 6.50, the second on 6.32 and 6.50. The doctor comparison, the gods and “speak ill” are left to their own lines so that no single-source detail becomes joint doctrine. “Turn me from it” does not refuse accommodation, which 6.32 allows.

empty.breaks: No passage in this section describes losing hold of my reason or my attention, or the way back; 6.32 only calls the first shocking.
empty.doubt: No passage in this section asks what still holds if my reason deserves no more respect than a craft does.

articles.title: Training, and the use of reason

claims.t: I am able where I have been trained. The left hand holds the bridle more firmly than the right, because the bridle is what the left hand has practised. In writing and reading I do not rule before I have been ruled, and this holds still more in life.
claims.shared: Restores the bridle image and keeps the source’s ‘rule’ and ‘ruled’. The first sentence is the joint claim. The bridle is from 12.5 alone and the saying on letters and life from 11.27 alone. Who rules is left unnamed, as in the source.

support.quote: the left hand, though for lack of practice it is no good at anything else, holds the bridle more firmly than the right, because this is what it has had practice in
support.follows: A hand that is no good at anything else is the stronger one at the single thing it has practised.
gives: I am able where I have been trained
The left hand holds the bridle more firmly than the right, because the bridle is what the left hand has practised

support.quote: In writing and reading you will not rule before you have been ruled. This is much more so in life.
support.follows: In writing and reading nobody gives the rules before having been given them, and this is even more true of life.
gives: I am able where I have been trained
In writing and reading I do not rule before I have been ruled, and this holds still more in life

support.quote: The art of living
support.follows: Living is called an art, as wrestling and dancing are.
support.note: Living is called an art, as wrestling and dancing are.

claims.t: I have reason, so I use it, whatever else I lack. When reason is doing its own work, I want nothing else. Others practise philosophy without a tunic, without a book, without bread. I lack the nourishment that comes from learning, and yet I hold to reason.
claims.shared: The first sentence is joint. Sufficiency stays conditional on reason doing its own work, from 4.11 alone. The tunic, book and bread belong to others in 4.25, so they are not claimed as my own lacks. Learning stays ‘nourishment’, a real privation.

support.quote: “Do you have reason?” “I do.” “Then why do you not use it?
support.follows: Someone who agrees that he has reason is asked why, then, he does not use it.
gives: I have reason, so I use it, whatever else I lack

support.quote: For when it is doing its own work, what else do you want?
support.follows: Once reason is doing its own work, there is nothing else to want.
gives: When reason is doing its own work, I want nothing else

support.quote: One person practises philosophy without a tunic, another without a book. Here is another, half naked: “I have no bread,” he says, “and yet I hold to reason.” And I, for my part, do not have the nourishment that comes from learning, and yet I hold to reason.
support.follows: People practise philosophy and hold to reason while lacking a tunic, a book, bread, or the nourishment that learning gives.
gives: I have reason, so I use it, whatever else I lack
Others practise philosophy without a tunic, without a book, without bread
I lack the nourishment that comes from learning, and yet I hold to reason

claims.t: The art of living is more like wrestling than dancing, in that it stands ready for what falls on it unforeseen and does not fall. I count myself better by how I stand in the face of what happens, not by throwing an opponent.
claims.shared: Keeps the comparison as ‘more like’ and limited by ‘in that’. The joint phrase takes ‘better’ and ‘in the face of what happens’ from 7.28 and standing from 7.33. Setting throws aside as the measure is our reading of 7.28 alone, which does not condemn wrestling skill.

support.quote: The art of living is more like the art of wrestling than the art of dancing
support.follows: Living is an art, and it resembles wrestling more than it resembles dancing.
gives: The art of living is more like wrestling than dancing

support.quote: Better at throwing an opponent
support.follows: Someone can be better at throwing an opponent and no better in the ways the sentence goes on to list.
gives: not by throwing an opponent

support.quote: nor better disciplined in the face of what happens
support.follows: Being better at throwing an opponent does not make a person better disciplined in the face of what happens.
gives: I count myself better by how I stand in the face of what happens

support.quote: in that it stands ready for the things that fall on it and are not foreseen, and does not fall
support.follows: The likeness to wrestling is this: the art of living stands ready for what falls on it unforeseen, and does not fall.
gives: in that it stands ready for what falls on it unforeseen and does not fall
I count myself better by how I stand in the face of what happens

single.label: A practice
single.t: I practise even the things I have given up on.
single.quote: Practise even the things you have given up on.
single.why: Single source, 12.5. The original stands verbatim. It names no particular pursuit and none is added.
single.follows: I should practise even what I have given up as hopeless.

single.label: Putting it off
single.t: If I would rather become good tomorrow than be good today, I deserve what is happening to me.
single.quote: You deserve these things that are happening to you; you would rather become good tomorrow than be good today.
single.why: Single source, 8.21. Kept as a conditional self-rebuke about delay, not a doctrine that misfortune is punishment and not a vow.
single.follows: A person who prefers becoming good tomorrow to being good today is told that he deserves what is happening to him.

single.label: Winning without improving
single.t: I can be better at throwing an opponent and no more social, no more modest, no better disciplined in the face of what happens, and no kinder towards the oversights of those near me.
single.quote: but not more social, nor more modest, nor better disciplined in the face of what happens, nor kinder towards the oversights of those nearby
single.why: Single source, 7.28. Restores the fourth item, discipline, which the original dropped. ‘Be’ replaces ‘become’ because the fragment has no verb. It states a possibility, not a verdict on any person.
single.follows: Being better at throwing an opponent is not being more social, more modest, better disciplined, or kinder towards the oversights of those nearby.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. In modern editions 12.5 is 12.6, 11.27 is 11.29 and 11.30, 4.11 is 4.13, 4.25 is 4.30, 8.21 is the second half of 8.22, 7.28 is 7.52 and 7.33 is 7.61.

Shorter than the original and removes the unclear ‘it’. Each phrase rests on two passages: art and training on 7.33, 11.27 and 12.5, reason in use on 4.11 and 4.25, readiness on 7.33 and 7.28. It does not claim that practice makes one good.
articles.limit: The link between training and reason or goodness is editorial: 12.5 and 7.33 mention neither. ‘Be ruled first’ in 11.27 and ‘be good today’ in 8.21 remain in unresolved tension, and no passage names the ruler. The wrestling image is used only for readiness and not falling. Counting myself better by steadiness and not by throws is our reading of 7.28, which has no stated subject and does not condemn wrestling skill.

statement.t: Living is an art I train in. I use the reason I already have, and I stand ready for what happens.

parts.words: Living is an art I train in
I use the reason I already have
I stand ready for what happens

statement.kind: A likeness, with its means and its use
statement.form: Shorter than the original and removes the unclear ‘it’. Each phrase rests on two passages: art and training on 7.33, 11.27 and 12.5, reason in use on 4.11 and 4.25, readiness on 7.33 and 7.28. It does not claim that practice makes one good.

empty.doubt: No passage in this section asks what holds if living cannot be trained like a skill, or if reason is not enough for it.

articles.title: What I turn to

claims.t: I gain by going back. By continually going back to the harmony I get a firmer hold on it. I go back often to philosophy and rest in it. Because of philosophy the things at court seem bearable to me, and I seem bearable among them.
claims.shared: Gives the reason for returning. The gloss “my inner tuning” is removed as editorial, and the semicolon is gone. “At court” resolves the quote’s “there” from the same passage, 6.10. The gain is only “seem bearable”, and it cuts both ways. The firmer hold is from 6.9 alone, and the bearable court from 6.10 alone.

support.quote: For you will have a firmer hold on the harmony by continually going back to it.
support.follows: Continually going back to the harmony gives a firmer hold on it.
gives: I gain by going back
By continually going back to the harmony I get a firmer hold on it

support.quote: Go back here often and rest in philosophy. Because of it, the things there seem bearable to you, and you seem bearable among them.
support.follows: Marcus is to go back often to philosophy and rest in it; philosophy is why the court seems bearable to him and he seems bearable there.
gives: I gain by going back
I go back often to philosophy and rest in it
Because of philosophy the things at court seem bearable to me, and I seem bearable among them

claims.t: I want one thing only and I take pleasure in one thing. I want to move and to hold back as civic reason thinks right. My pleasure and my rest are in going from one social act to another social act, with god in mind.
claims.shared: Both passages say “one thing”, but they do not say it is the same thing, so the want (9.10) and the pleasure (6.6) stay distinct. The gloss “member of a community” is dropped. “With god in mind” and “hold back” are kept as part of the instructions. “Civic reason” is not a state authority.

support.quote: Take pleasure in one thing and rest in it: going from one social act to another social act, with god in mind.
support.follows: The one thing to take pleasure in and rest in is going from one act for the common life to the next, with god in mind.
gives: I want one thing only and I take pleasure in one thing
My pleasure and my rest are in going from one social act to another social act, with god in mind

support.quote: want one thing only: to move and to hold back as civic reason thinks right
support.follows: The one thing to want is to move and to hold back as civic reason thinks right.
gives: I want one thing only and I take pleasure in one thing
I want to move and to hold back as civic reason thinks right

claims.t: I go back quickly and continually. When circumstances force me to be, as it were, thrown into confusion, I go back quickly into myself and step out of the rhythm no more than I am forced to. I run to my own ruling part. At present I wait on the court as on a stepmother, and I keep going back to philosophy as to a mother.
claims.shared: Describes the practice of returning. “Quickly” is from 6.9 and “continually” from 6.10. The stepmother image stays a comparison, tied to “now” by “at present”, and the service to the court is kept. The disturbance is conceded as forced. The gloss on the ruling part is removed as commentary.

support.quote: When circumstances force you to be, as it were, thrown into confusion, go back quickly into yourself, and do not step out of the rhythm more than you are forced to.
support.follows: When circumstances shake me, I should go back into myself quickly and leave the rhythm no more than I am forced to.
gives: I go back quickly and continually
When circumstances force me to be, as it were, thrown into confusion, I go back quickly into myself and step out of the rhythm no more than I am forced to

support.quote: If you had a stepmother and a mother at the same time, you would wait on the stepmother, and still you would be continually going back to your mother. That is what the court and philosophy are to you now.
support.follows: Marcus waits on the court as one waits on a stepmother, and keeps going back to philosophy as to a mother.
gives: I go back quickly and continually
At present I wait on the court as on a stepmother, and I keep going back to philosophy as to a mother

support.quote: Run to your own ruling part
support.follows: I should go to my own ruling part, and go at a run.
gives: I run to my own ruling part

claims.t: Among the things that please, I set virtue apart. To cheer myself I think of the strong points of the people I live with, the energy of one, the modesty of another, the generosity of a third. Nothing cheers so much as the likenesses of the virtues showing in their characters, as many at once as possible, so I keep these likenesses ready to hand. I divide a tuneful voice into each of its notes and ask at each one whether this gets the better of me, and so I come to look down on delightful singing. Except for virtue and what comes from virtue, I run to the parts and by dividing them come to look down on them.
claims.shared: The fused point is that virtue is exempt from dissection (11.2) and that likenesses of virtue cheer (6.43). The cheering is a remedy for low spirits and speaks of likenesses, not of the companions being virtuous. The dissection is narrowed to what the quotes name and is not turned on people or the court.

support.quote: When you want to cheer yourself, think of the strong points of the people you live with: for example, the energy of one, the modesty of another, the generosity of a third, and something else in someone else.
support.follows: To cheer myself I should think of what is strong in each person I live with: one’s energy, another’s modesty, another’s generosity.
gives: To cheer myself I think of the strong points of the people I live with, the energy of one, the modesty of another, the generosity of a third

support.quote: For nothing cheers so much as the likenesses of the virtues showing in the characters of the people you live with, and coming together, as many at once as possible. And so they must be kept ready to hand.
support.follows: Nothing cheers like the likenesses of the virtues in the people I live with, many at once, so they are to be kept ready to hand.
gives: Among the things that please, I set virtue apart
Nothing cheers so much as the likenesses of the virtues showing in their characters, as many at once as possible, so I keep these likenesses ready to hand

support.quote: You will look down on delightful singing, on dancing and on the pankration, if you divide the tuneful voice into each of its notes and ask yourself at each one whether this gets the better of you
support.follows: I shall look down on delightful singing if I divide it into its notes and ask at each one whether this gets the better of me.
gives: I divide a tuneful voice into each of its notes and ask at each one whether this gets the better of me, and so I come to look down on delightful singing

support.quote: In general, then, except for virtue and what comes from virtue, remember to run to the parts, and by dividing them to come to look down on them
support.follows: Except for virtue and what comes from it, I should go to the parts of a thing and, by dividing them, come to look down on it.
gives: Among the things that please, I set virtue apart
Except for virtue and what comes from virtue, I run to the parts and by dividing them come to look down on them

claims.t: I do not complain. I toil, but not as someone miserable, and not as someone who wants to be pitied or admired. Let no one hear me finding fault with life at court any more, and let me not hear myself doing it either.
claims.shared: 8.8 is kept as a self-command, not a vow or a confession. “Any more” carries the implied past without my asserting it. The ban concerns court life and does not praise the court. Toil itself is accepted, and only its wretched or audience-seeking manner is refused (9.10).

support.quote: Toil, not as someone miserable, and not as someone who wants to be pitied or admired
support.follows: I should toil without being miserable about it and without wanting pity or admiration for it.
gives: I do not complain
I toil, but not as someone miserable, and not as someone who wants to be pitied or admired

support.quote: Let no one hear you finding fault with life at court any more, and do not hear yourself doing it either.
support.follows: Marcus, who has been finding fault with life at court, is to stop, both aloud to others and silently to himself.
gives: I do not complain
Let no one hear me finding fault with life at court any more, and let me not hear myself doing it either

single.label: Three ruling parts
single.t: I run to my own ruling part, to that of the whole, and to this person’s. To my own, so that I make it a just mind. To that of the whole, so that I remember along with it what I am a part of. To this person’s, so that I take note whether there is ignorance there or intent, and at the same time reckon that this ruling part is akin.
single.quote: and to that of the whole, and to this person’s. To your own, so that you make it a just mind. To that of the whole, so that you remember along with it what you are a part of. To this person’s, so that you take note whether there is ignorance there or intent, and at the same time reckon that it is akin.
single.why: Single source, 9.20 only, kept in the speaker’s own framing with three distinct purposes. “This person’s” stands as he wrote it. The ignorance-or-intent question is left open, kinship holds either way, and forgiveness is not stated. Semicolons are removed.
single.follows: Beyond my own ruling part, I should go to the whole’s, to remember what I am part of, and to another’s, to see whether ignorance or intent is there and count it akin.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. In modern editions 6.43 is 6.48, 6.9 is 6.11, 9.20 is 9.22, 9.10 is 9.12, 6.6 is 6.7, 6.10 is 6.12 and 8.8 is 8.9; 11.2 is the same.

Philosophy is named once, as where I rest (6.10), and the self is a separate object of return (6.9), not equated with it. “Each act for other people” is our plain rendering of “social act” in 6.6. Its full wording, with “going from one social act to another” and “with god in mind”, stays in c2 and the margin. “I rest too” joins the rest of 6.10 and 6.6, so return serves engagement and is not withdrawal. “Without complaint” joins 9.10’s ban on miserable, pity-seeking toil with 8.8’s ban on fault-finding, which in 8.8 concerns court life only.
articles.limit: The passages never identify the self, the harmony, the ruling part, philosophy, the whole and god as one object of return. The synthesis sets them side by side without equating them. Return serves engagement and is not withdrawal: the court is still served and is called only “bearable”, and that judgement cuts both ways. The opening’s “each act for other people” is our plain rendering of “social act” in 6.6. The opening leaves out “with god in mind” and the movement from one act to the next, both of which c2 and the margin preserve. “At court” in c1 resolves the word “there” from the same passage, 6.10. “Without complaint” and “I do not complain” generalise from two narrower bans: 8.8 forbids fault-finding with court life, aloud or inwardly, and 9.10 forbids toiling as someone miserable or seeking pity or admiration. The dissection of pleasures is not extended to people or the court. Companions show likenesses of virtues, which is not a claim that they are virtuous, and thinking of them is a remedy for low spirits. Kinship in 9.20 implies no rule of forgiveness, and 9.20b borrows “run” and “ruling part” from the start of its own sentence. The link between 6.43 and 11.2 in c4, and the pairing of the two “one thing” sayings in c2, are our editorial interpretation and not a stated doctrine.

statement.t: I keep going back to myself, and to philosophy to rest. I rest too in each act for other people, and I toil without complaint.

parts.words: I keep going back
to myself, and to philosophy to rest
I rest too in each act for other people
I toil without complaint

statement.kind: A habit, what it gives, and the work it serves
statement.form: Philosophy is named once, as where I rest (6.10), and the self is a separate object of return (6.9), not equated with it. “Each act for other people” is our plain rendering of “social act” in 6.6. Its full wording, with “going from one social act to another” and “with god in mind”, stays in c2 and the margin. “I rest too” joins the rest of 6.10 and 6.6, so return serves engagement and is not withdrawal. “Without complaint” joins 9.10’s ban on miserable, pity-seeking toil with 8.8’s ban on fault-finding, which in 8.8 concerns court life only.

empty.doubt: No passage in this section considers what holds if going back does not steady me or if the work stays hard to bear.

articles.title: The morning, and the question before each action

claims.t: When I find it hard to get up, I remind myself that I am getting up to do a human being’s work: social actions, which accord with my nature. Sleep I share with the animals that have no reason. What accords with my nature is more my own, more closely grown to me, and more agreeable too.
claims.shared: The semicolon is removed and the image “more closely grown” from 8.11b is restored. The contrast with animals and the claim of agreeableness come from 8.11 alone. Sleep is not called bad.

support.quote: When you find it hard to wake from sleep, remind yourself that rendering social actions accords with the way you are made and with human nature, whereas sleeping is shared with the animals without reason as well.
support.follows: When waking is hard, I should recall that social action suits the way a human being is made, while sleep is shared with animals.
gives: When I find it hard to get up, I remind myself
social actions, which accord with my nature
Sleep I share with the animals that have no reason

support.quote: And what accords with each one’s nature is more its own, more closely grown to it, and indeed more agreeable too.
support.follows: What fits a thing’s nature is more its own, and more agreeable to it as well.
gives: What accords with my nature is more my own, more closely grown to me, and more agreeable too

support.quote: At dawn, when you are reluctant to get up, have this ready to hand: “I am getting up to do a human being’s work.
support.follows: On a morning when I do not want to get up, I should keep ready the thought that I get up to do a human being’s work.
gives: When I find it hard to get up, I remind myself
I am getting up to do a human being’s work

support.quote: You do not run to what is according to your nature?
support.follows: I ought to hurry towards what is according to my nature, not hang back from it.
gives: social actions, which accord with my nature

support.quote: But do social actions seem cheaper to you, and worth less effort?
support.follows: I should not value social actions less, or think them less worth the effort, than others value the things they love.
gives: social actions, which accord with my nature

claims.t: The little plants, the little birds, the ants, the spiders and the bees do what is their own to do and, for their part, put the universe together. We are all working together towards one finished result. Each works in its own way: some knowingly, some without attending to it, even those who are asleep, even the one who finds fault and the one who tries to stand against what happens. What remains for me is to understand among which of these workers I am placing myself. I ask myself whether I am willing to do what belongs to a human being.
claims.shared: The fault-finder and the resister are restored as two figures, as 6.37b has them. The question from 5.1c now stands in its own sentence, so 6.37c’s “what remains” covers only the choice of place among the workers. The sleepers and the two opponents come from 6.37 alone, and the small creatures from 5.1 alone. The rebuke in 5.1 stays a question to myself, not a vow. The sleepers are not merged with literal rising.

support.quote: Do you not see the little plants, the little birds, the ants, the spiders, the bees doing what is their own to do and, for their part, putting the universe together? And then you are not willing to do what belongs to a human being?
support.follows: Plants and small creatures each do their own work and help put the universe together, so I should be willing to do the work of a human being.
gives: The little plants, the little birds, the ants, the spiders and the bees do what is their own to do and, for their part, put the universe together
Each works in its own way
I ask myself whether I am willing to do what belongs to a human being

support.quote: We are all working together towards one finished result, some of us knowingly and with awareness, others without attending to it, just as Heraclitus, I think, says that even those who are asleep are workers and fellow workers in the things that happen in the universe.
support.follows: Everyone works towards one finished result, aware of it or not; even sleepers are workers in what happens in the universe.
gives: We are all working together towards one finished result
some knowingly, some without attending to it, even those who are asleep

support.quote: One works together in one way, another in another, and, into the bargain, so does even the one who finds fault and the one who tries to stand against the things that happen and do away with them, for the universe had need of such a person too.
support.follows: Each works with the rest in a different way; even the one who finds fault with what happens does, since the universe needed him too.
gives: Each works in its own way
even the one who finds fault and the one who tries to stand against what happens

support.quote: What remains, then, is for you to understand among which of them you are placing yourself.
support.follows: Since everyone works for the whole somehow, what is left to me is to see which kind of worker I am making myself.
gives: What remains for me is to understand among which of these workers I am placing myself

claims.t: At each thing I do, I stop and ask: how does this stand with me, and will I come to regret it? A little while and I am dead, and everything is cleared away. Is death something terrible because it deprives me of this?
claims.shared: The per-action check is joint. The regret question and “cleared away” come from 8.2 alone. The question of 10.29 is left open, as its source leaves it.

support.quote: At each action ask yourself: “How does this stand with me? Will I come to regret it? A little while and I am dead, and everything is cleared away.
support.follows: At each action I should ask how it stands with me and whether I will regret it, remembering that I shall soon be dead.
gives: At each thing I do, I stop and ask
how does this stand with me, and will I come to regret it
A little while and I am dead, and everything is cleared away

support.quote: At each of the things you do, one by one, stop and ask yourself whether death is something terrible because of being deprived of this.
support.follows: At each thing I do, I should stop and ask whether death is terrible because it would take this thing away.
gives: At each thing I do, I stop and ask
Is death something terrible because it deprives me of this

claims.t: When I have done good and another has received it, I do not look for a third thing: to be seen to have done good, or to get a return. I do not shout about it but pass on to another thing, as a vine that has borne its grapes looks for nothing more and passes on to bearing them again in season. I do not tire of being benefited, and I am benefited in giving benefit.
claims.shared: “Pass on to the next good act” is narrowed to “another thing”, as 5.6 has it. The benefit lies in the giving itself, from 7.43 alone. The line does not claim I am unaware of the good I do, so the hedge “in a way” from 5.6 is left to the margin.

support.quote: When you have done good and another has had good done to them, why do you look for a third thing beside these, as fools do: to be seen to have done good as well, or to get a return?
support.follows: Once I have done good and someone has received it, it is foolish to want to be seen doing it as well, or to be repaid.
gives: When I have done good and another has received it
I do not look for a third thing
to be seen to have done good, or to get a return

support.quote: No one tires of being benefited, and benefit is action according to nature. So do not tire of being benefited, in that you give benefit.
support.follows: Giving benefit is itself a benefit to me, and no one tires of being benefited, so I should not tire of giving it.
gives: I do not tire of being benefited, and I am benefited in giving benefit

support.quote: A third, in a way, does not even know what they have done, but is like a vine that has borne its grapes and looks for nothing more after it has once borne its own fruit.
support.follows: The best kind of giver is like a vine that, having borne its grapes, looks for nothing more.
gives: I do not look for a third thing
as a vine that has borne its grapes looks for nothing more and passes on to bearing them again in season

support.quote: A horse that has run, a dog that has tracked, a bee that has made honey, and a human being who has done good, do not shout about it, but pass on to another thing, as a vine passes on to bearing its grapes again in season.
support.follows: A human being who has done good, like a horse that has run, does not shout about it but goes on to the next thing.
gives: I do not shout about it but pass on to another thing
as a vine that has borne its grapes looks for nothing more and passes on to bearing them again in season

support.quote: What more do I look for, if the work in hand is the work of a living being that has mind, is social, and is under the same law as god?
support.follows: If what I am doing is the work of a social being with a mind, under the same law as god, I need look for nothing more.
gives: I do not look for a third thing

claims.t: Whoever I meet, and as far as I can with everything that anyone does, I ask in my own mind about this person: what do they hold to be good and bad, and to what end are they doing this? Given the principles they hold, it will seem to me nothing surprising or strange that they act as they do, and I will remember that they are compelled to act so. But I begin with myself and examine myself first.
claims.shared: “Nothing they do seems strange” is narrowed to actions that follow from the principles held, as 8.13 conditions it. Non-surprise and compulsion come from 8.13 alone. “As far as I can” and self-examination first come from 10.37 alone. No approval or excuse is stated.

support.quote: Whoever you meet, say to yourself at once, beforehand: “What principles does this person hold about what is good and what is bad?
support.follows: Before dealing with anyone, I should ask myself what that person believes to be good and bad.
gives: Whoever I meet
I ask in my own mind about this person
what do they hold to be good and bad
Given the principles they hold, it will seem to me nothing surprising or strange that they act as they do

support.quote: it will seem to me nothing surprising or strange if they do such-and-such things, and I will remember that they are compelled to do so.
support.follows: Knowing what someone believes, I will find nothing strange in what they do, and will remember that they are compelled to do it.
gives: Given the principles they hold, it will seem to me nothing surprising or strange that they act as they do
I will remember that they are compelled to act so

support.quote: Train yourself, as far as you can, with everything that anyone does, to ask in your own mind: “To what end is this person doing this?” But begin with yourself, and examine yourself first.
support.follows: With anything anyone does, I should ask what it is for, and ask it of my own actions first.
gives: as far as I can with everything that anyone does
I ask in my own mind about this person
to what end are they doing this
I begin with myself and examine myself first

single.label: Whether my mind is enough
single.t: Before a task I ask whether my mind is enough for it. If my mind is enough, I use it for the work as a tool given by the nature of the whole. If it is not enough, I step back for someone who can carry the work out better, unless for some other reason the work is my duty. Or I do the work as best I can, taking on a helper who, by using my ruling part as well, can do what is timely and useful for the community now.
single.quote: Is my mind enough for this or not? If it is enough, I use it for the work as a tool given by the nature of the whole. If it is not enough, either I step back from the work in favour of someone who can carry it out better, unless for some other reason it is my duty, or I do it as best I can, taking on as a helper someone who, by making use of my ruling part as well, can do what is timely and useful for the community now.
single.why: Single source 7.5. The helper’s use of my ruling part and the aim of use to the community are restored. Permission to step back stays permission and is limited by duty.
single.follows: If my mind is equal to a task I use it; if not, I give the task to someone better or do it with help.

single.label: A morning question
single.t: As soon as I wake, I ask myself whether it will make any difference to me if someone else blames what is just and right. It will not.
single.quote: Ask yourself as soon as you come out of sleep: will it make any difference to you if what is just and right is blamed by someone else? It will not.
single.why: Single source 10.15. The existing line stands verbatim. It is limited to blame of what is in fact just and right, not to all criticism.
single.follows: If someone else blames what is just and right, that makes no difference to me.

single.label: Too much rest
single.t: Nature has given measures for rest, as it has for eating and drinking. When I go beyond those measures, beyond what is enough, and in action stop short of what I can do, I do not love myself. If I loved myself, I would love my nature too, and what it wills.
single.quote: Nature, though, has given measures for this as well; it has given them for eating and drinking as well; and yet you go beyond the measures, beyond what is enough. But in your actions it is not so: there you stop short of what you can do. For you do not love yourself, since otherwise you would love your nature too, and what it wills.
single.why: Single source 5.1. The semicolon is removed and “beyond what is enough” restored. Rest is measured, not denied. The self-rebuke is kept as a judgement on excess, not as a vow.
single.follows: Going past nature’s measure in rest while falling short in action shows that I do not love my nature, and so do not love myself.

single.label: Waking again
single.t: I sober up and call myself back. When I have woken again and understood that it was dreams that were troubling me, then, awake, I look at the things before me as I looked at those dreams.
single.quote: Sober up and call yourself back. And when you have woken up again and understood that it was dreams that were troubling you, then, awake again, look at these things as you looked at those.
single.why: Single source 6.29. The waking is figurative. The source says only “these things” and “those”. Reading them as the things before me and the dreams is our editorial interpretation.
single.follows: Having seen that what troubled me were dreams, I should look at my waking troubles as I looked at the dreams.

single.label: Not a worthless part
single.t: The one who governs the whole will in any case use me well and take me in as some part of the fellow workers who help the work along. But I must not become a part like the cheap and ridiculous line in the play, the one Chrysippus mentions.
single.quote: For the one who governs the whole will in any case use you well, and will take you in as some part of the fellow workers and of those who help the work along. But you, do not become a part like the cheap and ridiculous line in the play, the one Chrysippus mentions.
single.why: Single source 6.37. The gloss about the line still adding to the play is dropped because the quote does not say it. The warning stays a warning.
single.follows: The one who governs the whole will use me well in any case, but I should not be the worthless line of the play.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. In modern editions 10.15 is 10.13, 8.11 is 8.12, 8.13 is 8.14–15, 7.5 is 7.5–7, 7.43 is 7.73–74, 6.37 is 6.42 and 6.29 is 6.31; 8.2, 5.1, 10.37, 5.6 and 10.29 have the same number.

115 characters. “The work I was made for” is replaced by the quoted wording of 5.1a, which 8.11a supports with waking and human nature. Each of the three phrases rests on two passages. No daily routine is implied beyond what the passages state.
articles.limit: The twelve passages share a practice of short questions put to oneself, but none sets them in one ordered daily routine, and this article does not build one. The figurative waking of 6.29 and the sleepers of 6.37 are kept apart from the literal rising of 5.1 and 8.11. The question of 10.29 is left unanswered. 10.15 covers only blame of what is just, and 8.13 gives non-surprise, not excuse. Looking for nothing more is conditional in 8.2 on the work being that of a rational and social being, and the unaware doing of good in 5.6 holds only “in a way”. Both limits are kept in the margin. The referents supplied in 6.29a are our editorial interpretation.

statement.t: I get up to do a human being’s work, I question each thing I do, and when I have done good I look for nothing more.

parts.words: I get up to do a human being’s work
I question each thing I do
when I have done good I look for nothing more

statement.kind: Three moments of a day
statement.form: 115 characters. “The work I was made for” is replaced by the quoted wording of 5.1a, which 8.11a supports with waking and human nature. Each of the three phrases rests on two passages. No daily routine is implied beyond what the passages state.

empty.doubt: No passage in this section asks what still holds if I was not made for this work or if questioning my actions does no good.

articles.title: Whose praise do I want?

claims.t: Before I fear people as judges, I pass right inside their ruling parts and picture their little souls naked. I see what they chase and what they run from, whom they want to please, and what they are like when they eat and sleep. I look at the wise as well.
claims.shared: The looking is joint across 9.16, 9.32 and 4.31. Fear of judges is 9.16 only. “Want to please” is now their wish, as 6.54 has it, not mine. The naked souls are 9.32 only and the wise are 4.31 only. Eating and sleeping come from 10.20, which never mentions praise, so the link to judges is editorial. No verdict is stated, because the sources leave it to the looking.

support.quote: What the ruling parts of these people are, what sort of things they are in earnest about, and what sort of things win their love and honour.
support.follows: I should consider what rules in these people, what they take seriously, and what they give their love and honour for.
gives: pass right inside their ruling parts

support.quote: Think of yourself as looking at their little souls naked.
support.follows: I should picture their small souls stripped bare, as they really are.
gives: picture their little souls naked

support.quote: Pass inside, right inside, into their ruling parts, and you will see what judges you are afraid of
support.follows: If I go deep into these people’s ruling parts, I will see what kind of judges I am afraid of.
gives: Before I fear people as judges
pass right inside their ruling parts

support.quote: Look closely into their ruling parts, and at the wise as well: what sort of things they run from, and what sort of things they chase.
support.follows: I should look closely into people’s ruling parts, and at the wise too, and see what they run from and what they chase.
gives: pass right inside their ruling parts
what they chase and what they run from
I look at the wise as well

support.quote: What sort of people those are whom they want to please, and for what sort of gains, and through what sort of activities.
support.follows: Anyone who wants to please people should consider what those people are like, what is gained, and what has to be done for it.
gives: whom they want to please

support.quote: What they are like when eating, sleeping, mating, emptying their bowels, and the rest.
support.follows: I should picture these people as they are when they eat, sleep, mate and empty their bowels.
gives: what they are like when they eat and sleep

claims.t: I ask how the people who judge me judge themselves. Do I want praise from a person who curses themselves three times an hour? Do I want to please a person who is not pleased with themselves? Do I want praise from people who know neither where they are nor who they are?
claims.shared: The unclear “it” in the last question is replaced by “praise”. The questions stay questions, since 8.51 asks and issues no blanket verdict. Only the self-judgment phrase is joint, in 9.16 and 8.51. The details are 8.51 alone. The quoted span 8.51b describes the people only, and its link to praise is carried by 8.51a and by the margin quote from the same passage.

support.quote: and what sort of judges they are of themselves as well.
support.follows: Looking into these people also shows what kind of judges they are of themselves.
gives: how the people who judge me judge themselves

support.quote: Do you want to be praised by a person who curses themselves three times an hour? Do you want to please a person who is not pleased with themselves?
support.follows: It makes no sense to want praise from someone who curses themselves, or to want to please someone who is not pleased with themselves.
gives: how the people who judge me judge themselves
praise from a person who curses themselves three times an hour
please a person who is not pleased with themselves

support.quote: people who know neither where they are nor who they are
support.follows: The people who clap know neither where they are nor who they are.
gives: people who know neither where they are nor who they are

claims.t: I make a gift of the present time to myself instead of chasing fame after death. Those who would remember me will be like the people I find hard to bear now, and they too are mortal. Each will very soon die, and then the one who takes over, until the whole memory goes out. What they say or think of me is nothing to me.
claims.shared: Wording unchanged. One anchor is added so that the rememberers are tied to 4.16a. Fame after death and mortality are joint in 8.42 and 4.16. The gift of the present, the hard-to-bear people and the closing judgment are 8.42 only. The succession of rememberers is 4.16 only. The image of lights going out lies outside the quoted span and is kept in the margin.

support.quote: Look: make a gift of this present time to yourself.
support.follows: I should give the time that is here now to myself.
gives: make a gift of the present time to myself

support.quote: People who instead chase fame after death do not take into account that those people will be others of the same kind as these whom they find hard to bear; and those people too are mortal.
support.follows: Those who would praise me later will be like the people I find hard to bear now, and they will die too.
gives: chasing fame after death
like the people I find hard to bear now
they too are mortal

support.quote: Whoever is worked up about fame after death does not picture that each of those who remember them will very soon die too; then in turn the one who takes over from that one, until the whole memory also goes out
support.follows: Everyone who remembers me will soon die, and the one after them too, until all memory of me is gone.
gives: chasing fame after death
Those who would remember me
they too are mortal
Each will very soon die, and then the one who takes over
until the whole memory goes out

support.quote: And what is it to you at all, if those people echo with sounds of such a kind, or hold a judgment of such a kind about you?
support.follows: What later people say about me, or what they think of me, is nothing to me.
gives: What they say or think of me is nothing to me

claims.t: I see how the wish for other people’s good opinion goes against itself. We love ourselves more than everyone else, yet we value other people’s judgment of us above our own. People despise one another yet fawn on one another, and wanting to be above one another they take the lower place. They will not speak well of those who live beside them, yet they prize the good word of those who come after, whom they will never see.
claims.shared: The sources’ own persons are restored: “we” for 12.3 and “they” for 11.13 and 6.17, so I do not confess to things the text says of others. The self-contradiction is joint in 12.3 and 6.17. The fawning paradox is 11.13 only and never mentions fame. No duty to praise contemporaries is stated.

support.quote: each person loves themselves more than everyone else, yet sets less value on their own judgment about themselves than on that of others
support.follows: People love themselves more than anyone, yet they value others’ judgment of them more than their own.
gives: the wish for other people’s good opinion goes against itself
We love ourselves more than everyone else, yet we value other people’s judgment of us above our own

support.quote: Despising one another, they fawn on one another; and wanting to be above one another, they take the lower place beneath one another.
support.follows: People who despise one another fawn on one another, and in wanting to be above one another they put themselves beneath.
gives: People despise one another yet fawn on one another
wanting to be above one another they take the lower place

support.quote: They are unwilling to speak well of the people who live at the same time as them and alongside them, yet they set great store by being spoken well of themselves by those who come after, whom they have never seen and never will see.
support.follows: It is odd to refuse to speak well of those who live beside me and yet care so much that people I will never see speak well of me.
gives: the wish for other people’s good opinion goes against itself
They will not speak well of those who live beside them
they prize the good word of those who come after, whom they will never see

claims.t: What is praised becomes neither worse nor better, and it is conceit to suppose that blame does harm. Whatever is beautiful is beautiful of itself and does not have praise as a part of itself. Nothing beautiful is ruined when it is blamed. I take my own good to be my own action, not another person’s activity.
claims.shared: Semicolon removed. The first phrase is joint in 4.16 and 9.32, and the conceit is 9.32 only. The claim about blame is narrowed to the beautiful, as 4.16 frames it. The good as my own action is 6.46 only, and it names action, not self-approval.

support.quote: At any rate, what is praised becomes neither worse nor better.
support.follows: Being praised makes a thing neither worse nor better.
gives: What is praised becomes neither worse nor better

support.quote: Which of these is beautiful because it is praised, or is ruined when it is blamed?
support.follows: Nothing is beautiful because it is praised, and nothing is ruined because it is blamed.
gives: Nothing beautiful is ruined when it is blamed

support.quote: When they suppose that they do harm by blaming or do good by singing praises, how much conceit.
support.follows: People who think their blame does harm, or their praise does good, think far too much of themselves.
gives: What is praised becomes neither worse nor better
conceit to suppose that blame does harm

support.quote: Everything that is beautiful in any way at all is beautiful of itself and ends in itself, and does not have praise as a part of itself.
support.follows: Whatever is beautiful is beautiful of itself, and praise is no part of its beauty.
gives: beautiful of itself and does not have praise as a part of itself

support.quote: The lover of fame takes their own good to be another person’s activity; the lover of pleasure, their own feeling; the person who has sense, their own action.
support.follows: Whoever loves fame puts their good in what someone else does; a sensible person puts it in their own action.
gives: my own good to be my own action, not another person’s activity

single.label: Slaves a little while ago
single.t: When people lord it, give themselves airs and scold from above, I remember that a little while ago they were slaves, to how many and for what things. In a little while they will be in the same sort of case.
single.quote: Then what they are like when lording it and giving themselves airs, or getting angry and scolding from a position of superiority. Yet a little while ago they were slaves, to how many, and for what sort of things. And in a little while they will be in the same sort of case.
single.why: Single source, 10.20. It never mentions praise or fame, and “the same sort of case” is not specified as death, so the line leaves it open.
single.follows: Those who give themselves airs and scold from above were slaves to many not long ago, and soon they will be in the same case.

single.label: Even if memory lasted
single.t: Even if those who remember me were immortal, and the memory immortal, what would that be to me? To the living, what is praise, except perhaps for the sake of managing some matter?
single.quote: But suppose even that those who will remember are immortal, and the memory immortal: what then is that to you? And I do not speak of its being nothing to the dead; but to the living, what is praise, except perhaps for the sake of managing some matter?
single.why: Single source, 4.16. Its question form and its “perhaps” are kept, so the practical use of praise stays a concession and becomes neither a rule nor a denial.
single.follows: Even an undying memory would be nothing to me; to the living, praise is at most useful for managing some matter.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. In modern editions 9.32 is 9.34, 8.42 is 8.44, 6.54 is 6.59, 4.16 is 4.19–20, 6.17 is 6.18, 8.51 is 8.52–53, 10.20 is 10.19, 12.3 is 12.4, 4.31 is 4.38, 9.16 is 9.18, 11.13 is 11.14 and 6.46 is 6.51; 10.10 is the same.

Semicolon removed and blame added, since 9.32 deflates praise and blame equally. “Want” and “fear” are left to the claims because each has only one witness. The three arguments stand side by side without being merged. “Ruins nothing” rests on 4.16, which speaks of beautiful things, and on 9.32.
articles.limit: Three separate arguments stand side by side: the quality of the judges, the transience of memory, and the self-sufficiency of the beautiful. The sources do not merge them. They do not tell me to despise people, withdraw from them, withhold praise or make self-approval my standard. 6.46 names my own action as my good, and 12.3 only observes, in the first person plural, that one’s own judgment is undervalued. 8.51 asks questions and faults fleeing praise as much as chasing it. 4.31 includes the wise. 4.16 leaves praise a possible practical use and sets the gift of nature aside. Passages 10.20, 11.13 and 10.10 never mention praise or fame, so their place in this article is editorial inference, and “the same sort of case” in 10.20 is not specified as death.

aside.10.10: About pride in a capture, from a spider’s fly to the Sarmatians Marcus himself fought. It shares with claim 1 the act of examining people’s principles, but turns it on pride in conquest, not on those whose praise or judgment I care about.

statement.t: I look into the minds that judge me. Praise makes nothing better, blame ruins nothing, and fame after death is nothing to me.

parts.words: I look into the minds that judge me
Praise makes nothing better
blame ruins nothing
fame after death is nothing to me

statement.kind: One question answered from three sides
statement.form: Semicolon removed and blame added, since 9.32 deflates praise and blame equally. “Want” and “fear” are left to the claims because each has only one witness. The three arguments stand side by side without being merged. “Ruins nothing” rests on 4.16, which speaks of beautiful things, and on 9.32.

articles.title: Wrongdoing harms the wrongdoer

claims.role: Where the harm of a wrong lies
claims.t: The evil of a wrong lies with the one who does it. It harms them and makes them bad, and they have the power to be rid of it as soon as they wish. The wrong does no harm to the universe or to the other person.
claims.shared: The first two phrases are joint across 8.53, 9.4 and 9.37. The power to be rid of the wrong and the absence of harm to the universe or the other person are 8.53 alone. The universe is restored from the source.

support.quote: It is harmful only to the one who has also been given the power to be rid of it, as soon as they wish to.
support.follows: Wickedness harms only the one who has it, and that one can be rid of it as soon as they wish.
gives: The evil of a wrong lies with the one who does it
It harms them and makes them bad
they have the power to be rid of it as soon as they wish

support.quote: Whoever does wrong does wrong at their own cost.
support.follows: The cost of a wrong falls on the one who does it.
gives: The evil of a wrong lies with the one who does it

support.quote: Whoever acts unjustly does injustice to themselves, making themselves bad.
support.follows: Whoever acts unjustly wrongs themselves, by making themselves bad.
gives: It harms them and makes them bad

support.quote: If the person did wrong, the evil is there.
support.follows: If someone did wrong, the evil is there, with the one who did it.
gives: The evil of a wrong lies with the one who does it

support.quote: Wickedness in general does no harm to the universe, and wickedness in the particular case does no harm to the other person.
support.follows: Wickedness does no harm to the universe, and a particular wicked act does no harm to the person on the receiving end.
gives: The wrong does no harm to the universe or to the other person

claims.t: Another person’s wrong is not an evil for me, and my being unfortunate does not depend on someone else. I leave that wrong where it is.
claims.shared: The two passages share only the subject, another person’s wrong. The reasoning is 8.53 alone and the leaving is 9.18 alone. 9.18 gives no reason and no instruction about the wrongdoer, so none is added.

support.quote: Otherwise my neighbour’s wickedness would be an evil for me, which god decided against, so that my being unfortunate should not depend on someone else.
support.follows: My neighbour’s wickedness is not an evil for me: god decided that my being unfortunate should not depend on anyone else.
gives: Another person’s wrong
is not an evil for me
my being unfortunate does not depend on someone else

support.quote: Another person’s wrongdoing must be left there.
support.follows: Someone else’s wrongdoing is to be left where it is, with them.
gives: Another person’s wrong
I leave that wrong where it is

single.label: Each mind rules itself
single.t: Another person’s power of choice is neither good nor bad for mine, any more than their bit of breath or their bit of flesh. We have come to be for one another’s sake, but each of us has a ruling part with its own authority.
single.quote: To my faculty of choice, my neighbour’s faculty of choice is just as much a matter of indifference as their bit of breath and their bit of flesh. For however true it is that we have come to be for one another’s sake, still each of our ruling parts has its own authority.
single.why: Single source, 8.53. The image of breath and flesh is kept, as is the concession that we exist for one another’s sake, so the line does not license indifference to people. “Neither good nor bad” is our rendering of “a matter of indifference”.
single.follows: My neighbour’s power of choice is neither good nor bad for mine; though we exist for one another, each mind has its own authority.

single.label: Perhaps no wrong
single.t: When I think someone has done wrong, I also allow that perhaps they did not.
single.quote: But perhaps they did not do wrong.
single.why: Single source, 9.37. The existing wording stands. It is a caution about my own judgement of the act and does not deny that something happened.
single.follows: It may be that the person did not do wrong at all.

single.label: Nothing new
single.t: When I meet wickedness, and with everything else that happens, I keep this at hand: this is what I have often seen.
single.quote: What is wickedness? This is what you have often seen. And with everything that happens, keep this at hand: this is what you have often seen.
single.why: Single source, 7.1. The line speaks of familiarity only. It does not say wickedness is harmless or acceptable.
single.follows: Wickedness is what one has often seen, and the same thought is to be kept at hand for whatever happens.

single.label: Wrong done for pleasure
single.t: A wrong done with pleasure is open to a greater charge than a wrong done with pain. The angry person is more like someone first treated unjustly and forced by pain into anger. The person who does wrong from desire is moved by an impulse of their own.
single.quote: the wrong done with pleasure is open to a greater charge than the wrong done with pain. And in general the one is more like a person who has first been treated unjustly and has been forced by pain into anger; the other is moved to do injustice by an impulse of their own, carried towards doing something from desire.
single.why: Single source, 2.7, where Marcus endorses a comparison by Theophrastus. It is kept in the third person, with “more like” as a comparison. Both remain wrongs and anger is not excused.
single.follows: Theophrastus, whom Marcus approves, holds that a wrong done with pleasure deserves a greater charge than a wrong done in the pain of anger.

single.label: Wrong by not acting
single.t: Injustice often lies in not doing something, and not only in doing something.
single.quote: Often the one who does not do something acts unjustly, not only the one who does something.
single.why: Single source, 9.4. “Often” is restored from the source. It stops “I leave another person’s wrong where it is” from being read as a rule of inaction.
single.follows: Leaving something undone can be unjust, as well as doing something.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. In modern editions 8.53 is 8.55–56, 9.4 is 9.4–5, 2.7 is 2.10, 9.18 is 9.20, 9.37 is 9.38 and 8.9 is 8.10; 7.1 is the same.

Both halves rest on two passages each. “Not the one it is done to” was dropped from the opening because only 8.53 says it, and it now sits in c1. The leaving comes from 9.18, and 9.37 supports only where the evil lies.
articles.limit: The article says where the evil of a wrong falls. It does not say how to treat the wrongdoer, and “left there” in 9.18 is not expanded into ignoring, forgiving or declining to correct. The opening’s “I leave” rests on 9.18 alone, with 9.37 supporting only where the evil lies. In c2 the two passages share only the subject, and the reasoning is 8.53 alone. 8.9 concerns pleasure and regret and stays aside.

aside.8.9: About regret: it argues that pleasure is neither useful nor good. It says nothing about wrongdoing or about whom a wrong harms.

statement.t: A wrong harms the one who does it, and I leave another person’s wrong where it is.

articles.title: Upright on my own, and not becoming like those I fight

unfused.reason: The five passages of this section are separate short sayings, and no two of them say the same thing, so nothing here is fused. Four are kept side by side, each on its own; the fifth is half a sentence and is set aside.

single.label: Up or down
single.t: For a stone thrown upward, it is nothing bad to be carried down and nothing good to be carried up.
single.quote: For a stone that has been thrown upward, it is nothing bad to be carried down, and nothing good to be carried up.
single.why: Single source 9.15, kept as the speaker’s third-person image. Supplied quote: “For a stone that has been thrown upward, it is nothing bad to be carried down, and nothing good to be carried up.” “Carried” is kept because the motion comes from outside the stone. No application to fortune, fate or death is added.
single.follows: For a thrown stone, falling is not bad and rising is not good.

single.label: Hive and bee
single.t: What is not good for the hive is not good for the bee either.
single.quote: What is not good for the hive is not good for the bee either.
single.why: Single source 6.49, kept verbatim. Supplied quote: “What is not good for the hive is not good for the bee either.” The claim is negative and runs one way only, so no rule that the hive’s good is the bee’s good is stated. The existing “in it” is dropped as an addition.
single.follows: A bee cannot gain from what does not benefit its hive.

single.label: Upright on my own
single.t: Upright, not held upright.
single.quote: Upright, not held upright.
single.why: Single source 7.9, kept verbatim in its own terse form. Supplied quote: “Upright, not held upright.” The existing “by someone else” is removed because the saying does not say who or what would do the holding.
single.follows: Uprightness should be one’s own, not something that another keeps in place.

single.label: Fighting back
single.t: When I fight back against people, the best way is not to become like them.
single.quote: The best way to fight back is to not become like them.
single.why: Single source 6.5. Supplied quote: “The best way to fight back is to not become like them.” The frame of fighting back is kept, so this is resistance and not passivity. “People” is added only to give “them” a referent. Nothing is said about forgiving or correcting them.
single.follows: The best way to fight back against someone is to not become like them.

decisions: The editor recommended that this section get no article, since no two of its passages share a claim. It stands instead as four said-once items, so that the article numbers stay as planned; whether the section keeps an article is the owner’s decision.

Unfused opening that sets two separate sayings side by side, each with one witness (7.9 and 6.5). “On my own” is dropped because 7.9 does not reject help or name who would do the holding. “Those I fight” gives the source’s unspecified “them” a referent taken only from “fight back”.
articles.limit: Nothing in this article is fused. It keeps four separate sayings side by side, each on its single witness. The opening only juxtaposes two of them (7.9 and 6.5), so the lines 7.9a and 6.5a restate those sayings in the speaker’s own frame and do not add new doctrine. “Those I fight” and “people” are editorial referents for the source’s unspecified “them”, drawn only from “fight back”. “Them” is not identified with members of the hive. The thrown stone is passively carried while uprightness is precisely not held, so the images must not be merged. The hive saying is negative and runs one way only. Reading it as a limit on self-possession is our interpretation, not the source’s wording. The 8.40 fragment stays in the margin without a subject or a consequence. Fate, death, nature, reason and the gods appear in none of the passages.

aside.8.40: The quoted words are half a sentence: what becomes a “rounded sphere” (the mind) and the main clause (nothing touches it) are in the part of the passage left out, so the words cannot stand alone.

articles.title: The sameness and foulness of things

claims.t: All things are the same and come from the same. Everything now is as it was in the time of those we have buried, and to watch it for a hundred years or for three comes to the same.
claims.shared: Adds the buried and the hundred years to the opening’s sameness. Limit: 9.36 says only ‘these things’, so reading ‘it’ as everything is our interpretation. No verdict on the worth or length of life is drawn.

claims.role: The life in me is matter too
claims.t: The little breath is one more thing of the same kind as other matter. The breath changes out of that matter and into that matter. The saying goes: “little breaths carrying corpses”.

single.label: Out of season
single.t: To ask for a fig in winter is mad. I am as mad if I ask for my child when my child is no longer given.
single.quote: To ask for a fig in winter is the act of someone mad. Such is the person who asks for their child when it is no longer given.
single.why: Single source, resting on the supplied quote 11.29a and turned to the first person. The fault is demanding what is no longer given. Love of the child is not faulted, and the saying is about loss, not sameness or filth.
single.follows: Asking for a child who is no longer given is as mad as asking for a fig in winter.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. In modern editions 9.12 is 9.14, 9.34 is 9.36, 6.41 is 6.46, 8.23 is 8.24, 4.23 is 4.28–29 (the sentence quoted opens 4.29), 9.22 is 9.24, 12.10 is 12.13, 9.36 is 9.37 and 11.29 is 11.33.

Two short sentences keep sameness and material foulness as separate judgements, then state the warning. ‘Dirt and rot’ says plainly what looking at the materials shows: filth in 9.12, rottenness in 9.34, dirt in 8.23. ‘Fail to recognise’ covers both not knowing what happens (4.23) and being surprised by it (12.10). It stays a warning, not a vow, and gives no reason for the lack of surprise because 12.10 gives none. ‘World’ stands for ‘universe’ in 4.23 and ‘life’ in 12.10. The marble, gold and bath images stay in c2 and c3. 134 characters.
articles.limit: Sameness and material foulness are separate grounds. The opening states them as two judgements in one sentence, and c3 sets them side by side, each sentence with its own witness. ‘These things’ in 9.12 and 9.36 has no stated referent, so reading it as the things of life is editorial. ‘Stranger’ rests on ignorance in 4.23 and on surprise in 12.10. The opening’s ‘fail to recognise’ gathers both, and c4 keeps them apart. The opening’s ‘world’ stands for ‘universe’ in 4.23 and ‘life’ in 12.10. C4 states the result of 4.23’s conditional directly, with the premise kept in the margin. The corpse saying is from 9.22 alone, and what it describes is not named. 11.29 is a single-source saying about asking for what is no longer given, not about sameness or filth. No passage says what should be valued instead, and none concludes for withdrawal or death. The fragments 11.28, 11.20 and 6.51 and the character list of 4.23 are left outside the doctrine.

aside.11.28: Two lines of verse with no comment, a heart that laughed and people who will find fault with virtue; they belong with other people’s blame, not with the sameness of things.
aside.11.20: A bare mention of the fable of the mountain mouse and the house mouse, with no verb and no comment; any lesson drawn from it would be the editor’s.
aside.6.51: An exclamation at how many of those born with me have already died; it belongs with the sections on death and time and says nothing of sameness or of matter.

articles.title: How my soul uses itself

claims.t: My soul can see itself and analyse itself. It can shine with a light by which it sees the truth of all things and the truth within itself. It can go round the whole universe, and it can know beginning and end and the reason that runs through the whole of substance.
claims.shared: Self-sight is joint (11.1, 11.11). The light is 11.11 alone, and “can” marks it as a capacity because the source grants it only when the sphere is true to its form. That condition is quoted in the margin. Knowledge of beginning and end is 5.26 alone, where it defines the skilled soul, so it too stays a capacity.

support.follows: The reasoning soul sees itself and analyses itself.

claims.role: What is mine and what is not
claims.t: I am made of a little body and a soul, a little soul carrying a corpse, as Epictetus used to say. Whatever is not my mind’s own activity is indifferent to it, and all of its own activity is in its power. Everything lies in that activity. The rest, whether within choice or outside it, is dead things and smoke.
claims.shared: Body and soul are joint (6.30, 4.34). The corpse image keeps its attribution to Epictetus and is 4.34 alone. Indifference is 6.30 alone. Reading the “that” of 12.26 as the mind’s own activity is our interpretation, since 12.26 speaks of the ruling part using itself. The line keeps 12.26’s point that things within choice also belong to the rest.

claims.t: At every turn I ask what I am using my soul for now, and how my ruling part is using itself. I ask whose soul I have now: not a small child’s, surely, nor a tyrant’s, nor a farm animal’s, nor a wild beast’s. I ask whether my ruling part is playing a part or running with the herd.
