single.label: Things say nothing
single.t: Things stand outside the doors, themselves by themselves. They know nothing about themselves and pronounce nothing. My ruling part pronounces on them.
single.quote: Things stand outside the doors, themselves by themselves, knowing nothing about themselves and pronouncing nothing. What, then, pronounces on them? The ruling part.
single.why: Single source 9.13, kept close to its image. It says things are silent and judgement is mine. It does not say things are unreal or that any judgement will do.
single.follows: Things say nothing about themselves; whatever is said about them is said by the ruling part.

single.label: Its own virtues
single.t: Love of those near me, truthfulness and a sense of shame are my rational soul’s own.
single.quote: The rational soul’s own are also love of those near it, and truthfulness, and a sense of shame
single.why: Single source 11.1. “My rational soul’s own” keeps the source’s framing of what belongs to the rational soul. The link to law and justice is left to the margin.
single.follows: Love of those near it, truthfulness and a sense of shame belong to the reasoning soul.

single.label: Following reason
single.t: If I follow reason in everything, I am at once unhurried and quick to move, at once cheerful and composed.
single.quote: Someone who follows reason in everything is something at once unhurried and quick to move, at once cheerful and composed.
single.why: Single source 10.14. The conditional keeps the dependence on “in everything”, and both pairs of opposites are held together as the source holds them.
single.follows: Whoever follows reason in everything is unhurried yet quick to move, cheerful yet composed.

single.label: A reasoned readiness
single.t: My readiness to be released from the body should come from a judgment of my own, not from bare opposition. It should be reasoned and dignified, able to convince someone else too, and without theatrics.
single.quote: this readiness should come from a judgment of one’s own, not by way of bare opposition, as with the Christians, but in a reasoned and dignified way, and so as to convince someone else too, without theatrics
single.why: Single source 11.3. The criticism concerns the ground and manner of readiness, not readiness itself. The example of the Christians is kept in the margin only.
single.follows: Readiness to die should rest on one’s own reasoned judgment, not on bare defiance or on show.

single.label: Time is short
single.t: Each person has one life, and mine is almost finished. Soon I will have no chance left to honour myself.
single.quote: you will have no chance left to honour yourself. For each person has one life, and yours is almost finished
single.why: Single source 2.3, limited to its supplied quote. “Soon” rests on “almost finished”. The ironic command to do violence to the soul is left to c4, where its quote belongs. The urgency is personal and tied to the speaker’s age, not a general rule.
single.follows: Each person has one life; Marcus’s is almost over, and soon he will have no chance left to honour himself.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. In modern editions 2.14 is 2.16, 2.3 is 2.6, 11.11 is 11.12, 4.17 is 4.21, 4.34 is 4.41, 5.26 is 5.32, 9.39 is 9.39b, 6.30 is 6.32, 8.44 is 8.45b, 12.26 is 12.33, 6.16 is 6.17, 8.57 is 8.60, 10.14 is 10.12b, 9.13 is 9.15 and 3.16 is 3.15–16a; 11.1, 5.11 and 11.3 are the same.

“What I use my soul for” takes the plain question of 5.11 and joins it to 12.26, where everything lies in how the ruling part uses itself. Treating soul and ruling part as one here is our interpretation. The truth of all things and of itself is 11.11’s wording, with self-sight shared by 11.1 and knowledge of the whole by 5.26. Self-violence is joint (2.14, 2.3). Pretence is named because it alone among the harms has two witnesses (2.14, 9.39) and it is the direct opposite of seeing the truth. It is one example, not the whole list. “Can” keeps both sight and harm as possibilities, not achievements. 132 characters.
articles.limit: The sources do not use “soul”, “mind” and “ruling part” as one settled term. The article’s treatment of them as near neighbours is our interpretation, as are the opening’s joining of 5.11’s question to 12.26’s “everything lies in that” and c2’s reading of that “that” as the mind’s own activity. The opening names pretence as one way the soul does violence to itself because two passages witness it. It is an example, not the full list. Of the five forms of self-violence in 2.14, vexation at what happens and hostility to a person appear only in the margin. What follows death is left open, and 4.17 speaks only on a supposition. Many of the sources are questions or ironic self-address, so the lines state capacities, tests and warnings, not achievements or vows, and they claim no immunity from disturbance. The images of sphere, arrow, road and circuit each make a separate point and do not form one geometry.

aside.3.16: Its first sentence is about the many senses of ordinary words and a sight that is not of the eyes. Its second divides a person into body, soul and mind, each with its own share (sensations, impulses, principles), and it is the one passage here that keeps soul and mind apart; the article reads them as one and divides a person only into soul and body.

articles.title: All things pass

claims.t: I am in continual alteration, and so is the whole universe. Eternity is a kind of river with a violent current, and each thing is carried past as soon as it has been seen.
claims.shared: Adds continuity and the river image to the opening. The river of eternity is from 4.35 alone. The torrent of 9.27 supports only the carrying. The hedged perishing of 9.17 is left for the margin.

support.quote: All things are in change.
support.follows: Everything is changing.
support.note: Everything is changing.

support.quote: You yourself too are in continual alteration and, in a certain respect, in perishing, and so is the whole universe.
support.follows: I too am always being altered, and in a way perishing, and so is the whole universe.
gives: I am in continual alteration

support.quote: Then earth itself will change, and those things too will change without end, and those again without end.
support.follows: Even the earth will change, and what it changes into will change again, without end.
support.note: Even the earth will change, and what it changes into will change again, without end.

support.quote: Flows and alterations renew the universe continually
support.follows: The universe is renewed all the time by flows and alterations.

support.quote: Each person’s life itself, too, is something of the kind: like the vapour that rises from blood and the breath drawn in from the air.
support.follows: A person’s life is a passing thing too, like vapour rising from blood or a breath drawn in.
support.note: A person’s life is a passing thing too, like vapour rising from blood or a breath drawn in.

support.quote: How quickly all things vanish, the bodies themselves into the universe, the memories of them into eternity.
support.follows: All things vanish quickly: bodies into the universe, and the memory of them into eternity.
support.note: All things vanish quickly: bodies into the universe, and the memory of them into eternity.

support.quote: Eternity is a kind of river of things that come to be, and a violent current. For as soon as each thing has been seen it has been carried past, and another is being carried past, and yet another will be carried along.
support.follows: Time is like a fast river: each thing is swept past as soon as it is seen, and others follow it.
gives: Eternity is a kind of river with a violent current
each thing is carried past

support.quote: The substance of the whole is a torrent: it carries everything along.
support.follows: The stuff of which everything is made is like a torrent that sweeps all things along.

support.quote: It is as if someone began to love one of the little sparrows flying past, and it has already gone out of sight.
support.follows: Loving something that passes is like beginning to love a sparrow that has already flown out of sight.
support.note: Loving something that passes is like beginning to love a sparrow that has already flown out of sight.

claims.role: Nature’s work, always of one kind
claims.t: The work of the nature of the whole is to change what exists and to make new things like the old. The nature of the whole loves this work. What will be is of the same kind as what has been, so I need not fear something new.
claims.shared: The love of change belongs to the nature of the whole and is not prescribed as my feeling. Freedom from fear of novelty is from 8.5 alone and stays a permission.

support.quote: The nature of the whole has this as its work: to move what is here over there, to change it, to lift it from here and carry it there.
support.follows: The work of the nature of the whole is to move things from one place to another and to change them.
gives: The work of the nature of the whole is to change what exists

support.quote: the nature of the whole loves nothing so much as to change the things that exist and make new things like them
support.follows: Nothing pleases the nature of the whole more than changing what exists and making new things like it.
gives: The work of the nature of the whole is to change what exists
to make new things like the old
The nature of the whole loves this work

support.quote: And in this the nature of the whole delights, the nature in accordance with which all things come about well, and from eternity have come about in the same kind of way, and without end there will be others like them.
support.follows: The nature of the whole delights in change, and things of the same kind as before will keep coming about without end.
gives: to make new things like the old
The nature of the whole loves this work

support.quote: All things are transformations, not so that one need fear something new. All things are familiar
support.follows: All things are changes of what was, so nothing new and strange comes that one need fear.
gives: I need not fear something new

support.quote: Whoever has seen what is now has seen everything: all that has come to be from the everlasting past and all that will be without end. For all things are of the same stock and of the same kind.
support.follows: Whoever has seen the present has seen all past and future, since all things are of the same kind.
gives: What will be is of the same kind as what has been

support.quote: It is possible to foresee what will be as well. For it will certainly be of the same kind, and it cannot step out of the rhythm of what is happening now.
support.follows: The future can be foreseen, because it will be of the same kind as what happens now.
gives: What will be is of the same kind as what has been

claims.t: When I reflect on wave after wave of change and on its speed, I look down on everything mortal. Only a small part of eternity and of the whole of substance is portioned out to me. I do not prize a thing running past in the river, because I cannot stand on it. What lures with pleasure, frightens with pain or is celebrated through vanity is cheap and quick to perish.
claims.shared: The disdain is aimed at mortal and sensory things, not at the whole or at conduct. The three classes of lure, fright and vanity are from 2.9 alone. The footing image is from 6.14 alone.

support.quote: For a person who reflects on wave after wave of changes and alterations, and on their speed, will look down on everything mortal.
support.follows: Whoever thinks about how fast changes follow one another will look down on everything mortal.
gives: When I reflect on wave after wave of change and on its speed
I look down on everything mortal

support.quote: How small a part of boundless, gaping eternity has been portioned out to each one: for it vanishes very quickly into the everlasting. And how small a part of the whole of substance, and how small a part of the whole of soul.
support.follows: Each of us has been given a tiny share of endless time, of all substance and of all soul.
gives: Only a small part of eternity and of the whole of substance is portioned out to me

support.quote: Reflecting on all this, picture nothing as great
support.follows: Whoever reflects on how small their share is should picture nothing as great.
gives: I do not prize a thing running past in the river

support.quote: In this river, then, which of these things running past would anyone prize, a thing it is not possible to stand on?
support.follows: Nothing running past in this river is worth prizing, since no one can stand on it.
gives: I do not prize a thing running past in the river
because I cannot stand on it

support.quote: What all the things perceived by the senses are like, and above all those that lure with pleasure or frighten with pain or are loudly celebrated through vanity: how cheap and contemptible and filthy and quick to perish and dead.
support.follows: The things of the senses, above all what tempts, frightens or is famous, are cheap, quick to perish and dead.
gives: I look down on everything mortal

claims.t: I keep the whole of eternity and the whole of substance constantly in mind. Set against substance, each particular thing is a fig seed. Set against time, each particular thing is a turn of a drill. I fix my attention on each thing and think of it as already dissolving and in change.
claims.shared: A mental exercise with no moral drawn, as in 10.19 and 9.31. The fig seed and the drill are from 10.19 alone and are kept as written.

support.quote: An impression, constantly, of the whole of eternity and the whole of substance, and that all particular things are, set against substance, a fig seed, and set against time, a turn of a drill.
support.follows: I should keep all of time and all substance always in view, and see each thing against them as a fig seed or a moment.
gives: I keep the whole of eternity and the whole of substance constantly in mind
Set against substance, each particular thing is a fig seed
Set against time, each particular thing is a turn of a drill

support.quote: Fixing attention on each object, think of it as already dissolving and in change
support.follows: Whatever I look at, I should think of as already changing and coming apart.
gives: I fix my attention on each thing
think of it as already dissolving and in change

support.quote: By having encompassed the whole universe in thought, and by surveying everlasting eternity, and by thinking of the swift change of each particular thing
support.follows: One holds the whole universe and all of time in thought, and thinks of how fast each thing changes.
gives: I keep the whole of eternity and the whole of substance constantly in mind
think of it as already dissolving and in change

support.quote: Observe continually that all things come about by change
support.follows: I should keep observing that everything comes about through change.
support.note: I should keep observing that everything comes about through change.

claims.t: Loss is nothing other than change, and to perish is to be altered. I have no ground to say that all things have gone badly and always will. Nothing is bad for a thing in the course of change, just as nothing is good for a thing that comes to exist out of change. The elements of the universe and of me change too, and those elements do not grumble.
claims.shared: The loss happens. Only the judgement that it is bad is refused. The symmetry about good is from 4.35 alone and keeps the line from being mere consolation. The uncomplaining elements of 8.16 are an example, not a vow.

support.quote: Why then do you say that all things have come about badly and all things will always go badly
support.follows: It is wrong to say that everything has gone badly and always will.
gives: I have no ground to say that all things have gone badly and always will

support.quote: Loss is nothing other than change.
support.follows: When something is lost, it has only changed.
gives: Loss is nothing other than change

support.quote: The parts of the whole, all that are by nature contained by the universe, must perish; but let “perish” be said in the sense of “be altered”.
support.follows: The parts of the universe must perish, and here perishing means being altered.
gives: Loss is nothing other than change
to perish is to be altered

support.quote: Now if this is by nature both bad and necessary for them, the whole would not be well managed
support.follows: If being altered were bad for the parts, the whole would be badly managed, which is not believable.
gives: I have no ground to say that all things have gone badly and always will
Nothing is bad for a thing in the course of change

support.quote: There is nothing bad for things that are in the course of change, just as there is nothing good for things that come to exist out of change.
support.follows: Being changed is not bad for a thing, just as coming out of a change is not good for it.
gives: Nothing is bad for a thing in the course of change
nothing is good for a thing that comes to exist out of change

support.quote: which are the elements of the universe and of you. And these too change, and do not grumble.
support.follows: My elements, which are also the universe’s, change and do not complain of it.
gives: The elements of the universe and of me change too
those elements do not grumble

claims.t: Suppose I leave nature out and explain things by the way they naturally are. Even so, the parts of the whole are such as to change, and each part dissolves into the things out of which it was put together. What grew from earth goes back to earth, or else the interlockings among the atoms dissolve and the elements scatter. On either account it would be ridiculous for me to be surprised or annoyed, as though dissolution were against nature. What has died does not fall outside the universe.
claims.shared: Restores the bridge from 10.7, explaining things by the way they naturally are, so that “against nature” makes sense after nature is left out. The physics stays open between elemental return and atomic scattering, as in 7.27 and 10.7. The earth line is verse quoted in 7.27. The last sentence is from 8.16 alone and its condition is kept in the margin.

support.quote: And if someone were to leave nature out of it and explain these things by the way they naturally are, even so it would be ridiculous to say that the parts of the whole are naturally such as to change, and at the same time to be surprised or annoyed as though at something happening against nature, especially when the dissolution is into the things out of which each is put together.
support.follows: Even without nature as the one who orders things, it is absurd to expect change and then be annoyed when a thing comes apart into its parts.
gives: Suppose I leave nature out and explain things by the way they naturally are
Even so, the parts of the whole are such as to change
each part dissolves into the things out of which it was put together
it would be ridiculous for me to be surprised or annoyed, as though dissolution were against nature

support.quote: For it is either a scattering of the elements out of which it was compounded, or a turning of the solid into the earthy and of the breath-like into the airy, so that these too are taken back up into the reason of the whole
support.follows: Dissolving either scatters a thing’s elements or turns them into earth and air, which the whole takes back.

support.follows: What dies stays in the universe, changes there, and is dissolved into its own parts.

single.label: Without lament
single.t: The sailing wind that blows from the gods must be borne, in toil and without lament.
single.quote: But the sailing wind that blows from the gods must be borne, in toils without lament.
single.why: Single source. A line of verse quoted in 7.27, kept in the third person with its wind image and not recast as a personal vow.
single.follows: What the gods send must be borne, with toil and without lament.

single.label: Everything a seed
single.t: Everything that exists is in a way the seed of what will come from it. To picture as seeds only those cast into earth or womb is a layman’s view.
single.quote: For everything that exists is, in a way, the seed of what will come from it. But you picture as seeds only those that are cast into earth or womb, and that is very much a layman’s view.
single.why: Single source, 4.29. Keeps the hedge “in a way” and the rebuke of the narrow picture of seeds.
single.follows: Whatever exists is a seed of what will follow it, not only seeds sown in earth or womb.

single.label: Old and young alike
single.t: Everything I see will very quickly perish, and those who watched it perish will very quickly perish too. Whoever dies in extreme old age will be brought level with whoever died before their time.
single.quote: Everything you see will very quickly perish, and those who have looked on as it perished will very quickly perish themselves, and whoever dies in extreme old age will be brought level with the one who died before their time.
single.why: Single source, 9.31. The levelling is by comparison with boundless time, and the passage draws no further moral.
single.follows: Since everything and everyone perishes quickly, dying very old comes to the same as dying young.

single.label: What is great
single.t: I picture nothing as great except this: to act as my own nature leads and to undergo things as the common nature brings them.
single.quote: except this: to act as your own nature leads, and to undergo things as the common nature brings them.
single.why: Single source. Only 12.25 states the positive exception to smallness, so the line stands alone and is not presented as joint doctrine.
single.follows: The only thing to picture as great is acting as one’s own nature leads and undergoing what the common nature brings.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. In modern editions 7.27 is 7.49–51, 6.14 is 6.15, 4.29 is 4.35–36, 10.19 is 10.17–18, 9.31 is 9.32b–33, 9.27 is 9.28b–29a, 9.17 is 9.19, 2.9 is 2.12a, 12.25 is 12.32, 6.34 is 6.37–38, 4.35 is 4.42–43, 8.5 is 8.6, 9.33 is 9.35 and 8.16 is 8.18; 10.7 is the same.
Removes the semicolon and gives each sentence its own subject. The judgement is limited to what changes, as 4.35 frames it. The opening is 136 characters.
articles.limit: The passages agree that all particular things change quickly within a whole renewed by change, and that this change is not bad for what changes. They do not share one physics or one tone. Atoms or elements, conflagration or exchange, are left open. Providence is asserted in 9.33 and 10.7 but set aside in the argument of c6. The delight in change belongs to the nature of the whole, not to me. Disdain is for mortal and sensory things only. The positive ethic rests on 12.25 alone. Nothing here asserts personal survival. Quotation 10.7b is the premise of a reductio, and it supports “not bad” only because the passage goes on to reject that premise. Anchors mark which words a quotation supports. The joining of quotations into one line is our editorial reading.

articles.title: The same matter, reshaped

claims.t: The nature of the whole works substance like wax: it shapes a little horse, melts it down and uses the material for a little tree, then for a little human. Each shape lasts the briefest time, and all existing things will very quickly change. Every part of me will pass through change to some part of the universe, and that part to another, without end.
claims.shared: Restores the wax image, which explains the idea better than the abstract original. Brevity and speed are jointly witnessed by 7.17 and 6.4. The wax image is 7.17 alone, and the endless reassignment of parts is 5.13 alone.

support.quote: The nature of the whole, out of the whole of substance as if out of wax, at one moment shaped a little horse; then it melted that down and used its material for a little tree, then for a little human, then for something else.
support.follows: Nature makes one thing after another out of the same substance, melting each down and using its material for the next.

claims.t: I am made of what is causal and what is material. Neither came out of nothing, and neither will perish into nothing. What is material very quickly vanishes into the substance of the whole. Every cause is very quickly taken back up into the reason of the whole, through change.

claims.role: Death, the same change as birth
claims.t: My death is the same kind of thing as my birth, a mystery of nature: a combining out of the same elements, a dissolving into the same. I came to be as a part within something, through change, as my parents did. I go back into what gave birth to me. I breathe my last into what I draw breath from every day. I fall on what gave my father the bit of seed, my mother the bit of blood and my nurse the bit of milk, and on what has fed and watered me every day for so many years.
claims.shared: Keeps the seed, blood and milk image from 5.4 alone, with its source left unnamed. Coming to be as a part through change is joint (4.12, 5.13), as is the return to the source (4.12, 5.4). The sameness of death and birth is 4.5 alone and promises no survival.

claims.t: There is nothing terrible for a little box in being taken apart, just as there is nothing good in its being put together. My ending is not contrary to the sequence proper to a living being with mind, to the reason on which I am built or to nature’s aim. Nature has aimed at the ending of each thing no less than at its beginning and its course.

The fittingness of my ending is joint (4.5, 8.18). The judgement is neutrality, not praise of death or a command against fear.

single.t: I make my way through the things that accord with nature until I fall and rest.
single.quote: I make my way through the things that accord with nature until I fall and rest
single.why: Single-source line from 5.4, kept verbatim for its distinctive wording. It describes a course and its rest, and carries no argument or cosmology.
single.follows: I go on through what accords with nature until I fall and rest.

single.label: One whole or not
single.t: Existing things will either go up in vapour, if substance is indeed a unity, or be scattered.
single.quote: either they will go up in vapour, if substance is indeed a unity, or they will be scattered
single.why: Single-source line from 6.4. The conditional is kept and the physics is left open as Marcus leaves it. The original’s “one continuous whole” gloss is dropped.
single.follows: If the stuff of the world is one continuous whole, things will go up in vapour; if not, they will be scattered.

single.label: Even in finite cycles
single.t: For anyone who goes back through the changes that made me, the line runs on into an infinity of its own. Nothing prevents me from saying so, even if the universe is governed in finite cycles.
single.quote: and for anyone who goes back, the line runs on into another infinity. For nothing prevents one from saying so, even if the universe is governed in finite cycles.
single.why: Single-source line from 5.13. “The changes that made me” supplies the referent from the surrounding passage. The last clause is a hedge that neither asserts nor denies finite cycles.
single.follows: Going back through one’s ancestors leads into another infinity, and one may say so even if the universe runs in finite cycles.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. In modern editions 7.17 is 7.23, 6.4 is 6.4–5, 7.7 is 7.10, 4.12 is 4.14–15 and 8.18 is 8.20a; 5.13, 4.5 and 5.4 are the same.
Shortened so the line stands alone when read aloud. The ending as nature’s aim is left to c4. “Go back” covers both vanishing and being taken back up without choosing between them.
articles.limit: The synthesis promises no personal survival: what continues is material and cause, redistributed through change. It leaves the physics open (vapour or scattering, finite cycles or not, vanishing or being taken back up). Its judgement is neutrality about composition and dissolution alike, not comfort or a command against fear. The box in c4 stands as a third-person comparison, as 7.17 frames it, and no line states it of me. Reading my own ending under 4.5 and 8.18 in the first person is our editorial step, since 4.5 speaks of a living being with mind and 8.18 of each thing.

statement.t: I came out of the whole through change, and through change I go back into it.

parts.words: I came out of the whole through change
and through change I go back into it

statement.kind: One cycle traced, and what it means for the end
statement.form: Shortened so the line stands alone when read aloud. The ending as nature’s aim is left to c4. “Go back” covers both vanishing and being taken back up without choosing between them.

empty.practice: No passage in this section gives an exercise to repeat; they describe what happens to what I am made of.
empty.breaks: No passage in this section describes what failing looks like here or how to come back from it.

articles.title: The dead and the forgotten

claims.t: People of every kind and occupation are dead. Those who treated the sick died, and so did those who foretold other people’s deaths and those who killed many in war. A whole court has died and, in a way, whole cities have died.
claims.shared: Split into short sentences. “Everyone dies” is narrowed to what 6.42 says. The court is singular as in 8.29, and “in a way” keeps 4.39’s qualification about cities.

support.quote: Keep in mind continually that people of every kind, of every kind of occupation and from every sort of nation, are dead
support.follows: I should keep in mind that people of every kind, every occupation and every nation are dead.
gives: People of every kind and occupation are dead

support.quote: Keep in mind continually how many doctors have died, after knitting their brows time and again over the sick
support.follows: I should keep in mind how many doctors have died after frowning over the sick many times.
gives: Those who treated the sick died

support.quote: Hippocrates, after curing many illnesses, fell ill himself and died.
support.follows: Hippocrates cured many illnesses and still fell ill and died.
gives: Those who treated the sick died

support.quote: how many astrologers, after foretelling other people’s deaths as if that were something great
support.follows: Astrologers who made much of foretelling other people’s deaths are among the many who have died.
gives: those who foretold other people’s deaths

support.quote: The Chaldaeans foretold the deaths of many, and then what was fated caught up with them too.
support.follows: The Chaldaeans foretold many deaths, and then their own fated end caught up with them.
gives: those who foretold other people’s deaths

support.quote: how many champions, after killing many
support.follows: Champions who killed many are among the many who have died.
gives: those who killed many in war

support.quote: after so often wiping out whole cities completely and cutting down in battle many tens of thousands of horsemen and foot soldiers, one day went out of life themselves as well
support.follows: Conquerors who destroyed cities and cut down tens of thousands in battle one day left life themselves.
gives: those who killed many in war

support.quote: how many whole cities have, so to speak, died
support.follows: Even whole cities have, so to speak, died.
gives: in a way, whole cities have died

support.quote: The death of a whole court.
support.follows: A whole court, such as that of Augustus with all its people, has died.
gives: A whole court has died

claims.t: I shall soon be dead, and those who bury me or remember me will soon follow. One person buries another and dies in turn, and a little later not even my name is left.
claims.shared: The lost name rests on 4.6 alone, so “our names” is narrowed to “my name”. In 4.6 the thought serves to deflate annoyance at another man.

support.quote: within a very short time both you and this man will be dead, and a little later not even your names will be left
support.follows: Very soon both I and the man who annoys me will be dead, and a little later even our names will be gone.
gives: I shall soon be dead
a little later not even my name is left

support.quote: A little while and you will close your eyes
support.follows: In a little while I shall close my eyes in death.
gives: I shall soon be dead

support.quote: already someone else will be mourning the one who carried you out
support.follows: Soon after I die, the one who carried me out to burial will be mourned by someone else.
gives: those who bury me or remember me will soon follow

support.quote: Short-lived is the one who praises and the one who is praised, the one who remembers and the one who is remembered.
support.follows: Whoever praises or remembers is as short-lived as whoever is praised or remembered.
gives: those who bury me or remember me will soon follow

support.quote: little leaves in the same way are those who will receive in succession the fame that comes after death
support.follows: Those who will in turn keep a person’s fame after death fall like leaves as well.
gives: those who bury me or remember me will soon follow

support.quote: One buried this person and was then laid out, another buried that one, and all of it in a short time.
support.follows: One person buries another and is soon laid out himself, and all of it happens in a short time.
gives: One person buries another and dies in turn

support.quote: Lucilla buried Verus, then Lucilla.
support.follows: Lucilla buried Verus, and then it was Lucilla’s turn.
gives: One person buries another and dies in turn

claims.t: Even those who shone soon turn into tales, and then fade even from the tales. The rest are forgotten the moment they die. Everlasting remembrance is itself empty.
claims.shared: Three distinct steps kept as three sentences. The fate of “the rest” and the emptiness of everlasting remembrance rest on 4.28 alone.

support.quote: For all things quickly fade and turn into tales, and quickly too complete forgetting buries them. And I say this of those who shone in some wonderful way; for the rest, the moment they have breathed their last, are “unseen, unheard of”.
support.follows: Even those who shone quickly become tales and are then wholly forgotten; everyone else is unheard of from the moment they die.
gives: Even those who shone soon turn into tales
The rest are forgotten the moment they die

support.quote: And what is everlasting remembrance at all? All of it empty.
support.follows: Even a remembrance that lasted for ever would be wholly empty.
gives: Everlasting remembrance is itself empty

support.quote: some not remembered even for a short while, some changed into tales, and some by now faded even out of the tales
support.follows: Of the dead, some were not remembered even briefly, some became tales, and some have faded even out of the tales.
gives: Even those who shone soon turn into tales
then fade even from the tales

support.quote: Smoke and ash and a tale, or not even a tale.
support.follows: Those who were at the height of fame or fortune are now smoke, ash and a tale, or not even a tale.
gives: Even those who shone soon turn into tales
then fade even from the tales

claims.t: Nothing is terrible for the dead in being long dead, whether they were famous or never named. It does a ball no good to rise and no harm to have fallen. It does a bubble no good to hold together and no harm to have burst. Having ended harms none of them.
claims.shared: The last sentence states what both witnesses imply. 6.42 asks what is terrible in death for the dead, and 8.19 asks what harm it is to have fallen or burst. Both put the point as a question, so the plain statement and the pairing of the dead with the ball and bubble are our reading. 8.19 is fragmentary.

support.quote: What, then, is terrible in this for them? And what for those who are not even named at all?
support.follows: Being long dead is nothing terrible for the famous dead, nor for those never named.
gives: Nothing is terrible for the dead in being long dead, whether they were famous or never named
Having ended harms none of them

support.quote: So what good is it to the little ball to be carried upward, or what harm to be carried downward, or even to have fallen? And what good is it to the bubble to hold together, or what harm to have burst?
support.follows: A thrown ball is not harmed by falling, nor a bubble by bursting.
gives: It does a ball no good to rise and no harm to have fallen
It does a bubble no good to hold together and no harm to have burst
Having ended harms none of them

claims.t: One thing deserves my serious effort: just thought, social action and speech that never lies. I live life through with truth and justice, kindly towards liars and the unjust, and without affectation.
claims.shared: Restores 4.28’s social action. Kindness to liars and the unjust is from 6.42 alone, and “without affectation” from 12.20 alone.

support.quote: What then is there that one should put serious effort into? This one thing: thought that is just, actions that are social, speech such as never to lie
support.follows: What deserves serious effort is just thought, social action and speech that never lies.
gives: One thing deserves my serious effort
just thought, social action and speech that never lies

support.quote: One thing here is worth a great deal: to live life through with truth and justice, kindly towards the liars and the unjust.
support.follows: The one thing of great worth is to live with truth and justice, and to be kind to liars and the unjust.
gives: One thing deserves my serious effort
I live life through with truth and justice
kindly towards liars and the unjust

support.quote: how much more philosophical it is, in the material one has been given, to show oneself just, self-controlled, following the gods, without affectation
support.follows: It is wiser to be just, self-controlled and without affectation in the life one has been given.
gives: I live life through with truth and justice
without affectation

claims.role: Leaving when the time is done
claims.t: When my time is done, I leave life. I pass through this instant in accord with nature and come to rest with good grace, as a ripe olive falls, speaking well of the earth that bore it and grateful to the tree that grew it. When I have sailed and come to harbour, I get off.
claims.shared: The first sentence carries what both passages share: the olive falls when ripe and the passenger gets off at the harbour. Good grace, the olive and its gratitude are from 4.39 alone. The voyage is from 3.3 alone.

support.quote: So pass through this instant of time in accord with nature and come to rest with good grace, as an olive might fall when it has grown ripe, speaking well of the earth that bore it and grateful to the tree that grew it.
support.follows: I should live this brief time according to nature and end it with good grace, as a ripe olive falls, grateful to its tree.
gives: When my time is done, I leave life
I pass through this instant in accord with nature and come to rest with good grace
as a ripe olive falls, speaking well of the earth that bore it and grateful to the tree that grew it

support.quote: You went on board, you sailed, you came to harbour: get off.
support.follows: When the voyage of my life has reached harbour, I should get off.
gives: When my time is done, I leave life
When I have sailed and come to harbour, I get off

claims.t: Again and again I go over those who stood at the height of fame or fortune, and those I know, one after another. Then I ask where they are now: nowhere, or wherever it may be.
claims.shared: Adds 10.31’s own answer, which leaves open what follows death. That answer is from 10.31 alone.

support.quote: Go back continually over those who were exceedingly indignant at something, those who were at their height in the greatest fame or disasters or enmities or fortunes of whatever kind.
support.follows: I should keep going back over people who were once furious, famous or in great fortune or disaster.
gives: Again and again I go over those who stood at the height of fame or fortune

support.quote: Go over as well all those you know, one after another.
support.follows: I should go over, one after another, the dead I know of.
gives: those I know, one after another

support.quote: Then stop and consider: where is all that now?
support.follows: Having recalled them, I should stop and ask where all that is now.
gives: Then I ask where they are now

support.quote: where, then, are those people? Nowhere, or wherever it may be.
support.follows: The people of earlier times are nowhere now, or wherever it may be.
gives: Then I ask where they are now
nowhere, or wherever it may be

claims.t: When I look at a person now, or at myself, I picture the one from an earlier time who corresponds. I set whole plays and scenes of the same kind before my eyes. The things that happen now happened before and will happen again, only with other people.
claims.shared: Text unchanged and anchors corrected. The picturing drill is from 10.31 alone. That things will happen again, the plays and “only with other people” are from 10.27 alone. Only the sameness of past and present is joint, from 10.27 and 4.27. Recurrence here is sameness of human scenes, not a cosmological doctrine.

support.quote: when you look at yourself, picture one of the Caesars; and with each person the one who corresponds
support.follows: For each person I see, myself included, I should picture someone of the past who corresponds.
gives: When I look at a person now, or at myself, I picture the one
from an earlier time
who corresponds

support.quote: set before your eyes whole plays and scenes of the same kind, all that you have come to know from your own experience or from older history
support.follows: I should picture whole scenes of the same kind, from my own experience and from history.
gives: from an earlier time
I set whole plays and scenes of the same kind before my eyes

support.quote: Think continually how all things of the kind that happen now happened before as well, and think of them as going to happen.
support.follows: What happens now happened before, and it will happen again.
gives: The things that happen now happened before
will happen again

support.quote: For all of those were of this kind, only with other people.
support.follows: Those past courts were just like the present, only with other people.
gives: only with other people

support.quote: Think, for example, of the times of Vespasian, and you will see all the same things
support.follows: In the times of Vespasian I would see all the same things that happen now.
gives: The things that happen now happened before

claims.t: When I go wrong, I strain after things. I run from things and chase things as if they would last for ever. Those who strained with all their strength soon fell, and what people strain after is cheap. The way back is to do what fits my own constitution, hold on tight to that and be content with that. It is enough to get across this short stretch in good order.
claims.shared: The opening states the reproach both passages address to oneself: 10.31 asks why you strain, and 10.34 says you chase all things. “When I go wrong” and “the way back” are editorial framing. 10.31 puts the last point as a question, read here as its implied answer. Running from things and the illusion of permanence are from 10.34 alone, and the constitution is from 4.27 alone.

support.quote: Why then do you strain? Why is it not enough for you to get across this short stretch in good order?
support.follows: There is no need for me to strain; getting across this short stretch in good order should be enough.
gives: When I go wrong, I strain after things
It is enough to get across this short stretch in good order

support.quote: you run from all things and chase all things as if they were going to last for ever
support.follows: I avoid and chase everything as if it would last for ever, though life is short for all.
gives: When I go wrong, I strain after things
I run from things and chase things as if they would last for ever

support.quote: see how many people strained with all their strength and a little later fell and were broken up into the elements
support.follows: Many people strained with all their strength and soon fell and were broken up into the elements.
gives: Those who strained with all their strength soon fell

support.quote: how cheap everything is that people strain after
support.follows: Everything people strain after is cheap.
gives: what people strain after is cheap

support.quote: and neglected to do what fits their own constitution, to hold on tight to that and to be content with that
support.follows: Those I knew went wrong by neglecting what fitted their constitution instead of holding to it and being content with it.
gives: The way back is to do what fits my own constitution, hold on tight to that and be content with that

claims.role: Whatever death turns out to be
claims.t: Death may be an end for me, or a move somewhere else. Either my little compound will be scattered, or my little breath will be put out, or it will move away and be posted somewhere else. If death leads to another life, nothing there is empty of gods. If death leads to a state without sensation, I stop putting up with pains and pleasures and stop being a slave to a vessel worse than the thing that serves it.
claims.shared: The first sentence states the fork both passages hold open, without choosing. In 8.24 the options are scattering, the breath put out or a posting elsewhere. In 3.3 they are no sensation or another life. The two-way summary is ours. The three-way form stays in full from 8.24 alone, and the gods and the vessel are from 3.3 alone.

support.quote: either your little compound will have to be scattered, or your little breath be put out, or else move away and be posted somewhere else
support.follows: At death my little compound will be scattered, or my little breath put out, or the breath will move and be posted elsewhere.
gives: Death may be an end for me, or a move somewhere else
Either my little compound will be scattered, or my little breath will be put out, or it will move away and be posted somewhere else

support.quote: If to another life, nothing is empty of gods there either. And if in a state without sensation, you will stop putting up with pains and pleasures and being a slave to a vessel that is so much worse than the thing that serves it
support.follows: If death leads to another life, there are gods there too; if to no sensation, I am freed from pains, pleasures and the body.
gives: Death may be an end for me, or a move somewhere else
If death leads to another life, nothing there is empty of gods
If death leads to a state without sensation, I stop putting up with pains and pleasures and stop being a slave to a vessel worse than the thing that serves it

single.label: A small corner
single.t: Praise and remembrance live in a corner of this region. Not even here do all agree, nor does any one person agree with themselves. And the whole earth is a point.
single.quote: And besides, in a corner of this region, and not even here do all agree, nor does any one person even agree with themselves; and the whole earth is a point.
single.why: Single source, 8.19. The supplied quote has no subject, so “praise and remembrance” is supplied from the sentence before it in 8.19. That is our reading, and the passage is fragmentary. The claim of personal possession is dropped.
single.follows: Praise and memory live in a small corner, among people who disagree, on an earth that is itself a point.

single.label: Attention in proportion
single.t: I remember that the attention I give each action has its own worth and proportion. If I do not occupy myself with lesser things more than is fitting, I shall not give up in frustration.
single.quote: And here it is necessary to remember that the attention given to each action also has its own worth and proportion. For in this way you will not give up in frustration, if you do not occupy yourself with the lesser things more than is fitting.
single.why: Single source, 4.27. This is a rider about proportion in attention, not a point about mortality. Wording stays close to the source’s “worth and proportion”.
single.follows: Attention to an action has its proper measure; not overspending it on lesser things keeps me from giving up in frustration.

single.label: Kissing my child
single.t: Epictetus used to say that a person kissing their small child should add inwardly: “Tomorrow, perhaps, you will die.” Nothing is of ill omen that points to a work of nature. Otherwise reaping the ears of grain would be of ill omen too.
single.quote: A person kissing their small child, Epictetus used to say, should add inwardly: “Tomorrow, perhaps, you will die.” “Those are words of ill omen.” “Nothing is of ill omen,” he said, “that points to some work of nature. Otherwise reaping the ears of grain is of ill omen too.”
single.why: Single source, 11.30, a saying reported from Epictetus and left in his third-person framing. The earlier “I may say” weakened “should add”. “Perhaps” and “inwardly” are kept.
single.follows: Epictetus taught that thinking of a loved child’s death is not ill-omened, since death is nature’s work, like the harvest.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. In modern editions 4.39 is 4.48, 6.42 is 6.47, 4.28 is 4.33–34, 10.31 is 10.31a, 4.27 is 4.32, 12.20 is 12.27, 8.24 is 8.25, 8.19 is 8.20b–21, 8.29 is 8.31 and 11.30 is 11.34–35, while 3.3, 4.6, 10.27 and 10.34 are the same. Of the passages set aside, 4.37 is 4.46, 7.15 is 7.18 and 8.35 is 8.37. In 8.24 “Lucilla buried Verus, then Lucilla” the Greek has no verb, and “buried” is supplied by the translators; 4.39 has “buried” for the first act and “laid out” for the second, so claim 2 says only that the burier dies in turn.
Keeps the existing opening but replaces “all before me” with 6.42’s “people of every kind”. It asserts nothing about what follows death.
articles.limit: The article states what the passages share: people of every kind pass and are forgotten, and the answer is to live the short stretch justly, truthfully and with good grace. It asserts neither annihilation nor survival, because 3.3, 8.24 and 10.31 leave that open and 11.30 speaks of change into “what is not now”. The joint sentences added to c4, c6, c9 and c10 are our plain statements of what two passages imply, and several of those passages put the point as a question. Several passages (10.27, 8.29, 8.35, most of 8.19) draw no ethical conclusion of their own, so their use under the opening is our arrangement. The harsh images do not license contempt for people or for life. 8.19 is fragmentary and 8.29 has a gap. 4.27e concerns proportion in attention, 4.6 concerns annoyance at another person, and 11.30a is a reported saying of Epictetus.

aside.4.37: Heraclitus on the death of each element into the next belongs with the chapter on change; the rest of the passage is about people who live as if asleep and do what was handed down.
aside.7.15: About change being necessary to the nature of the whole; it says nothing of the dead or of being forgotten, and belongs with the chapter on change.
aside.8.35: That those who sat by the coffins of Verus and Hadrian died too is said more plainly by 4.39 and 8.24. Its questions about whether the dead would be aware of such mourners, or pleased by them, are set aside: they mock the mourning and say nothing of fame, and 6.42 and 8.19 already ask what harm ending does.

articles.title: The length of a life and the use of its time

claims.t: The longest life comes to the same thing as the shortest. It makes no difference whether I see the same things for a hundred years or for time without limit. I ask what difference there is between a child three days old and a Nestor of three generations. I think it nothing great to die many years from now rather than tomorrow.
claims.shared: Drops the unanchored ‘does not matter’. The equality of longest and shortest is joint between 2.12 and 4.42. The Nestor image is 4.42 alone and stays a question as Marcus framed it. ’Nothing great’ is 4.38 alone and is not strengthened to ‘no difference’. No urgency is drawn from these passages.

support.quote: it makes no difference whether a person will see the same things for a hundred years, or for two hundred, or for time without limit
support.follows: All things are of one kind and come round again, and it makes no difference whether one sees them for a hundred years, for two hundred, or without end.
gives: It makes no difference whether I see the same things for a hundred years or for time without limit

support.quote: So the longest comes to the same thing as the shortest.
support.follows: The longest life and the shortest come to the same thing.

support.quote: In this, then, what difference is there between a child three days old and a Nestor of three generations?

support.quote: so too think it nothing great that it should be many years from now rather than tomorrow

claims.role: The time is limited and running out
claims.t: A limit of time has been marked out for me. I am not upset that I weigh so many pounds and not three hundred, and I am just as content with my share of time. My life is being used up day by day. I come nearer to death at every moment, and what must come hangs over me.
claims.shared: The marked limit is joint between 2.1 and 6.44. The body-weight image and the contentment are 6.44 alone, and 6.44 says nothing about hurrying. Daily using up is 3.1 alone. ‘What must come’ is 4.14 alone and is left unnamed as in the source.

support.quote: a limit of time has been marked out for you
support.follows: A limit has been set to my time, and I must come to see that it has.
gives: A limit of time has been marked out for me

support.quote: For just as you are content with the amount of matter that has been marked off for you, so too with time.
support.follows: As I am content with the body marked off for me, so I am to be content with the time marked off for me.
gives: A limit of time has been marked out for me
just as content with my share of time

support.quote: You are not upset, are you, that you weigh so many pounds and not three hundred?
support.follows: I am not upset that I weigh so many pounds and not three hundred.

claims.t: I hurry. While I live, while it is possible, I become good. If I care at all about myself, I come to my own rescue. If I do not use my time to clear away the clouds, that time will be gone, I will be gone, and the clearing will not be possible again.
claims.shared: Semicolon removed and the pronouns given referents. Hurry is joint between 3.1 and 3.15, and ‘while it is possible’ between 4.14 and 3.15. Becoming good is 4.14 alone, the conditional self-rescue is 3.15 alone, and the clouds and the warning are 2.1 alone. The warning stays a conditional and is not made a vow.

support.quote: So one must hurry
support.follows: Because death comes nearer and the mind may give out first, one must hurry.
gives: I hurry

support.quote: So hurry to the end
support.follows: Since he will not read what he saved for old age, Marcus must hurry on to the end.
gives: I hurry

support.quote: While you live, while it is possible, become good.
support.follows: While I am alive and still able to, I am to become good.

while it is possible

support.quote: come to your own rescue, if you care at all about yourself, while it is possible

If I care at all about myself, I come to my own rescue

support.quote: If you do not use it to clear away the clouds, it will be gone, you will be gone, and it will not be possible again.
support.follows: If I do not use my time to clear away the clouds, my time will be gone, and so will I, with no second chance.
gives: If I do not use my time to clear away the clouds
that time will be gone, I will be gone, and the clearing will not be possible again

claims.t: I remember how long I have been putting things off. Many times I was given a set time and made no use of it. I accept that I am not going to read the notebooks and extracts I was putting away for my own old age. I stop wandering and let go of empty hopes.
claims.shared: Deferral is joint between 2.1 and 3.15. The unused set times are 2.1 alone, with the gods as givers kept for the margin. The unread notebooks are 3.15 alone and are framed as acceptance, so the prediction is not read as a vow against reading.

support.quote: Remember how long you have been putting these things off, and how many times you have been given a set time by the gods and have made no use of it.
support.follows: Marcus has long put these things off, and has again and again been given time and not used it.
gives: I remember how long I have been
putting things off
Many times I was given a set time and made no use of it

support.quote: For you are not going to read either your little notebooks or the deeds of the ancient Romans and Greeks and the extracts from the writings, which you were putting away for your own old age.
support.follows: Marcus will not read the notes, histories and extracts he was saving for his old age.
gives: putting things off
I am not going to read the notebooks and extracts I was putting away for my own old age

support.quote: Stop wandering.
support.follows: Marcus tells himself to stop wandering.
gives: I stop wandering

support.quote: letting go of empty hopes
support.follows: Marcus is to let go of empty hopes.
gives: let go of empty hopes

claims.t: Even if I were to live three thousand years, I would lose only the present, for no one could lose either the past or the future. The one who lives longest and the one who dies soonest lose an equal amount. And if I live longer, it is at least unclear whether my mind will stay equal to the understanding of things. The grasp of things and the power to follow them can give out first, while breathing and taking nourishment go on.
claims.shared: Semicolon removed and the long sentence split. Only the supposition of a longer life is joint. The equal loss of the present is 2.12 alone, and 2.12 makes it conditional in the source. The failing mind is 3.1 alone and keeps its hedge ‘at least unclear’.

support.quote: Even if you are going to live three thousand years, or even three times ten thousand
support.follows: Marcus supposes a life of three thousand years, or even thirty thousand.
gives: Even if I were to live three thousand years
if I live longer

support.quote: the one who lives longest and the one who will die soonest lose an equal amount
support.follows: Whoever lives longest loses no more than whoever dies soonest.
gives: The one who lives longest and the one who dies soonest lose an equal amount

support.quote: For the present is the only thing a person is going to be deprived of
support.follows: The only thing anyone is going to be deprived of is the present.
gives: I would lose only the present

support.quote: For no one could lose either the past or the future
support.follows: No one can lose the past or the future, since no one has them.
gives: no one could lose either the past or the future

support.quote: if a person were to live longer, it is at least unclear whether their mind will later on be equal, unchanged, to the understanding of things
support.follows: If I live longer, it is not certain that my mind will still be fit to understand things.
gives: if I live longer

support.follows: The grasp of things and the power to follow them give out before the rest of a person does.
gives: The grasp of things and the power to follow them can give out first

support.quote: there will be no lack of breathing, of taking nourishment
support.follows: A person who begins to lose their wits still goes on breathing and taking food.
