single.label: Recalling the long-lived dead
single.t: As a layman’s help towards contempt of death, and an effective one all the same, I call back to mind those who clung on and lingered in life. I ask what more they have than those who died before their time.
single.quote: A layman’s help towards contempt of death, but an effective one all the same, is to call back to mind those who clung on and lingered in life. What more do they have, then, than those who died before their time?
single.why: Single-source practice from 4.42, kept in the speaker’s own framing as a layman’s help. It supports thinking little of death and gives no instruction to hurry.
single.follows: Recalling people who held on to life a long time is a plain but effective help towards thinking little of death.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. In modern editions 2.12 is 2.14, 4.42 is 4.50, 2.1 is 2.4, 4.14 is 4.17, 3.15 is 3.14, 4.38 is 4.47 and 6.44 is 6.49; 3.1 is the same.

Replaces ‘does not matter’ with ’no great thing’, because 4.38 calls the difference not great rather than nil and 3.1 values time with reason intact. Semicolon removed. The hurry is anchored only in 3.1 and 3.15. ‘Become good’ is 4.14 alone and is paired with the self-rescue of 3.15 through the shared ’while it is possible’.
articles.limit: The sources form two groups, and the claims set them side by side. 2.12, 4.42, 4.38 and 6.44 argue that length of life is not worth distress and never say to hurry. 3.1, 2.1, 3.15 and 4.14 urge present use, and 3.1 alone assumes that time with reason intact matters. The four grounds for indifference are distinct, and 4.38 says the difference is not great, which is weaker than saying it is nil. The aims of haste also differ: understanding in 2.1, trained reasoning and duty in 3.1, self-rescue in 3.15 and goodness in 4.14. Joining the two groups in the opening is our editorial interpretation, and so is attaching the hurry of 3.1 and 3.15 to the becoming good of 4.14. In c3, “the clearing” is our gloss on an unspecified “it” in 2.1, and “hurry” drops the unglossed “to the end” of 3.15. In c5, “can give out first” reads the flat statement in 3.1 in the light of its earlier hedge, and the only joint element is the supposition of a longer life. Nothing here states that death is no evil, speaks of an afterlife, urges pleasure, endorses suicide or rejects learning.

statement.t: I count a longer life no great thing. My time has a limit, and I hurry to become good and come to my own rescue while it is possible.

parts.words: I count a longer life no great thing
My time has a limit
I hurry
become good and come to my own rescue while it is possible

statement.kind: Two grounds that seem to pull apart, and the conduct that answers both
statement.form: Replaces ‘does not matter’ with ’no great thing’, because 4.38 calls the difference not great rather than nil and 3.1 values time with reason intact. Semicolon removed. The hurry is anchored only in 3.1 and 3.15. ‘Become good’ is 4.14 alone and is paired with the self-rescue of 3.15 through the shared ’while it is possible’.

articles.title: Meeting death well

claims.t: I judge dying to be one of nature’s works, and something good for nature too.
claims.shared: Three passages call dying natural. Only 2.10 calls it good for nature, and that is a benefit to nature, not to the person dying.

support.quote: since this too is one of the things nature wills
support.follows: Death too is one of the things that nature wills.
gives: dying to be one of nature’s works

support.quote: for this too is one of the things that accord with nature
support.follows: Being untied from my own people at death, without being pulled back, is one of the things that accord with nature.
gives: dying to be one of nature’s works

support.quote: This, though, is not only a work of nature but also something good for nature.
support.follows: Dying is a work of nature, and it is also good for nature.
gives: dying to be one of nature’s works
something good for nature

claims.t: I have already lived through many endings: activities that stopped, and ages of my life that gave way to the next. Each change was a kind of death, and none was terrible. Neither is the ending of my whole life.
claims.shared: This is an argument by analogy that reaches ‘not terrible’, not ‘good’. Calling each change a death is 9.19 only. 12.17 adds the condition of stopping at the right time, which c3 carries.

support.quote: For as it is with being young and growing old, with growing and reaching one’s prime, with getting teeth and a beard and grey hair, with begetting and carrying a child and giving birth, and with all the other natural activities that the seasons of life bring, so it is with being dissolved.
support.follows: Dying is a change like growing old, getting grey hair or giving birth: one of the natural activities the seasons of life bring.
gives: ages of my life that gave way to the next

support.quote: The ending of an activity, the stopping and, as it were, the death of an impulse, of a judgment: nothing bad.
support.follows: When an activity, an impulse or a judgment ends, nothing bad has happened.
gives: I have already lived through many endings
activities that stopped
none was terrible

support.quote: Now pass on to the ages of life: childhood, for example, adolescence, youth, old age. For every change of these too is a death. Surely that is nothing terrible?
support.follows: Each passage from one age of life to the next is a kind of death, and none of them is terrible.
gives: I have already lived through many endings
ages of my life that gave way to the next
Each change was a kind of death
none was terrible

support.quote: In the same way, then, neither is the ending and stopping and change of your whole life.
support.follows: The ending of my whole life is no more terrible than the smaller endings before it.
gives: the ending of my whole life

support.quote: Any single activity, whichever it is, that stops at the right time suffers nothing bad in that it has stopped
support.follows: An activity that stops at the right time suffers nothing bad by having stopped.
gives: activities that stopped

support.quote: In the same way, then, the sum made up of all the actions, which is a life, if it stops at the right time, suffers nothing bad just in this respect, that it has stopped
support.follows: A life, the sum of a person’s actions, suffers nothing bad by stopping, if it stops at the right time.
gives: the ending of my whole life

claims.t: Nature sends me away, not a tyrant or an unjust judge. Nature, not I, fixes the right time and the limit. My death is not a bad thing if it is outside my choice and not against the community. My death is a good thing if it comes at the right time for the whole, benefits the whole and is carried along with the whole.
claims.shared: The semicolon is removed and the sentences shortened. The tyrant and judge are 12.27 only. Both conditional judgements are 12.17 only, and their ‘if’ conditions are kept, including ‘outside my choice’.

support.quote: sent away from the city not by a tyrant, nor by an unjust judge, but by nature, which brought you in
support.follows: It is nature, which brought me into life, that sends me out of it, not a tyrant or an unjust judge.
gives: Nature sends me away, not a tyrant or an unjust judge

support.quote: For what is complete is fixed by the one who was responsible then for the putting together and is responsible now for the dissolving; you are responsible for neither.
support.follows: What is complete is fixed by the one responsible for the putting together and the dissolving, and neither is my doing.
gives: Nature, not I, fixes the right time and the limit

support.quote: The right time and the limit are given by nature
support.follows: It is nature that gives the right time and the limit of a life.
gives: Nature, not I, fixes the right time and the limit

support.quote: So for each person the stopping of life is not a bad thing, since it is not a shameful thing either, if indeed it is both outside one’s choice and not unsocial; and it is a good thing, if indeed it comes at the right time for the whole, benefits the whole and is carried along with the whole.
support.follows: An end of life outside one’s choice and not against the community is not shameful, so not bad; it is good if timely for the whole, useful to it and carried with it.
gives: not a bad thing if it is outside my choice and not against the community
a good thing if it comes at the right time for the whole, benefits the whole and is carried along with the whole

claims.t: When my death comes I go graciously, friendly and gentle towards the people I leave. I withdraw from them not as one torn away, but as the soul slips easily from the body in an easy death.
claims.shared: The text is unchanged. The anchor now covers the withdrawal from these people, which with ‘not torn away’ and the image of the soul slipping from the body is 10.36 only. Gracious going is joint in 12.27 and 10.36, and friendliness and gentleness are joint in 10.36 and 9.3.

support.quote: So go away graciously, for the one who dismisses you is gracious too.
support.follows: I should leave graciously, since the one who dismisses me is gracious too.
gives: I go graciously

support.quote: Still, do not for that reason go away less kindly towards them, but keeping to your own habit: friendly, well-disposed and gracious.
support.follows: Even towards people who are glad to see me go, I should leave as I always was with them: friendly, well-disposed and gracious.
gives: I go graciously
friendly and gentle towards the people I leave

support.quote: not as one being torn away; rather, just as in a person who dies an easy death the little soul slips easily out of the body, so too must the withdrawal from these people take place.
support.follows: I should leave the people of my life not as one torn away, but as easily as the soul slips from the body in an easy death.
gives: I withdraw from them not as one torn away
as the soul slips easily from the body in an easy death

support.quote: rather one must even care for them and bear with them gently
support.follows: One must care for the people one is leaving and bear with them gently.
gives: friendly and gentle towards the people I leave

claims.t: To go more easily, I look at what I am about to leave. The release will not be from people who share my principles, and only life among such people could hold me back, if anything could. Even partners I struggled for may want me gone, so I do not cling to a longer stay.
claims.shared: ‘Nothing here to hold on to’ is narrowed, because 9.3 names like-minded company as the one thing that could hold me. ‘May’ avoids asserting what others want. 9.3 calls this a layman’s rule, and c4 carries the kindness both passages require.

support.quote: what will most put you at ease about death is to stop and look at the things you are about to leave
support.follows: What most eases a person about death is to stop and look at what they are about to leave.
gives: To go more easily
I look at what I am about to leave

support.quote: So you will think of this as you die, and you will go out more easily, reasoning: “I am leaving a life of this kind, in which my very partners, for whom I struggled so much, prayed, cared, those very people want me to go
support.follows: Dying, I will go more easily if I remember that even the partners I struggled and prayed for want me to go.
gives: To go more easily
Even partners I struggled for may want me gone

support.quote: remember that the release will not be from people who hold the same principles as you
support.follows: The people death releases me from are not people who share my principles.
gives: The release will not be from people who share my principles

support.quote: For this alone, if anything at all, would pull one back and hold one in life: if one were allowed to live together with those who have made the same principles their own.
support.follows: The one thing that could hold a person in life is living with people who share their principles.
gives: only life among such people could hold me back, if anything could

support.quote: Why, then, would anyone hold on to a longer stay here?
support.follows: There is no reason to hold on to a longer stay in such a life.
gives: I do not cling to a longer stay

single.label: A rest
single.t: Death is a rest from the impacts on my senses, from impulse tugging the puppet strings, from the step-by-step course of thought, and from service to the flesh.
single.quote: Death is a rest from the impacts on the senses, from the tugging of impulse on the puppet strings, from the step-by-step course of thought, and from service to the flesh.
single.why: Single source, 6.26, kept close to its wording and its puppet image. Thought is among the things that stop, so the rest is not a promise of felt relief.
single.follows: Death ends the blows on the senses, the pull of impulse, the step-by-step working of thought and the service of the body.

single.label: When I am afraid
single.t: I look at dying by itself and take apart what I have imagined into it, until I judge it to be nothing but a work of nature. Whoever fears a work of nature is a child.
single.quote: if a person looks at it by itself alone and, by dividing up the notion, dissolves the things imagined into it, they will no longer judge it to be anything other than a work of nature; and if anyone is afraid of a work of nature, they are a child.
single.why: Single source, 2.10. The practice comes first, and the saying about the child stays a third-person warning as the speaker framed it, not a vow.
single.follows: Looked at by itself, with what was imagined into it taken away, dying is only a work of nature, and fearing it is childish.

single.label: Either way
single.t: If I fear death, I fear either having no sensation or having sensation of another kind. With no sensation, I will sense nothing bad. With sensation of a different kind, I will be a different kind of living thing and will not have stopped living.
single.quote: Whoever fears death fears either the absence of sensation or sensation of another kind. But if you no longer have sensation, you will have no sensation of anything bad either; and if you acquire a rather different kind of sensation, you will be a different kind of living thing, and you will not stop living.
single.why: Single source, 8.55. The dilemma leaves open which alternative is true and asserts no survival. The semicolon is removed.
single.follows: Whatever death is, it brings either nothing to feel, so nothing bad, or a new kind of feeling and a life that goes on.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. In modern editions 12.27 is 12.34–36, 2.10 is 2.12b, 12.17 is 12.23, 9.19 is 9.21, 8.55 is 8.58 and 6.26 is 6.28, while 9.3 and 10.36 are the same.

The comparison is now stated plainly as growing up and growing old, from 9.3 and 9.19. ‘Stay kind’ follows 10.36’s ‘keeping to your own habit’ and 9.3’s gentle care. The line claims only that death is natural, not that it is good for me.
articles.limit: Most passages support only that death is natural and not bad or terrible. ‘Good’ appears only in 2.10 and conditionally in 12.17, and always by reference to nature or the whole. The conditions in 12.17, including ‘outside one’s choice’, are kept, and nothing here licenses self-chosen death or settles what follows death. The thought about uncongenial company comes from 9.3 and 10.36 alone, is framed in 9.3 as a layman’s aid, and is bound to continued care and gentleness. The lines for 6.26, 2.10 and 8.55 are single-source. The first and third do not use the nature argument, and none is offered as joint doctrine.

statement.t: My death is nature’s work, like growing up and growing old, so I go graciously and stay kind to the people I leave.

parts.words: My death is nature’s work
like growing up and growing old
I go graciously
stay kind to the people I leave

statement.kind: A ground and the conduct that follows from it
statement.form: The comparison is now stated plainly as growing up and growing old, from 9.3 and 9.19. ‘Stay kind’ follows 10.36’s ‘keeping to your own habit’ and 9.3’s gentle care. The line claims only that death is natural, not that it is good for me.

articles.title: What I learned, and from whom

claims.t: I keep free of anger and give no sign of it. I am not irritable when I explain, and I am at once most free of passion and most affectionate.
claims.shared: Freedom from anger is shared by 1.1, 1.6 and 1.12. The pairing of calm with affection is Sextus alone (1.6) and is kept so that calm is not read as coldness. Patience in explaining is Apollonius alone (1.5). Semicolon removed.

support.quote: From my grandfather Verus: good character and freedom from anger.
support.follows: Marcus took good character and freedom from anger from his grandfather Verus.
gives: free of anger

support.quote: never giving so much as a sign of anger or of any other passion, but being at once most free of passion and most affectionate
support.follows: From Sextus, Marcus took this: never to show even a sign of anger or other passion, and to be both free of passion and most affectionate.
gives: free of anger
give no sign of it
at once most free of passion and most affectionate

support.quote: never hurrying or hanging back or at a loss or downcast or putting on a grin, or again angry or suspicious
support.follows: Maximus, as Marcus saw him, was never in a hurry or hanging back, never downcast, and never angry or suspicious.
gives: free of anger

support.quote: and not being irritable when explaining
support.follows: From Apollonius, Marcus took this: not to be irritable when explaining things to others.
gives: not irritable when I explain

claims.t: I stay the same in sharp pain, at the loss of a child and in long illness, and I keep good spirits in illness as in other hardship. After an attack of headache I go straight back to my usual work at full strength.
claims.shared: Steadiness is shared by 1.5 and 1.12. The three trials are restored from Apollonius (1.5) in place of the vaguer “grief”. The headache detail is the father’s alone (1.13) and is now named, so “attack” has a clear referent.

support.quote: being always the same, in sharp pains, at the loss of a child, in long illnesses
support.follows: From Apollonius, Marcus took this: to be always the same, whether in sharp pain, at the loss of a child or in long illness.
gives: I stay the same
in sharp pain, at the loss of a child and in long illness

support.quote: From Maximus: self-mastery and being carried off course in nothing; and good spirits in illness as in other hard circumstances
support.follows: From Maximus, Marcus took self-mastery, and good spirits in illness as in any other hardship.
gives: I stay the same
good spirits in illness as in other hardship

support.quote: after his attacks of headache, coming straight back fresh and at full strength to his usual work
support.follows: Marcus’s father, after attacks of headache, went straight back to his usual work, fresh and at full strength.
gives: After an attack of headache I go straight back to my usual work at full strength

claims.t: I am slow to accept slander and slow to assent to glib talk, and I disbelieve tales of spells. I do not rest content with a rough grasp of a matter or with the impressions that lie to hand.
claims.shared: Refusing to be content too soon is shared by 1.4 (reading) and 1.13 (inquiry in council). Slander is 1.2 alone, and “slow” is not “never”. Disbelief is aimed at sorcerers’ claims about spells (1.3 alone), not at religion.

support.quote: and being slow to accept slander
support.follows: From the man who brought him up, Marcus learned to be slow to accept slander.
gives: slow to accept slander

support.quote: and reading with care, and not being content with a rough grasp of the whole, nor quickly assenting to glib talkers
support.follows: From Rusticus, Marcus took this: to read with care, not to rest content with a rough grasp, and not to agree quickly with glib talkers.
gives: slow to assent to glib talk
do not rest content
a rough grasp of a matter

support.quote: and disbelieving what is said by those who deal in marvels and by sorcerers about spells and about the driving out of spirits and things of that kind
support.follows: From Diognetus, Marcus took this: not to believe what marvel-mongers and sorcerers say about spells and driving out spirits.
gives: disbelieve tales of spells

support.quote: and careful inquiry in council, and persistence, and not “he gave up the search too soon, content with the impressions that lay to hand”
support.follows: Marcus’s father inquired with care in council and kept at it; no one could say he stopped too soon, content with first impressions.
gives: do not rest content
the impressions that lie to hand

claims.t: I do good, and I share readily and unsparingly.
claims.shared: Doing good is shared by 1.11 and 1.12, and readiness to share by 1.1 and 1.11. “Unsparingly” is Severus alone (1.11). “What I have” is dropped as an unsupported addition.

support.quote: From my mother: reverence for the gods, and readiness to share
support.follows: From his mother, Marcus took reverence for the gods and a readiness to share.
gives: share readily

support.quote: and doing good and sharing readily, unsparingly
support.follows: From his brother Severus, Marcus took this: doing good, and sharing readily and unsparingly.
gives: I do good
share readily
unsparingly

support.quote: and doing good
support.follows: Among the things Marcus took from Maximus is doing good.
gives: I do good

claims.t: I train myself to live plainly, far from the way the rich live, and to need little. When comforts are there I take them without affectation, and when they are not I do not need them.
claims.shared: Plain living and few needs are shared across 1.1, 1.2, 1.3 and 1.13. The second sentence is the father’s alone (1.13) and keeps simplicity from hardening into asceticism. “Without affectation” replaces “without fuss” as the source’s own wording.

support.quote: and also plain living, far from the way the rich live
support.follows: From his mother, Marcus took a plain way of living, far from the way the rich live.
gives: train myself to live plainly
far from the way the rich live

support.quote: From the man who brought me up: becoming neither a Green nor a Blue, nor a Small-Shield or a Big-Shield man; and bearing hard work, and needing little
support.follows: From the man who brought him up, Marcus learned to bear hard work and to need little.
gives: to need little

support.quote: and wanting a pallet bed and an animal skin, and everything of that kind that belongs to the Greek training
support.follows: From Diognetus, Marcus took the wish for a pallet bed, an animal skin and the rest of the Greek training.
gives: train myself to live plainly

support.quote: using the things that add to the ease of life, of which fortune gave him plenty, without conceit and at the same time without apology, so that when they were there he took them without affectation, and when they were not he did not need them
support.follows: Marcus’s father used the comforts fortune gave him without conceit or apology, and did not need them when they were not there.

when they are not I do not need them

claims.t: When a friend finds fault with me, even without reason, I do not make light of it, and I try to bring my friend back to their usual self. I am easy to reconcile with those who were angry and did wrong, as soon as they are willing to come back, and I forgive.
claims.shared: Wording unchanged and anchors corrected. Forgiving is the jointly held phrase: 1.12 names it outright, and 1.4 shows it as being won back by those who did wrong. Ease of reconciliation and the condition of the other person’s willingness are Rusticus alone (1.4). The fault-finder is a friend, and the attempt to restore them is Catulus alone (1.10). No promise is made that the other person returns.

support.quote: and, towards those who have been angry and have done wrong, being easy to win back and easy to reconcile, as soon as they themselves are willing to come back
support.follows: From Rusticus, Marcus took this: to be easily won back and reconciled with those who were angry and did wrong, once they want to return.
gives: easy to reconcile
those who were angry and did wrong
as soon as they are willing to come back
I forgive

support.quote: not making light of a friend who finds some fault, even if they happen to be finding fault without reason, but trying even to bring them back to their usual self
support.follows: From Catulus, Marcus took this: not to brush off a friend’s complaint, even an unfounded one, but to try to bring the friend back to their usual self.
gives: When a friend finds fault with me, even without reason, I do not make light of it
bring my friend back to their usual self

support.quote: and forgiving
support.follows: Among the things Marcus took from Maximus is forgiving.
gives: I forgive

single.label: Reason alone
single.t: I look to nothing other than reason, not even for a little while.
single.quote: and looking to nothing other than reason, not even for a little while
single.why: Single source: Apollonius (1.5), “and looking to nothing other than reason, not even for a little while”. Existing line stands verbatim. It is not presented as joint doctrine.
single.follows: From Apollonius, Marcus took this: to look to nothing but reason, not even for a short time.

single.label: The mark of a sound soul
single.t: To be strong, to hold out and stay sober both in going without and in enjoying, is the mark of a soul that is sound and unbeaten.
single.quote: What is recorded of Socrates would fit him: that he was able both to go without and to enjoy those things which most people are weak at going without and give way in enjoying. To be strong, and to hold out and stay sober in each of the two, is the mark of a man who has a soul that is sound and unbeaten
single.why: Single source: the father, with the Socrates comparison (1.13), “To be strong, and to hold out and stay sober in each of the two, is the mark of a man who has a soul that is sound and unbeaten”. The existing line split holding out and sobriety between the two cases, but the source applies both to each. Left in the third person as the speaker framed it.
single.follows: Being able both to go without and to enjoy, holding out in the one and staying sober in the other, is the mark of a sound and unbeaten soul.

single.label: Needing correction
single.t: I accept that my character needs correcting and treatment.
single.quote: From Rusticus: getting the impression that my character needed correcting and treatment
single.why: Single source: Rusticus (1.4), “getting the impression that my character needed correcting and treatment”. The source records an impression received, so “I keep in mind” is replaced by acceptance, which is not a vow.
single.follows: From Rusticus, Marcus got the impression that his character needed correcting and treatment.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. In modern editions 1.1 is 1.1–4, 1.2 is 1.5, 1.3 is 1.6, 1.4 is 1.7, 1.5 is 1.8, 1.6 is 1.9, 1.10 is 1.13, 1.11 is 1.14, 1.12 is 1.15 and 1.13 is 1.16.

Kept close to the existing opening. “And taught me” is dropped because the anchored quotes name family and the man who brought him up, not teachers as such. The three traits are the ones the claims develop.
articles.limit: These passages are a list of debts to particular people, mostly observed example, not a system. Marcus does not claim to possess the qualities, and 1.4 says his character needed correction. The first-person present is therefore an editorial framing of what he records learning. Calm is always paired with affection, simplicity with unapologetic use of comforts, and scepticism about sorcerers with reverence for the gods. Reconciliation is conditional on the other person’s willingness. “Reason alone” appears only in 1.5 and is not a programme for the whole article.

statement.t: I live as the people who brought me up showed me: even-tempered, careful in what I believe, and needing little.

parts.words: I live as the people who brought me up showed me
even-tempered
careful in what I believe
needing little

statement.kind: Lessons from many people aligned into one
statement.form: Kept close to the existing opening. “And taught me” is dropped because the anchored quotes name family and the man who brought him up, not teachers as such. The three traits are the ones the claims develop.

empty.doubt: No passage in this section asks what would hold if these lessons were wrong; Book 1 is a record of thanks, not an argument.

articles.title: Socrates, Plato and other models

claims.t: Staying alive is not the great thing, and I do not cling to life or count death terrible. Where I have taken up a post, judging it best, or been posted there, I stay and run the risk. I take nothing into account ahead of disgrace, not even death.
claims.shared: Restores the post “judged best” or assigned, and the source’s “ahead of disgrace” in place of “shameful”. The post is a single-source detail from 7.26. Limit: 7.26 hedges with “perhaps” and 7.23 is conditional on a great mind.

support.quote: see whether what is noble and what is good may not be something other than saving and being saved. For perhaps this, living for whatever length of time, is what one who is truly a man must let go, and he must not cling to life
support.follows: What is noble and good may be something other than staying alive, and perhaps a true man must let go of how long he lives.
gives: Staying alive is not the great thing
I do not cling to life

support.quote: do you think human life seems anything great to the one who has it?’ ‘Impossible,’ he said.
support.follows: To a mind with a view of all time and of all being, human life cannot seem anything great.
gives: Staying alive is not the great thing

support.quote: Wherever a person has taken up a post, judging it to be best, or has been posted by a commander, there, as it seems to me, they must stay and run the risk, taking nothing into account, neither death nor anything else, ahead of disgrace
support.follows: Whoever has taken up a post, or been posted there, must stay and run the risk, counting nothing, death included, ahead of disgrace.
gives: Where I have taken up a post, judging it best, or been posted there, I stay and run the risk
I take nothing into account ahead of disgrace, not even death

support.quote: such a person will not count death a terrible thing either
support.follows: Whoever has a view of all time and of all being will not count death a terrible thing.
gives: count death terrible

claims.t: I look at what kind of soul a person has. I ask what Alexander, Gaius and Pompey are beside Diogenes, Heraclitus and Socrates, who saw things, their causes and their matter. A more glorious death and nimbler argument do not prove that Socrates was better than Telauges.
claims.shared: Removes the unsupported “hardly anyone has heard of him” and the verdict “little”. Both comparisons stay as the questions the sources ask. The Telauges question is from 7.37 alone and is not a verdict against Socrates.

support.quote: what has to be looked at is this: what kind of soul Socrates had
support.follows: The thing to look at in Socrates is what kind of soul he had.
gives: I look at what kind of soul a person has

support.quote: For the latter saw things and their causes and their matter, and their ruling parts were the same.
support.follows: The reason given for setting the philosophers higher is what they saw and the state of their ruling parts.
gives: I look at what kind of soul a person has
who saw things, their causes and their matter

support.quote: Alexander, Gaius and Pompey: what are they beside Diogenes, Heraclitus and Socrates?
support.follows: Alexander, Gaius and Pompey amount to little when set beside Diogenes, Heraclitus and Socrates.
gives: what Alexander, Gaius and Pompey are beside Diogenes, Heraclitus and Socrates

support.quote: it is not enough that Socrates died a more glorious death, and argued more nimbly with the sophists
support.follows: A more glorious death and more skill in argument are not enough to show that Socrates was the better man.
gives: A more glorious death and nimbler argument do not prove

support.quote: How do we know that Telauges was not better than Socrates in his disposition?
support.follows: We do not know that Telauges was not the better man in his inner disposition.
gives: that Socrates was better than Telauges

claims.t: When I act I look at this alone: whether I am doing what is just or unjust, the deeds of a good person or of a bad one. I find it enough to be just in my dealings with people and devout in my dealings with the gods.
claims.shared: Keeps the source wording and restores the good and bad deeds. Limit: in 7.37 “enough” is a test put to Socrates’ soul, adopted here as my own standard. Devotion to the gods is from 7.37 alone.

support.quote: look at this alone whenever he acts: whether he is doing what is just or unjust, and the deeds of a good man or of a bad one
support.follows: Whenever a man acts he should look at one thing only: whether what he is doing is just or unjust.
gives: When I act I look at this alone
whether I am doing what is just or unjust, the deeds of a good person or of a bad one
I find it enough to be just in my dealings with people

support.quote: whether he could find it enough to be just in his dealings with human beings and devout in his dealings with the gods
support.follows: The question about Socrates is whether being just to people and devout to the gods was enough for him.
gives: I find it enough to be just in my dealings with people
devout in my dealings with the gods

claims.t: I do not turn on people for what they get wrong. I do not get idly angry at vice, and I do not pounce reproachfully on a wrong word or a slip of grammar. If we say we have sound souls, I ask why we fight and fall out.
claims.shared: The existing line vowed not to quarrel, but 11.32 ends on a question, so the question stands. “Souls” is supplied from the fuller exchange in 11.32. 1.7 covers errors of language only and is named as such.

support.quote: neither getting idly angry at vice
support.follows: The soul this passage asks about does not get angry at vice to no purpose.
gives: I do not turn on people for what they get wrong
I do not get idly angry at vice

support.quote: not to find fault, and not to pounce reproachfully on people who have come out with a wrong form of a word, a mistake in grammar or a jarring sound
support.follows: From Alexander the grammarian: not to find fault with people or pounce on them for a slip in their speech.
gives: I do not turn on people for what they get wrong
I do not pounce reproachfully on a wrong word or a slip of grammar

support.quote: “Sound ones.” “Then why do you not look for them?” “Because we have them.” “Then why do you fight and fall out?”
support.follows: Socrates asks people who say they already have sound souls why, then, they fight and fall out.
gives: If we say we have sound souls, I ask why we fight and fall out

claims.t: I take the wide view of all time and all being. When I speak of human beings, I look down at the things on earth as if from somewhere above. I look round at the courses of the stars as if running round with them, and I think continually of the elements changing into one another. These impressions wash away the dirt of life on the ground.
claims.shared: Removes the semicolon and restores “running round with them” and the condition about speaking of human beings. The star and dirt images are from 7.26 alone. The view cleanses and does not express contempt.

support.quote: a mind that has greatness and a view of all time and of all being
support.follows: There is a mind that has greatness and a view of all time and of everything that exists.
gives: I take the wide view
of all time and all being

support.quote: whoever is talking about human beings must also look down at the things on earth as if from somewhere above
support.follows: Anyone who talks about human beings should also look down at earthly things as if from above.
gives: I take the wide view
When I speak of human beings, I look down at the things on earth as if from somewhere above

support.quote: Look round at the courses of the stars as if running round with them, and think continually of the changes of the elements into one another. For the impressions of these things wash away the dirt of life on the ground.
support.follows: Picturing the stars’ courses and the elements changing into one another washes away the dirt of life on earth.
gives: I look round at the courses of the stars as if running round with them
I think continually of the elements changing into one another
These impressions wash away the dirt of life on the ground

claims.t: I guard against slavery of two kinds. One is to be a slave to anyone’s ignorance. The other is to have many things to take thought for and to be a slave to many.
claims.shared: The existing vow named the three commanders, but this claim’s quote from 8.3 says only “the others”, so the names stay in c2. The observation is kept as a guard, not a vow. Each kind of slavery has one witness.

support.quote: nor yet being a slave to anyone’s ignorance
support.follows: The soul this passage asks about is not a slave to anyone’s ignorance.
gives: I guard against slavery
a slave to anyone’s ignorance

support.quote: But with the others, how many things to take thought for, and slavery to how many!
support.follows: The others, the three conquerors, had a great many things to take thought for and were slaves to a great many.
gives: I guard against slavery
to have many things to take thought for and to be a slave to many

single.label: The mind’s own boundary
single.t: Nature did not blend my mind with my body in such a way that my mind is not allowed to draw a boundary round itself and bring what is its own under its own control.
single.quote: Nature did not blend the mind with the compound in such a way that it is not allowed to draw a boundary round itself and to bring what is its own under its own control.
single.why: Single source 7.37. “In such a way that” follows the source and prevents hearing a purpose clause that would reverse the sense. The permission “not allowed” is kept, and “my mind” is repeated so the referent is clear. “Body” renders the source’s “compound”.
single.follows: The mind is not so mixed with the compound it lives in that it cannot mark itself off and take charge of what is its own.

single.label: Bogeys
single.t: Socrates used to call the principles of the many “Lamias”, things to frighten children.
single.quote: Socrates used to call the principles of the many, too, “Lamias”, things to frighten children.
single.why: Single source 11.21, left as the speaker framed it. The existing “when they frighten me” and “live by” were additions. The source does not say which principles.
single.follows: Socrates called what most people hold and live by “Lamias”, things that frighten children.

single.label: The next question
single.t: How long I live I leave to god, trusting the saying that no one escapes what is fated. I consider what comes next: how I might best live the time I am going to live.
single.quote: leaving these matters to god and trusting the women who say that not even one person could escape what is fated, he must consider what comes next: how he might best live the time he is going to live
single.why: Single source 7.26, an unattributed speech. Restores the trust in the saying about fate that the existing line dropped. “How long I live” is our reading of “these matters”.
single.follows: Perhaps a true man must leave the length of his life to god and ask how to live the time he has as well as possible.

single.label: “I am busy”
single.t: I do not say “I am busy” to anyone, or write it in a letter, often or without need. I do not keep pleading the business around me to excuse myself from what I owe the people I live among.
single.quote: not to say “I am busy” to anyone, or write it in a letter, often or without need; and not to keep excusing oneself in this way from the duties that come with one’s relations to those one lives among, by pleading the business that surrounds one
single.why: Single source 1.9, Alexander the Platonist. Keeps “often or without need”, so only the habitual or needless plea is ruled out.
single.follows: From Alexander the Platonist: seldom to say “I am busy”, and not to plead business to get out of duties to those one lives among.

single.label: A kindness I cannot return
single.t: Socrates would not go to Perdiccas. “So that I may not die the worst of deaths,” he said, that is, so that he would not, after receiving a kindness, be unable to do one in return.
single.quote: Socrates to Perdiccas, on not going to him: “So that I may not die the worst of deaths,” he said, that is, so that I may not, after receiving a kindness, be unable to do one in return.
single.why: Single source 11.23. The spoken “he said” marks the quoted “I” as Socrates when the line is read aloud, and the gloss moves to the third person. It concerns a kindness he could not return and does not refuse all kindness. The unsupported “King” stays out.
single.follows: Socrates would not go to Perdiccas, so as not to receive a kindness he could not return, which he called the worst of deaths.

single.label: Correcting without reproach
single.t: When someone says a thing wrongly, I deftly come out with just what should have been said: in my answer, in backing them up, or in discussing with them the matter itself, not the expression.
single.quote: deftly to come out with just the very thing that should have been said, by way of an answer, or of backing them up, or of a joint discussion about the matter itself, not about the expression
single.why: Single source 1.7, Alexander the grammarian. Restores “deftly”. The scope is errors of language, and correction still happens indirectly.
single.follows: From Alexander the grammarian: to correct a slip by deftly using the right form oneself, in an answer or in discussing the matter.

single.label: What a tyrant is like
single.t: I have taken note of what a tyrant’s envy, shiftiness and play-acting are like, and that the people we call patricians are, on the whole, somehow rather lacking in affection.
single.quote: to have taken note of what a tyrant’s envy, shiftiness and play-acting are like, and that on the whole these people we call patricians are somehow rather lacking in affection
single.why: Single source 1.8, Fronto. Restores both hedges, “on the whole” and “somehow rather”. It is a social observation and is not joined to either strand.
single.follows: From Fronto: to have noticed what a tyrant’s envy, shiftiness and play-acting are like, and that patricians are on the whole rather lacking in affection.

single.label: The king and the mule driver
single.t: Alexander of Macedon and his mule driver came to the same state once they were dead. Either both were taken back into the same seed-reasons of the universe, or both were scattered alike into atoms.
single.quote: Alexander of Macedon and his mule driver, once dead, came to the same state: for either they were taken back into the same seed-reasons of the universe, or they were scattered alike into atoms.
single.why: Single source 6.22. Removes the editorial opening and the gloss on seed-reasons, and splits the overlong sentence. The either/or stays open. This is not the Alexander of 1.7 or 1.9.
single.follows: Once dead, the king and the man who drove his mules were in the same state, whether the universe took them back or they were scattered into atoms.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. In modern editions 7.26 is 7.44–48, 7.37 is 7.66–67a, 7.23 is 7.35, 11.23 is 11.25, 11.32 is 11.39, 1.9 is 1.12, 11.26 is 11.28, 11.21 is 11.23, 1.8 is 1.11, 6.22 is 6.24, 1.7 is 1.10, 6.12 is 6.13b and 11.22 is 11.24; 8.3 is the same.

Keeps the existing opening’s measure but drops its colon gloss. Each phrase rests on two passages. “Fame” is from 7.37 and “power” is our reading of the three commanders in 8.3. The death clause joins 7.26’s ranking of disgrace with 7.23, which speaks only of a great mind.
articles.limit: This is not a single portrait of Socrates. He is named only in 7.37, 8.3, 11.21, 11.23, 11.26 and 11.32. The speeches in 7.23 and 7.26 are unattributed here, and 7.37 asks an open question about his worth without ruling against him. 7.23 is conditional on a great mind and 7.26 hedges with “perhaps”, so the first-person lines on death are our adoption of those views. 11.32 ends on a question, and c4 keeps it as a question. The tests of the soul in 7.37 are put to Socrates, and the first-person lines in c3, c4 and c6 adopt them as a standard. “Body” in 7.37g renders the source’s “compound”. The three Alexanders are different people. Fronto’s remark in 1.8 stands alone and joins neither strand. 11.26 and 6.12 supply no content and support nothing, and 11.22 is kept only in the margin.

aside.11.26: A note pointing at a story about Socrates in a sheepskin. Marcus does not give what Socrates said, and the story does not survive elsewhere.
aside.6.12: One sentence cut from the end of a chapter: “See what Crates says about Xenocrates.” The saying itself is not given, so there is nothing to build on.
aside.11.22: An example of hosts giving their visitors the better seats. Unlike 11.23 it gives no saying or reason in anyone’s words, and unlike 1.8 Marcus does not name it as something he learned; no other passage of the section speaks of guests.

rights.basis: The English quoted on the page is this project’s own translation from the Latin, so no translator’s rights apply. The Latin is an older public-domain text. Gummere’s 1917–25 English is kept privately and used only to find passages by similarity; none of its words are published. The facts gathered on Gummere’s rights are kept below for the record.
rights.decision: Settled on 23 November 2026: the owner chose to translate Seneca within the project (“let’s translate seneca ourselves?”).

gummere.basis: Richard Mott Gummere died on 3 December 1969. His Loeb translation appeared in three volumes, 1917, 1920 and 1925. Works published before 1 January 1931 are in the public domain in the United States. In the European Union, the United Kingdom and Turkey the general term is the translator’s life plus 70 years, counted to the end of the year, so the translation is protected there through 31 December 2039. Each of those laws also compares the term with the work’s country of origin; that comparison was not worked out. Each allows quotation of a published work with its source named, within conditions (EU Directive 2001/29/EC art. 5(3)(d); UK CDPA s.30(1ZA); Turkey Law 5846 art. 35). This is a record of facts for the owner, not legal advice.
